text:
The Trump administration informed Congress in September that it will once again reserve its refugee admissions “primarily” for white South Africans and set a limit of just 17,500 for fiscal year 2027. The determination extends White House refugee policy established last year that has all but closed the program to people fleeing war and persecution anywhere else.

The move provoked concern from Catholic leaders who advocate for more merciful treatment of refugees.

“This announcement comes as no surprise,” Mario Russell, the executive director of the Center for Migration Studies of New York, wrote, responding to an email from America. “The administration’s mass deportation of law-abiding, working migrant families and barring of refugees—with the exception of a few pre-selected thousand—are distorted and inhumane policies.”

“When today’s U.S. Refugee Admissions Program reflects an 80 percent decrease from the historical average across decades of both Republican and Democratic presidential administrations alike, we should ask ourselves whether the current approach is truly living up to our history and values,” David Spicer, the director of policy and engagement for migration at the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, wrote in an email to America.

The U.S. Refugee Admissions program historically has accepted about 80,000 refugees each year, allowing admissions from around the world, often from nations stricken by humanitarian crises or conflict. The president annually sets a threshold for total refugee admissions.

During his first administration, President Donald Trump dramatically reduced the refugee threshold to just 15,000, and in the first days of his second administration he effectively shut the refugee resettlement system altogether. In the fall of 2025, Mr. Trump set the refugee ceiling for fiscal year 2026 at 7,500—the lowest on record.

Admissions in FY 2026 were primarily reserved for Afrikaners, white South Africans who descended mainly from Dutch settlers. In May, invoking a law that allows a midyear change for emergencies, he raised the cap to 17,500.

Washington media reports that in a letter to Congress arguing for the prioritizing of white South African farmers, the State Department repeated administration claims that the group faced “the seizure of agricultural property without compensation; government policies designed to dismantle equal opportunity in employment, education, and business; and hateful rhetoric fueling disproportionate violence against racially disfavored minorities.”

Those charges and other allegations of “white genocide” in South Africa have been repeatedly challenged by the nation’s leaders.

The president has insisted on a course of “America First” in his domestic and international policymaking, but for Catholics, a focus on the homeland need not and cannot correspond with a neglect of all other people, Mr. Spicer said.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church states that “more prosperous nations are obliged, to the extent they are able, to welcome the foreigner in search of the security and the means of livelihood which he cannot find in his country of origin.”

“Our Catholic faith simply does not accept the false premise of choosing between two goods when it comes to doing what is right,” Mr. Spicer said. “Meanwhile, the demonstrated contributions to American communities of past refugees, economic and otherwise, show this is not merely one-sided charity.”

And “as the most prosperous and powerful country in the history of the world,” the United States must accept a role as a global paragon, Mr. Spicer added.

If its policies have the power to influence other nations, then the example set by the Trump administration on refugees is a dangerous one, Mr. Russell said.

The administration’s stance on immigration and refugee welcome comes “from a distorted perception of human experience,” he said. “They ignore facts, they dismiss history, and they are, sadly, indifferent to suffering and basic human dignity.”

Mr. Russell shared a hope “that in time the United States will be able to reaffirm its commitment to protection and the fair and compassionate treatment of migrants.”

“As the U.S. bishops have long said, we can continue to be a beacon of hope and defender of those who are persecuted, including our brothers and sisters in Christ, while also addressing the challenges faced by everyday Americans,” Mr. Spicer said. “The Refugee Admissions Program offers a lawful, secure and proven way to do that.”

text:
On a bright, breezy Saturday morning in late September, Eliott Rodriguez, a congressional candidate in Florida’s Twenty-seventh District, walked the streets of Little Havana with two of his campaign volunteers. They were in the throes of a debate over the best translation for “Sorry I missed you,” an essential phrase in the door-knocking lexicon, eventually settling on “Perdona que no nos vimos” (“I’m sorry we didn’t see each other”). Nearby, roosters scampered along the edge of Cuba Memorial Boulevard Park. Rodriguez, a trim, seventy-year-old Cuban American, is a Democrat and former local news anchor, which makes him a well-known figure in the area. Predictably, he has spent much of the lead-up to Election Day working to win over Latino voters in the majority-Hispanic district, which covers much of central Miami—a group that, in recent years, has moved to the right. In 2020, despite voting for Joe Biden, the district narrowly elected Republican María Elvira Salazar, who had been endorsed by Donald Trump, to Congress. In 2022, she was reëlected, and, in 2024, Trump carried the district, and Salazar cruised to victory, winning by more than twenty points. But Salazar, who, amazingly, is also a Cuban American former news anchor, is now reckoning with her district increasingly turning on the President amid economic pressure and an immigration crackdown that is extremely unpopular among Latinos.

At the onset of the race, it seemed as if Salazar’s campaign strategy was to continue her embrace of Trump and the MAGA movement, even alongside a surge in deportations in Miami, the nation’s leader in ICE arrests. Last year, she declared that the facilities at Alligator Alcatraz, the infamous immigrant-detention center in the Everglades, met the “highest standards,” and she avoided criticizing the Trump Administration when it announced the terminations of Temporary Protected Status for Venezuelans, Haitians, and Nicaraguans, upending countless lives and businesses in her district.

But, a few weeks ago, Salazar released an ad breaking with Trump over immigration enforcement and warning him that the Latino voters who helped him win in 2024 felt betrayed—“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far.”—joining the ranks of several G.O.P. candidates nationwide attempting to distance themselves from the President. As Election Day approaches, Trump’s approval rating has hit a record low, currently hovering in the mid- to low thirties, and a recent poll from NBC News showed that a higher percentage of voters consider their vote this November to be a signal of opposition to the White House than in any other midterm in nearly thirty years. Perhaps because of this, Salazar’s ad seemed to barely make a dent. In fact, as Rodriguez explained, Salazar’s turnabout had seemed to spark a fund-raising windfall for his campaign from national donors, who saw the dysfunction as a sign that the seat was potentially flippable. Shortly after, their premonitions were borne out: political forecasters shifted the seat from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican,” whereas other pollsters even went as far as to call it a toss-up.

We crossed Calle Ocho, where tourists milled around Domino Park and perused souvenir shops selling rooster T-shirts and Cuban-flag magnets, before eventually making our way a few blocks north, to a neighborhood of modest, low-slung apartment buildings. With a little more than a month to go, Rodriguez’s campaign was relentlessly targeting voters with no party affiliation (N.P.A.s, as his staffers called them), who make up thirty per cent of the district and more than twenty-four per cent of Florida’s registered voters. The canvassers were in high spirits: in contrast to the district’s more affluent neighborhoods, where they were often met with silence and Ring cameras, they told me that people in Little Havana still opened their doors, and, more often than not, they were excited to see Rodriguez at their doorstep.

“Rodriguez is essentially a household name for Miamians of a certain age,” Carlos Odio, a researcher focussing on Latino voter sentiment who grew up in Miami, told me. “I remember him being on television as a kid.” When I asked Rodriguez if it felt like he was back on the local-news beat, he smiled and nodded. “Same skill, talking to people.” As a campaign volunteer filmed with an iPad, Rodriguez introduced himself in his mellifluous anchorman’s voice to residents and passersby, asking how they were doing. “La situación está difícil, no?” he said. (“Things are hard, right?”) Fidelia, a woman in her sixties who had arrived in the U.S. from Cuba seven years ago, mentioned how difficult life was for her family back on the island but wasn’t critical of the Trump Administration, or of Salazar. “This country has been a blessing for me,” she said. At Rodriguez’s pitch, one older man in a fedora and sunglasses held up his hands as if it had nothing to do with him: he was only a resident. Another Cuban woman was more forthcoming. “I don’t like her,” she said when I asked about Salazar. “I don’t think she’s sincere.”

As the South Florida heat intensified, we passed a pair of Jehovah’s Witnesses across the street. “We got some competition,” Rodriguez murmured. When Rodriguez approached Melba, a middle-aged Nicaraguan woman walking her dog, she told him that she had swum over the southern border with her son in the eighties but proudly declared herself a Republican, mainly owing to her Christian values. She had voted for Trump but wasn’t happy with the state of the country. “The things that he’s doing, or the things that ICE is doing, that’s sad,” she said, also mentioning the Iran war and gas prices. She liked the Democrats but was turned off by the “gender stuff,” adding that she was too old to change her beliefs. “I’m with you on that,” Rodriguez replied. After he moved on, I asked if Melba knew who she’d be voting for, and she said that she’d have to think hard about it.

The Twenty-seventh District has been referred to as the at-large seat of the Americas, and, increasingly, the matchup between Rodriguez and Salazar has taken on an international dimension. During that morning’s canvassing shift, Rodriguez and several campaign volunteers walked by a monument to the Bay of Pigs invasion, and a member of the group mused that Trump and the Secretary of State, Marco Rubio (a native of the Twenty-seventh), seemed to be plotting a repeat of the operation. The notion isn’t far-fetched. Recently, a Wall Street Journal report revealed that, in June, a group of wealthy Cuban Americans met at a mansion in the district, just a few miles south of Little Havana, to plot Cuba’s post-Communist future. Meanwhile, Rubio has openly discussed direct intervention, threatening that the Cuban regime would “learn the lesson the hard way” if it didn’t capitulate to American demands.

The current Administration’s crushing sanctions and blockade on oil shipments to the island have made Trump popular among Miami Cubans. And some right-wing politicians in Latin America allied with the White House have endorsed Salazar, including María Corina Machado, the exiled Venezuelan politician who won the Nobel Peace Prize, and the Colombian President, Abelardo de la Espriella. But, in this election, both candidates have attempted to claim the mantle of anti-communism. Rodriguez, in addition to covering Miami’s biggest stories, such as the Mariel boatlift and Hurricane Andrew, had also reported from inside Communist regimes such as Venezuela, Nicaragua, and Cuba, once even interviewing Fidel Castro, and recently attacked Salazar in a Spanish-language social-media post over the Trump Administration’s partnership with the socialist government in Venezuela. (He isn’t a fan of Zohran Mamdani’s plan for government-owned bodegas, either.)

In a reflection of the race’s tricky political balancing act between long-term and more recent exiles, Rodriguez said that he still has family in Cuba and believes that the Administration’s economic strangulation of the island is hurting citizens more than the government. “I think people have opened their eyes that Trump’s policy toward Cuba is not about restoring democracy—it’s about enriching himself,” Rodriguez told me. In response to de la Espriella’s and Machado’s endorsements of Salazar, he said that he was more focussed on families struggling to make ends meet in Miami.

After all, the campaign would need more than Little Havana. Though Rodriguez’s campaign has gained momentum, fuelled by the same anti-Trump resentment that has powered the Republican-turned-Democrat former congressman David Jolly’s run for governor and the Democratic state legislator Angie Nixon’s Senate campaign, Republicans maintain a strong grip on the district and have been significantly outpacing Democrats in voter registration throughout the state. Since 2020, national Democrats and their allies have all but abandoned Florida financially. Susan Whitman-Helfgot, the co-finance chair of Democratic Hispanic Caucus of Florida, was motivated to get involved anyway. She helped found the West Miami Dems, a voter-registration group, after the 2024 Presidential election, newly determined to make Florida a swing state again. “You need to pull in the no-party voters. It’s not an easy sale, but it can be made,” she told me.

The stakes for voter engagement are particularly high for this year’s elections in Florida, she explained, in the face of recent Republican-led changes to state election laws that will de-register voters who do not participate, as well as a swell of disinformation aimed at disenfranchising Latino voters. Some Latinos told her that they thought they weren’t allowed to vote in congressional elections as independents. Others mentioned hearing at church that they simply couldn’t vote this year. She was also quick to point out that, although Latino voters were not a monolith, the Trump Administration’s immigration crackdown had increasingly become a political wake-up call for those affected by it. “It changes when it’s personal,” she said. “When you’re Venezuelan, and you’ve had a family member thrown out, it’s a whole different ballgame.”

That sentiment dovetailed with a 2025 poll of mostly long-term Venezuelan immigrants in Florida by Florida International University’s Latino Public Opinion Forum, which found that thirty-five per cent of respondents had family or a close friend affected by the termination of T.P.S. Of all the poll’s participants, a fifth of those who had voted for Trump now regretted it. Trump, for his part, did not seem concerned. After initially shrugging off questions about Salazar’s ad, he reposted more than a dozen posts attacking her on Truth Social: “She is nothing but a back stabber,” one post read. “I’m glad Latino support hasn’t wavered.” Another read, “So we need a NEW Republican to Replace Salazar.”

In the days after the ad, Salazar appeared on CBS News’ “Face the Nation,” saying that she spoke with Trump and had a “fantastic conversation” with him, adding that he was “courteous” and “very receptive.” It was unclear whether her ad was a reaction to any new voter data, but, since its release, she had been keeping a relatively low profile in Miami. Shortly after meeting with Rodriguez, I reached out to Salazar’s spokesperson for an interview, even visiting her office on Eighth Street, where a Cuban flag emblazoned with the word “Libertad” hung on the wall, but my repeated requests were unanswered. Then, a few days later, I received a tip that the congresswoman would appear at a Mass at Our Lady of Lebanon, a Maronite Catholic church back in Little Havana that serves a diverse community of Lebanese and of Latino descent. At the conclusion of an English-language service interspersed with hymns in Arabic, the priest introduced Salazar, who stood up in the front row, smiling and waving. She walked with him into an adjoining banquet hall, where she shook hands and posed for pictures. As I approached Salazar, a young woman stepped in front of me and began addressing her as a bearded man beside me filmed the exchange.

“You were talking about enforcement,” the woman said. “I wanted to interrupt. My name is Arianne Betancourt. My father was in Alligator Alcatraz. Myself and several of the people here went to your office several times. Your staff told us you were in full support of this Administration and its policies.”

Salazar nodded in response, a tight smile across her face as a small crowd formed around us. “Wait a minute, who did you talk to?” she said, glancing over her shoulder as two staffers approached. She began to introduce Reidel Nabut, her deputy district director. “This is, uh . . .”

“Yes, that’s who I spoke to,” Betancourt said. “But, you know, it’s been six months since that happened. And you really let the community down.” After some back and forth, with Salazar’s spokesperson looking on uneasily, the congresswoman turned to the priest. “Are they part of this community?” she asked him, indicating Betancourt and the man who was filming. “No,” he said.

“We are part of the community, and I’m one of your constituents,” Betancourt replied. Salazar smiled and nodded, pointing at the man who was filming, an activist named Thomas Kennedy. “Sí, that’s why you’re taping.”

Eventually, the priest and a few parishioners intervened, and Betancourt left. Salazar’s team told me that she wouldn’t be taking questions. I spoke briefly to the priest, Manuel Rahmeh, a native of Lebanon, who told me that the majority of his church congregants are immigrants. “They should be treated in a different way.”

A few days later, I met Betancourt for coffee in North Miami. The video of her exchange with Salazar had been posted online and had gone viral, so much so that Salazar had been forced to issue a statement, telling a local news station she believed that the encounter was politically motivated and that Betancourt had a “clear agenda.” Betancourt, who is half Cuban but also has Honduran and Salvadoran roots, told me that before her father was detained she wasn’t a political person at all—she had even voted for Salazar. She had worked as a tour guide in Little Havana and other parts of Florida before quitting her job to focus full time on getting her father released from detention and had been among the first to document human-rights abuses at the facility. Her father’s case was complicated; he had a criminal record, but she told me he had been following immigration protocol.

He was detained at a routine check-in at ICE’s Miramar field office. She had sat outside in her car all day waiting for him and finally received a call at 9 P.M. with his voice on the line telling her that he was in Alligator Alcatraz, shackled to a bed.

When she tried to get help from Salazar’s office, she said members of the staff told her that there was nothing they could do and that the congresswoman supported immigration enforcement. Eventually, with help from the Community Justice Project, Betancourt was able to get her father out. The congresswoman’s office disputed her account, saying that her team had met with Betancourt and claimed they had offered to help with her father’s case. A spokesperson for the congresswoman also said that her office has resolved many immigration-related cases for its constituents.

Betancourt now works for an immigrant-rights group called the Workers Circle, and she said that she’d confronted Salazar on behalf of nearly eight hundred families with loved ones detained in other South Florida facilities, such as Krome. Her phone was constantly pinging throughout our conversation, and at one point she received a call from a detention center. She showed me a WhatsApp group for Cubans who had been deported to Africa.

Later, Betancourt told me that advocating on her father’s and other detainees’ behalf had made her a target of far-right Cuban American influencers. It had also caused tension in her family. She’d been renting from her father’s sister, a Trump supporter, who she said called her a communist and kicked her out after seeing her attend a vigil. But she added that, over the past couple of months, she had felt a shift in her critics. “Some of the people who were against the work I was doing are now, like, ‘You know what, maybe you were right.’ ”

It echoed what I’d heard from others in the city. Although no one I spoke to in the Twenty-seventh District predicted a stampede of Republicans running to vote for Rodriguez, one longtime local politician told me that even his most vociferous MAGA friends had become quieter, steering their conversations away from politics. A lawyer I met related the story of a Republican colleague who had remained a Trump supporter until a few weeks ago, appalled by the lack of due process in immigration court. She asked her colleague if she planned to vote for Salazar.

“She told me she would probably stay home,” she said. ♦

description:

In its formal response, DHS argued that extending auto-activation to ICE "presents significant operational risks, including inadvertent or false activations during routine movement."
Two more men were killed later in the year during immigration enforcement vehicle stops — Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston on July 8, and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine, roughly a week later.
After the Houston and Maine shootings triggered protests across the country, Congress reversed that course and directed $20 million specifically toward the procurement, deployment, and operation of body cameras for immigration enforcement officers.
Neither ICE nor CBP had updated its body camera management plan since the programs were first established — ICE's dated to 2024, CBP's to 2022 — even as both agencies substantially expanded their workforces in the intervening years.
text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement has never issued a written reprimand to a single officer for failing to turn on a body camera — and the Trump administration this week dismissed the one safeguard that would have removed that choice from officers' hands entirely. The decision, formalized in a federal watchdog's report released publicly on Wednesday, deepens an accountability crisis at an agency where cameras were not recording during any of at least six fatal shootings involving ICE officers since President Trump's return to the White House.

A Federal Watchdog Finds a System Built Entirely on Officer Discretion

The October 14 report from the Government Accountability Office — conducted at the request of Democratic members of Congress — examined body-worn camera programs at ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection covering the period from February 2025 through September 2026. At its core, the audit concluded that neither agency had built the institutional controls needed to guarantee that agents actually press record when required.

Under current ICE policy, individual officers retain full discretion over when their cameras activate. Agency rules require recording during arrests, searches, and pre-planned enforcement operations — but without any automated enforcement mechanism, compliance rests entirely on human judgment during high-pressure encounters. ICE has not implemented the controls needed to ensure its own camera policies are being followed, the watchdog concluded — a finding the agency's zero-reprimand record makes difficult to challenge.

Same Hardware, Completely Different Rules: The CBP Divide

Among the GAO's most pointed observations: both ICE and CBP carry Axon body cameras that natively support automatic activation under preset conditions — when a firearm clears its holster, when emergency vehicle lights engage, or when a nearby camera begins recording. CBP deploys those features as standard practice. ICE does not.

In its formal response, DHS argued that extending auto-activation to ICE "presents significant operational risks, including inadvertent or false activations during routine movement." The department also raised privacy concerns, warning that accidental recording could capture sensitive conversations with informants or victims, or document bystanders engaged in First Amendment-protected activity. Critics note that CBP agents operate the identical Axon hardware in the field every day — making the gap between the two agencies less a technological problem and more a reflection of institutional resistance to being on the record.

Fatal Shootings Without Footage Drove the Congressional Probe

Democratic lawmakers launched the GAO review against a backdrop of deaths that drew national attention. Federal immigration agents have killed at least nine people and injured more than a dozen others in at least 30 shootings since Trump began his second term, according to a CBS News independent review — among them two people shot dead in Minneapolis: Renée Good on January 7 and Alex Pretti on January 24. Two more men were killed later in the year during immigration enforcement vehicle stops — Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston on July 8, and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine, roughly a week later. In each high-profile case, no cameras were running.

The program's funding history tracks the political turbulence surrounding those deaths. The Trump administration's fiscal 2026 budget had proposed cutting ICE's camera program funding by roughly 75 percent, from approximately $20.5 million down to $5.5 million. After the Houston and Maine shootings triggered protests across the country, Congress reversed that course and directed $20 million specifically toward the procurement, deployment, and operation of body cameras for immigration enforcement officers. DHS confirmed to the GAO that all ICE field offices had received their devices by August 5 — a distribution milestone that resolves the hardware gap but does nothing to enforce activation once the cameras are in agents' hands.

Zero Reprimands, No Performance Standards, Plans Years Out of Date

The GAO's criticism reaches well beyond the auto-activation dispute. Neither ICE nor CBP had updated its body camera management plan since the programs were first established — ICE's dated to 2024, CBP's to 2022 — even as both agencies substantially expanded their workforces in the intervening years. At multiple ICE field offices reviewed by auditors, officers reported confusion about basic activation requirements, including whether cameras had to be on during vehicle searches or when transporting detainees.

Most critically, neither agency has established any measurable performance standards by which to gauge whether its camera program is delivering the transparency and public trust it was designed to produce. Tens of millions in federal dollars have been allocated, but no formal benchmarks exist to determine whether that investment is working. DHS accepted six of the GAO's seven recommendations. The sole rejection was the only one that would have taken the activation decision entirely out of individual officers' hands.

Legislation Promised, but Its Path Through Congress Remains Unclear

Rep. Thompson chose direct language after the report's release. "This is completely unacceptable," he said in a statement, pledging to introduce mandatory auto-activation legislation "in the coming days." Whether that bill can advance in a divided Congress remains an open question. What the GAO report and DHS's response make clear is where the line has been drawn: agents will carry cameras into every enforcement encounter, but the choice to actually roll footage — even when drawing a weapon — will remain, for now, theirs alone.

Last week I drove to Edinburg in the Rio Grande Valley and back in one day.

I was shocked at the number of patrol cars, representing multiple law enforcement agencies, positioned on the side of the highway. I counted five within a 1-mile stretch.

You might think they were just cracking down on speeding in the RGV. But I wondered if they were hunting for immigrants.

Based on the prevalence of 287(g) agreements, combined with automatic license plate readers in the state of Texas, it’s a fair question.

Texas has implemented Senate Bill 8, one of the state’s most significant immigration enforcement laws, which passed in the last legislative session in 2025.

Senate Bill 8 mandates that every county with a jail enter into an agreement that allows local law enforcement to perform federal immigration enforcement activities.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

These are called 287(g) agreements, and they expand the reach and power of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Homeland Security in our communities. In addition to the mandated agreements, which applies to almost every one of the 254 counties in Texas, any local law enforcement agency is eligible to voluntarily apply for a 287(g) agreement.

Agencies can choose from three operational models of 287(g) agreements: the Warrant Service Officer Model, or WSO; the Jail Enforcement Model, or JEM; and the Task Force Model, TFM.

According to Texas Immigration Law Council, there are 541 active agreements in Texas, and not every county has adopted the agreement, including Travis County and Dallas County. The deadline set by SB8 to do so is Dec. 1.

Bexar County has adopted the mildest model available, the WSO, which allows local law enforcement to serve ICE warrants inside jails. But smaller jurisdictions within Bexar County have voluntarily opted into TFM agreements: Balcones Heights, China Grove, Hollywood Park, St. Hedwig, Sandy Oaks, Universal, Von Ormy and Bexar County Constable Precinct 3.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

TFM agreements make up the majority of the 287(g) agreements in Texas. They are the most aggressive.

A TFM essentially deputizes law enforcement officers to function like ICE. In a routine encounter, like a traffic stop, a task force officer has the power to stop, interrogate, arrest and transport a person to immigration detention on the spot.

You may wonder why so many agencies are voluntarily entering into these agreements. As usual, the answer lies in money.

Remember last summer when Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill and ballooned the budget for ICE? ICE now reimburses 100% of the salaries and benefits, plus equipment, overtime and additional stipends for each 287(g) officer.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Furthermore, individual officers are incentivized to help ICE meet President Donald Trump’s deportation goals. Quarterly performance-based bonuses are paid to each officer in an agency that locates and detains certain percentages of undocumented immigrants.

Officers under 287(g) are given direct access to federal databases to help locate undocumented immigrants who have been identified by ICE. And with the additional help from automatic license plate readers, such as the Flock cameras that track our every move, it’s easier than ever.

All someone would have to do is park on the side of a highway that automated license plate readers show is a regular route for someone on the list and start scanning the cars that drive by.

We should all be concerned by this, if not enraged. The people we entrust with protecting public safety are distracted by these carrots our government is dangling in front of them.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

I was in Edinburg to speak with Keyla Contador, whose father, Juan Mejia Contador, has been in immigration detention in Port Isabel since Aug. 15 after ICE pulled him over as he was on his way to work.

He may not have been pulled over by a 287(g) officer, but as these agreements take effect, more and more people will be.

Keyla and I discussed how so many in her community voted for Trump, believing he would only be going after criminals. They now feel betrayed.

Contador doesn’t have a criminal conviction, just like 70% of the immigrants who have been detained since 2025 (and 95% of those who do have only minor nonviolent convictions).

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Contador works, pays taxes and contributes to his community. He’s a property owner, a well-known mariachi player, and a husband and father of four, including a special needs adult.

The Contador family wants you to know his story and help them advocate for his return. For now, he is holding strong in detention, resisting the urge to sign self-deportation papers to his home country in hopes of being reunited with his family.

Texas has always found a way to live with our immigrant neighbors. Instead, Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton are enticing local agencies to do the bidding of the Trump administration.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Our country is not safer because people like Juan Contador are locked up. But we are far less safe because our law enforcement is consumed with hunting down immigrants like him instead of fulfilling their primary duties.

text:
A Biden-appointed judge dealt the Trump administration another legal blow Thursday, tossing its lawsuit seeking to upend New York City’s sanctuary policies after ruling that the Justice Department’s arguments amounted to a "backdoor around the Tenth Amendment."

The Trump administration sued New York City in July 2025, alleging that its sanctuary laws unlawfully hinder federal immigration enforcement by restricting local law enforcement’s cooperation with federal authorities.

The New York City case is one of more than two dozen lawsuits the Trump administration has filed against state and local jurisdictions over sanctuary and related policies restricting cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

But U.S. District Judge Ramón E. Reyes Jr. ruled that the federal government lacked standing to challenge New York City’s restrictions on honoring ICE detainers and rejected the Justice Department’s claims that the city’s sanctuary policies are preempted by federal law.

MAMDANI BLASTS FEDS FOR WAGING 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE AND TERROR' AGAINST NYC'S IMMIGRANTS

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani celebrated the ruling in a Friday post on X, accusing the administration of attempting to turn city employees into immigration enforcement agents.

"The federal government tried to turn our public servants into deportation agents and force New York City to carry out ICE’s cruel agenda. Today, a federal court rejected that effort and upheld our laws. Every New Yorker deserves to seek help from their city without fear of being targeted for deportation. We will stand by our immigrant neighbors, defend our laws and protect the promise that this city belongs to all of us," Mamdani wrote.

Reyes found the administration lacked standing because striking down the city’s restrictions would not remedy its alleged harm because separate state laws restricting cooperation would remain in place.

But Abhishek Kambli, a former federal prosecutor and current partner at Holtzman Vogel, disputed that reasoning, arguing that the city's laws independently harm the federal government's authority regardless of whether similar state restrictions exist.

"The sovereign harm is done just by the fact that New York City has the law in the books, no matter what other factors prevent practical application of the United States's position," Kambli told Fox News Digital.

FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS NEW YORK LAW BANNING ICE AGENTS FROM WEARING MASKS

Reyes also rejected the Justice Department's argument that New York City's sanctuary policies are overridden by federal immigration law.

"Even if the United States has standing — and it does not — its preemption claims fail," Reyes wrote. "All of the United States’ preemption claims — express, conflict and field — fail because the relevant federal statutes do not regulate private actors."

The judge pointed to the Tenth Amendment's anti-commandeering doctrine, which prevents the federal government from forcing state and local governments to use their own officials and resources to administer federal programs.

"If states cannot remain free to control their agencies and employees to resist federal immigration enforcement, which is within states’ constitutional prerogatives, the Tenth Amendment anticommandeering doctrine means nothing," Reyes wrote.

Kambli, however, argued that Reyes misinterpreted the distinction between forcing local governments to assist federal immigration enforcement and preventing them from actively obstructing it.

"Really what the 10th Amendment anti-commandeering means is you can't force states to go from doing nothing to affirmatively assisting. What these statutes are doing is basically preventing states from actively obstructing federal immigration enforcement," Kambli said.

He argued that the Justice Department was not seeking to force New York City officials to carry out federal immigration enforcement, but instead to prevent local laws from interfering with federal authorities' ability to enforce immigration law.

"That's different from the federal government saying a state or a city is required to actively assist ICE in operations," Kambli said.

HUNDREDS OF JAILED ILLEGAL ALIENS RELEASED BACK ONTO BLUE-STATE STREETS DESPITE ICE DETAINERS, RECORDS SHOW

The Justice Department also argued that New York City's sanctuary policies went beyond simply refusing to assist federal authorities by restricting information-sharing with ICE that is protected under federal law. The administration additionally claimed that the city unfairly singled out federal immigration officials for restrictions that did not apply to other law enforcement agencies.

Reyes, however, found that federal information-sharing protections apply specifically to information about an individual's citizenship or immigration status and do not require local governments to provide ICE with broader details, such as a person's release date or whereabouts.

"The United States’ assertion that information regarding release dates and custody status is information regarding immigration or citizenship status is contrary to law," Reyes wrote.

Kambli, however, argued that the distinction over what information is being withheld misses the greater issue at hand.

"The issue is mainly whether any state or locality that prohibits cooperation is preempted by federal law, regardless of what the information is," Kambli said.

text:
New York City successfully shut down the Trump administration’s lawsuit challenging the city’s decades-old policies that limit local law enforcement’s cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

A Brooklyn-based federal judge late Thursday dismissed the White House’s case, filed last year, that argued those policies — collectively known as the sanctuary city law — are unconstitutional and make it harder for federal immigration officers to do their jobs. The Justice Department said those statutes are preempted by federal law.

The government’s preemption arguments “amount to nothing more than a backdoor around the Tenth Amendment,” Judge Ramon E. Reyes Jr. of the US District Court for the Eastern District of New York said in his ruling. That amendment’s anticommandeering doctrine, which prevents federal agencies from compelling state action, precludes relief for the US, the judge added.

Ruling in favor of the US government would allow city agencies and individual employees to decide for themselves whether they comply with state and local law as part of their work, making it impossible for the municipality to control those entities, Reyes said.

That kind of system, he continued, would direct “the expenditure of municipal resources and obviously violate federalism, contravene due process, and foreclose efficiencies available through the implementation of uniform processes.”

The decision adds to a string of losses the Trump administration has faced in its effort to take down similar laws in cities across the country and pave the way for the White House to carry out its deportation plans. A federal judge in Rochester, N.Y., dismissed a similar lawsuit against the Western New York municipality in September.

“This is a victory for New Yorkers and a rebuke to ICE’s deportation agenda,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) said in a press statement. “The federal government came to court seeking to force New York City to turn its public servants into deportation agents and divert our resources toward carrying out ICE’s cruel agenda.”

The city will continue to “use every tool at our disposal to protect New Yorkers from ICE’s abuses,” he said.

The US Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Failing Cases Elsewhere

The law at issue prevents local law enforcement from honoring a civil immigration detainer without a judicial warrant. One provision says that no city agency should use its resources or “subject its officers or employees to the direction and supervision of the secretary of homeland security primarily” for immigration enforcement purposes.

The administration’s July 2025 complaint said those laws violate the federal government’s “well-established, preeminent, and preemptive authority to regulate immigration.” The Justice Department argued the laws should be declared invalid for violating the Supremacy Clause.

New York City over the past several months has filed multiple letters with the court pointing to other sanctuary city suits that have been dismissed across the country, including those in Rochester, Los Angeles, Boston, New Jersey, Minnesota, and Colorado.

Reyes’ ruling cited a Massachusetts federal court’s decision earlier this year that dismissed the White House’s case against Boston. There, Judge Leo T. Sorokin said a court ruling can’t “lessen or alleviate” the federal government’s alleged injuries.

“Other actors, not this Court, hold the authority to grant the United States the redress it seeks,” Reyes said, building on Sorokin’s rationale. The relief the US seeks must come from the state or city legislature or Congress, all of which could enact laws that authorize law enforcement officers to conduct civil immigration arrests, he added.

Direct Regulation

The US contends the city’s rejection of congressionally authorized means of enforcing federal immigration law constituted an unlawful direct regulation of the federal government.

The Second Circuit — which maintains jurisdiction over federal courts in New York, Connecticut, and Vermont — hasn’t defined direct regulation, Reyes said, and he declined “to define the bounds” himself.

The judge concluded that the “challenged provisions cannot be classified as functionally regulating the United States.” Enjoining New York City’s policies “would result in the commandeering of state and local resources,” in violation of the US Constitution, he added.

Reyes also rejected the administration’s argument that it’s been harmed by the city’s policies, which prohibit local law enforcement officers from sharing with immigration officers information about a person who has been in local custody, and from executing an ICE detainer request to maintain custody of a non-citizen for 48 hours without a judicial warrant.

Federal immigration officers must now engage in dangerous efforts to re-arrest immigrants who were previously in local custody, the US said in its complaint.

US law bars local governments from preventing their agencies and officials from disclosing information about a person’s citizenship or immigration status, Reyes said. However, that information isn’t the same as the information the US is seeking about immigrants who have been released from local custody, he explained.

The administration’s assertion that information about custody release is the same as immigration or citizenship status “is contrary to law,” Reyes said.

description:

text:
About this research

This Pew Research Center analysis focuses on Latino registered voters and the 2026 midterm election.

Why did we do this?

Pew Research Center conducts research to inform the public, journalists and decision-makers. This analysis builds on a larger body of work that explores the views and attitudes of Latino voters in U.S. elections and the attitudes and experiences of Latinos in the United States.

Learn more about Pew Research Center, our research on Hispanics in the U.S. and other research on race and ethnicity.

How did we do this?

We surveyed 5,062 U.S. adults, including 774 Hispanic registered voters, from Sept. 28 to Oct. 4, 2026. Everyone who took this survey is part of the Center’s American Trends Panel. The survey was conducted in English and Spanish and represents the views of the full U.S. adult population. Read more about the ATP’s methodology.

Here are the questions used for this analysis, detailed responses and the survey methodology.

List of key terms

The terms Hispanic and Latino are used interchangeably in this report.

In a previous survey, respondents were asked a question about their voter registration status. In this report, respondents are considered registered voters if they self-report being absolutely certain they are registered at their current address. Respondents are considered not registered to vote if they report not being registered or express uncertainty about their registration.

The terms “registered voters” and “voters” are used interchangeably in this report.

This analysis includes comparisons between Latino registered voters and other registered voters. In these cases, the terms other registered voters or other voters refer to those who are not Latino.

Validated voters are adult citizens who told us in a postelection survey that they voted in a given general election and have a record of voting in a commercial voter file. Trump voters are validated voters who self-reported that they voted for Republican Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election. Harris voters are validated voters who self-reported that they voted for Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

Nonvoters are those who did not vote in 2024 but were eligible to do so.

Several weeks out from the 2026 midterm election, Democratic congressional candidates have a sizable advantage among Latino registered voters. And while not all registered voters will cast ballots this year, Latino Democratic candidate supporters are more engaged with this year’s election compared with four years ago.

77% of Latino registered voters who support a Democratic candidate for their district in the House of Representatives say it really matters who wins control of Congress, up from 58% in 2022.

53% say they’re extremely motivated to vote, up from 41% four years ago.

45% say they’ve given a lot of thought to the upcoming elections, up from 24% in 2022.

Meanwhile, Latino voters who support Republican congressional candidates show lower levels of engagement this year compared with Latino voters supporting Democratic candidates.

Latino registered voters overall are more engaged in this year’s election than they were at a similar point before the 2022 midterms. Their current level of interest is similar to other registered voters. By contrast, in 2022, Latino voters were less engaged than other voters.

Latino voters have historically favored Democratic over Republican candidates in midterm elections, but the margin has narrowed in recent years: In 2022, Latino voters backed Democrats over Republicans by a 21 percentage point margin, down from a 47-point margin in 2018. Trump also made gains among Latino voters in presidential elections between 2016 and 2024, winning nearly half their votes two years ago. Previous Pew Research Center studies have found that differences in who turns out to vote, rather than voters switching their support between parties, have played a role in these shifts.

Two years into the second Trump administration, the president’s standing with Latino voters has deteriorated. His current job approval rating among Latino voters, at 24%, is down from 38% in February 2025. And majorities of Latino voters say the Trump administration’s policies harm Hispanics more than help them and that their situation as a group is worse than a year ago. (Jump to “Trump’s falling job approval rating among Latino registered voters.”)

The economy remains the top issue for Latino voters, who have grown more negative about economic conditions and are increasingly concerned about the cost of gas and unemployment. (Jump to “The Economy Is the Top Issue for Latino Voters in the 2026 Midterms.”)

These findings come from a new Pew Research Center survey of U.S. adults, including 774 Hispanic registered voters, conducted from Sept. 28 to Oct. 4, 2026.

Where do Hispanics who voted for Trump in 2024 stand today?

Donald Trump’s job approval rating as president has declined substantially among Hispanics voters who backed him in 2024: 57% approve of his job performance, down from 93% at the beginning of his second term.

Latino voters who supported Trump in 2024 are split over whether his policies help or harm Latinos overall (32% vs. 37%). At the same time, their views of economy have worsened: 34% now rate economic conditions as excellent or good, down from 57% at the start of the year.

On immigration enforcement, 30% of Hispanic voters who backed Trump in 2024 say his administration is doing too much on deporting immigrants who are living in the United States illegally. Still, a majority say it is either striking the right balance in their approach or not doing enough.

When it comes to this year’s midterms, about two-thirds (65%) of Hispanic voters who supported Trump in 2024 say they would vote for the Republican candidate in their district if the congressional election were held today. Meanwhile, 24% say they would support another candidate or are not sure whom they would support. And 11% say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House race.

Vote preferences among Hispanic voters in the 2026 midterm elections

Democrats hold a 27 percentage point advantage over Republicans among all Hispanic registered voters in the national race for the House of Representatives – 51% to 24%. Another 18% say they are not sure who they would vote for, and an additional 7% indicate they would support another candidate.

Meanwhile, 84% of Hispanic voters who supported Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 say they back the Democratic House candidate this year.

Among those who did not vote in 2024, 47% say they would choose the Democratic candidate and 18% the Republican candidate. An additional 31% say they are unsure who they would vote for, while 4% favor another candidate.

For more information, visit the detailed tables on voting preferences and presidential approval.

(Jump to “Latino Registered Voters See the Democratic Party More Favorably Than the Republican Party.”)

For many Latino voters, Trump is a factor in their congressional vote choices

A majority of Latino registered voters (55%) say they think of their vote for Congress this fall as a vote against Trump. Another 14% say their vote is in support of him, while 30% say he is not much of a factor.

This is a substantial change from four years ago, when 26% of Latino voters viewed their vote as support for Joe Biden and 23% viewed it as opposition to him. About half (48%) said he was not a factor in their congressional vote choice.

Hispanic voters who back a Republican candidate are about equally likely to say their vote for Congress is a vote for Trump or that Trump is not much of a factor for their vote (46% each). Only 7% say they think about their vote as a vote against Trump.

A strong majority (84%) of Hispanic voters who say they support a Democratic candidate for Congress this year view their vote as opposition to Trump. And 14% say Trump is not a factor in their vote for Congress.

Among Hispanic voters who backed Trump in 2024, 35% say their vote for Congress this year is a vote for the president. Yet 19% view their vote as opposition to Trump. Another 46% say he is not much of a factor in their vote choice.

Trump’s falling job approval rating among Latino registered voters

Today, 24% of Latino registered voters say they approve of Trump’s handling of his job as president. This number has fallen 14 percentage points from the start of his second term, when 38% approved of his job.

The president’s job approval rating has fallen more sharply among his 2024 Hispanic voters. At the start of his second term, 93% said they approved of his job as president. Now, 57% say this – a decline of 36 percentage points. Approval has also fallen among Trump’s 2024 non-Hispanic backers, though less sharply. In February 2025, 95% approved of his job performance, compared with 68% today.

The impact of Trump’s policies on Hispanics

Seven-in-ten Hispanic registered voters (70%) say the Trump administration’s policies have been harmful to Hispanics, while 12% say they have been helpful and 16% say they have had no effect. This is similar to their assessment from a year ago, when 74% said the administration’s policies were harmful to Hispanics.

Today, views differ sharply by how Hispanic registered voters say they will vote in the House election:

Republican candidate supporters are divided: 23% say the administration’s policies have been harmful, while 37% say they have been helpful. Another 38% say they have had no effect.

Almost all Democratic candidate supporters say the administration’s policies have been harmful to Hispanics (91%).

How Hispanic voters view the situation of Hispanics in the country

About six-in-ten Hispanic registered voters (61%) say the situation of Hispanics in the United States is worse than it was a year ago, while 11% say it is better and 26% say it is about the same.

The share who say Latinos’ situation in the U.S. is worse than a year ago is roughly the same as the share that said this a year ago (65%).

However, the reference periods differ. This year’s assessment asks respondents to compare the situation today with the first year of Trump’s second administration. Last year, they were comparing the first year of Trump’s second administration to the final year of the Biden administration.

This year’s negative assessment of Hispanics’ situation remains far above previous years: In 2021, only 28% said Hispanics’ situation had worsened in the previous year, and in 2019, 42% said this.

Hispanic registered voters’ choice of congressional candidate this year is related to how they see the situation of U.S. Hispanics.

Maine federal Judge Lance E. Walker Trump appointee

The judges ruled that there was no legal or factual basis for the government’s demand. They noted that the laws require states to keep accurate, up-to-date computerized voter lists that include confidential information. But the statutes give the federal government limited power to enforce those mandates.

Several judges accused the administration of using the election laws as a pretext to suppress voting.

“ The foundation upon which American democracy has been built is the right to vote. … Now it seems the Executive Branch of the United States government wants to abridge the right of many Americans to cast their ballots. … The Court does not take lightly DOJ’s obfuscation of its true motives.”

California federal Judge David O. Carter Bill Clinton appointee

“ Public statements from government officials reveal its intentions: to create a nationwide voter-database, for potential weaponization in future elections; as a ‘fishing expedition,’ hoped to advance unsubstantiated claims of non-citizen voting; and as a tool for immigration enforcement.”

Pennsylvania federal Judge Cathy Bissoon Barack Obama appointee

In an extraordinary rebuke (echoed by other courts around the country), the judge hearing the Oregon case wrote that the federal government’s actions undermined the judiciary’s longstanding trust in the Justice Department. He called them “chilling.”

text:
The Trump administration is escalating its fight with California ahead of next month’s midterm elections, warning that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution.

The letter on Friday from senior justice department officials and obtained first by the Associated Press is the latest salvo in an ongoing tussle with heavily Democratic California, coming just a day after the Trump administration sued the state to prevent it from counting mail-in ballots from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.

Noncitizen voting is extremely rare and the effort to investigate noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections has only turned up a handful of cases so far. The justice department has charged about 50 people who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens out of the more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.

“The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime – and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful,” warns the letter from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the justice department.

It adds: “If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime.”

The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles county counsel’s office and also is copied to the California secretary of state, Shirley Weber, and the Los Angeles county registrar, Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice.

Trump weighed in late Friday, sharing on Truth Social a link to a news story about the letter and adding: “They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!”

The justice department lawsuit was filed after California officials were given, and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the 3 November election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters.

Rick Hasen, a UCLA law professor, said the letter “ups the ante by threatening election officials with potential criminal prosecution”.

“It is deplorable that rather than work cooperatively and assist states in their election administration responsibilities, the federal government is making escalating threats and unreasonable demands beyond its power in the middle of an ongoing election,” he said.

Justin Levitt, a former deputy assistant attorney general who teaches at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, dismissed the idea that an attempted prosecution of an election official using the letter’s rationale would hold up.

“Courts haven’t been buying what DOJ has been selling, and nothing in this letter is calibrated to change course,” he said. “Fortunately, election officials – not just in Los Angeles, but across the country – are equipped to stand up to aggressive bullying. And the law is on their side.”

More than 23 million people are registered statewide, and a handful of competitive congressional races in other California districts could determine which party controls the US House for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidential term.

Earlier Friday, Alex Padilla, California Democratic senator, Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democratic senator and Dick Durbin, an Illinois Democratic senator, wrote to Todd Blanche, the attorney general, demanding that the justice department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified.

description:
“Our local laws make New York City safer.
“Today’s ruling is a win for New York City and immigrant New Yorkers,” Ali continued.
“These disturbing figures expose the deadly consequences of an immigration enforcement system increasingly defined by militarization, violence and a dangerous lack of accountability,” Jozef said.

text:
In his ruling, Judge Ramón Reyes, Jr., a judge in US District Court in Brooklyn, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, wrote that the Trump administration lacks standing to bring its 2025 lawsuit claiming New York City’s Sanctuary Laws are preempted by federal law.

“This is a victory for New Yorkers and a rebuke to ICE’s (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency) deportation agenda,” Mayor Mamdani said. “The federal government came to court seeking to force New York City to turn its public servants into deportation agents and divert our resources toward carrying out ICE’s cruel agenda. Today, they lost.

“The court made clear that the federal government has no standing to bring this case and cannot commandeer our city workers to do its bidding,” he added. “Our local laws make New York City safer. They allow us to focus our resources on protecting and serving our communities and ensuring that every New Yorker can turn to their city government without fear that asking for help will make them a target for deportation.

“The federal government wants to use fear to divide our city,” Mamdani continued. “We will not let them. We will continue to uphold our local laws and use every tool at our disposal to protect New Yorkers from ICE’s abuses.

“Our city belongs to all of us, and we will not abandon our neighbors to satisfy an inhumane, xenophobic agenda,” he said.

The New York City Mayor’s Office of Immigrant Affairs Commissioner Faiza N. Ali said that, “for decades, New York City’s Sanctuary Laws have helped build trust between immigrant New Yorkers and their local government.

“These local laws are essential to ensuring that all New Yorkers can access critical public services, including health care, housing and public education, without fear,” she added. “At a time when federal immigration enforcement is destabilizing and separating families and putting communities across the five boroughs at risk, defending these protections has never been more important.

“Today’s ruling is a win for New York City and immigrant New Yorkers,” Ali continued. “It affirms our right to determine how to best use resources to serve and protect our communities. The federal government’s attempt to undermine our laws has been rejected, and we will not back down from our commitment to protecting our immigrant neighbors.”

She said her office will “keep working to ensure immigrant New Yorkers know their rights, can access trusted support and have the opportunity to live with safety and dignity.”

Murad Awawdeh, president and CEO of New York Immigration Coalition (NYIC), an umbrella organization of over 200 immigrant and refugee groups in New York, lauded Judge Reyes for “upholding our constitutional rights and the state’s rights to pass laws that keep our communities safe.”

Awawdeh said Trump’s lawsuit was “a last-ditch attempt to make an end run around the Tenth Amendment.”

The Tenth Amendment to the US Constitution states: “The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.”

Awawdeh said: “Neither New York City nor New York State will be bullied by the federal government to give up our rights and protections.”

Judge Reyes wrote that, “even if the United States has standing — and it does not — its preemption claims fail.

“All of the United States’ preemption claims — express, conflict and field — fail because the relevant federal statutes do not regulate private actors,” he said, adding that “there is nothing within federal law that obligates states to participate in federal immigration enforcement or compels states to comply therewith,

“The United States’ preemption arguments amount to nothing more than a backdoor around the Tenth Amendment and rest on a false distinction between (a) compelling local governments’ participation in federal immigration enforcement and (b) prohibiting local governments from dictating how their personnel and other resources may be utilized towards federal immigration enforcement,” Judge Reyes continued.

In July 2025, under the administration of then New York City Mayor Eric Adams, Trump’s Department of Justice (DOJ) challenged New York City’s Sanctuary Laws, claiming that prohibition against honoring detainer requests from ICE had “resulted in countless criminals being released into the city who should have been held for immigration removal from the United States.”

Detainer requests, also referred to as “ICE holds,” are written requests from ICE or US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), requesting that state or local law enforcement agencies maintain custody of Caribbean and other immigrants for up to 48 hours after their release time, so ICE or CBP can detain them for subsequent deportation.

Judge Reyes’s ruling comes as the San Diego, CA-based Haitian Bridge Alliance (HBA) strongly condemned the Oct. 8 shooting of Oscar Belgal, 28, a Dominican Republic immigrant wounded by an ICE officer during an arrest operation in New York City, while his five-year-old son sat inside his vehicle.

“This latest shooting is not an isolated incident,” HBA Executive Director Guerline Jozef told Caribbean Life, pointing to reports in which US federal immigration agents have been involved in at least 32 documented shooting incidents since 2025, leaving nine people dead and 15 others injured.

In addition, Jozef noted that human rights and policy organizations have tracked over 60 total deaths inside ICE custody across this combined 2025–2026 period due to medical neglect, overcrowding and facility conditions.

“These disturbing figures expose the deadly consequences of an immigration enforcement system increasingly defined by militarization, violence and a dangerous lack of accountability,” Jozef said.

She said that, more recently, “Pierre Damas Bel, a brilliant 20-year-old immigrant from the Republic of Haiti and Wright State University student, committed suicide amid the termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for roughly 350,000 Haitian nationals and more than a million other nationals whose countries are facing severe humanitarian and security crises.”

Jozef said Bel had reportedly been placed under electronic monitoring by US immigration authorities and “had spoken publicly about the fear, shame, bullying, and emotional distress he experienced while wearing an ankle monitor.

“Far too many immigrants and Americans have been killed and shot by ICE, and now a five-year-old child has been exposed to gunfire during an ICE operation,” she said. “How many more families must be traumatized before we say enough is enough?

“This administration has unleashed a campaign of fear and violence against immigrant communities, particularly Black and Brown families,” Jozef added. “We cannot continue to accept a system where immigration enforcement becomes a license to terrorize communities, endanger children, and take human lives.

“Our humanity is not negotiable. Our dignity is not conditional on immigration status,” she continued. “We demand accountability, justice, and an immediate end to these dangerous enforcement practices.”

Jozef said that, “for Haitian and other Black immigrant communities already confronting discriminatory immigration policies, racial profiling, and the constant threat of family separation, these shootings represent an escalating human rights crisis that demands national attention.”

She said HBA calls for an immediate independent investigation into the New York shooting, the release of all relevant body-camera footage, full accountability for unlawful uses of force, and congressional intervention “to end militarized immigration enforcement practices that threaten civilian lives.”

Caribbean-American Democratic Congresswoman Yvette D. Clarke has demanded that ICE agents leave New York City after an ICE agent shot Belgal in the Marble Hill section of Manhattan.

Law enforcement authorities said the unidentified agent shot Belgal in the neck after ICE agents sought to detain him, with his 5-year-old son in the back of his car.

“For nearly two long and painful years, Americans have watched in helpless horror as our neighbors continue to be stolen from their homes and shot in the street by agents of the Trump administration,” Clarke, the daughter of Jamaican immigrants, who represents the 9th Congressional District in Brooklyn, told Caribbean Life.

The chair of the Congressional Black Caucus (CBC) said the “attempted murder of a New Yorker in front of his five-year-old son was far from the first disgraceful incident of its kind, but it must be the last.

“We demand that ICE leave our city immediately, and we are too disgusted to accept any delay,” she said. “While the Trump administration’s government-sanctioned abuses have shocked our collective conscience and sickened our society, we cannot say that we are surprised to see them befall our communities.”

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement is pushing back against a government watchdog agency’s suggestion ICE agents’ body cameras should turn on automatically.

Typically, ICE and Customs and Border Protection agents’ are required to turn on their cameras at the beginning of enforcement.

“We found some areas where they could improve,” Government Accountability Office Director Heather MacLeod said.

The nonpartisan watchdog released a report this week — “CBP and ICE should improve body-warn camera program management” — which found the agencies don’t always give clear guidance on the use of cameras.

Some CBP and ICE agents said they thought “camera use is not mandated,” “up to interpretation” and “has gray areas.”

Some ICE agents said they “had not begun using cameras … due to this uncertainty.”

“Body-worn cameras, they have the potential to promote public trust, accountability and transparency,” MacLeod said.

The GAO report urges ICE to make agents' cameras automatically start recording when they turn on their sirens or pull out a gun.

CBP cameras already have that function, but according to the report, ICE is reluctant, citing privacy concerns for civilians.

“There are no punitive measures,” MacLeod said about GAO suggestions. “Essentially, we'll continue following up with them, working with them.”

A New York Times analysis found at least 25 people have been shot at by federal immigration agents during President Donald Trump’s second term. Six of those people died, including Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis, and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston.

In some cases, ICE agents wore body cameras, but in other cases, they didn’t.

Border czar Tom Homan told Fox News over the summer he supports the use of body cameras.

“They exonerate more law enforcement than they convict, and I want officers to wear body cameras, ‘cause I want the American people to see what the officer saw when they took that action,” he said.

According to the GAO, the Department of Homeland Security did agree with the other recommendations in the report, as far as the need to give agents clearer guidance on when to turn on their cameras.

A DHS official submitted a letter saying, “These programs are designed to enhance officer safety, transparency, accountability, and public trust. CBP and ICE continue to refine their policy frameworks and training to ensure these systems effectively support officers and agents while upholding these core values.”

text:
U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries joined Democratic congressional candidate Eliott Rodriguez at a Pinecrest bakery Friday to rally support as Rodriguez tries to unseat Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar in Florida's 27th Congressional District.

Salazar has held the seat since 2021. Rodriguez said the national Democratic support shows confidence that it could change hands.

"They identify seats that can be flipped, and we are proud to say that we are on that list," Rodriguez said.

Both candidates have named immigration and affordability as top concerns for district residents, but their campaign stops showed different approaches.

Rodriguez called for a change in direction and criticized the economy and the Trump administration's immigration policies.

"We did not vote for this immigration policy that is cruel, inhumane, and it is impacting our community," Rodriguez said. "We need a change of direction."

Jeffries also criticized the administration's approach to immigration enforcement.

"We also believe that Donald Trump's violent mass deportation machine is out of control," Jeffries said. "It's not what was promised."

District resident Tamara McKeown said immigration enforcement, particularly ICE detentions, is motivating her vote. She said she would vote for Rodriguez.

"This is not just criminals, people that are legitimately seeking asylum that are being deported, families being torn apart," McKeown said.

Salazar, who campaigned Thursday in South Miami, said she expects an immigration bill to become law under Trump.

"I think that before Donald Trump leaves the White House, there will be an immigration reform law signed by him, the president," Salazar said.

She said her proposed Dignity Act would play an important role. Salazar also pointed to housing, saying she helped get a law signed that allows abandoned buildings to be converted into apartments. She said the conversions could increase the housing supply in the 27th District.

Voter Nicholas Alexander said the ability of future generations to afford homes in the community is a priority. He said he would vote for Salazar.

"I want my kids to have that opportunity to buy homes where we grew up," Alexander said.

Early voting begins Monday, Oct. 19. Election Day is Nov. 3.

text:
Immigrant advocacy groups representing migrant children have sued the Trump administration to stop what they call a "cruel and unlawful scheme" to fast-track migrant children's asylum cases.

In a complaint filed Thursday night, the groups allege that new government policies have transformed the asylum process for migrant children into a "deportation assembly line depriving them of their rights."

The lawsuit comes as immigration attorneys and advocates say unaccompanied migrant children are being rushed through the immigration system and that their deportations have been accelerated as part of the Trump administration's aggressive immigration crackdown.

Trump administration offering migrant children $3,000 to self-deport

"A system that moves faster and that is by design made so that children are unable to access lawyers and are railroaded into deportation orders is not justice. It's assembly line deportation of the most vulnerable among us," said Lindsay Toczylowski, co-founder of the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, during a press call.

The groups said unaccompanied children are facing rushed hearings, difficulty finding lawyers, and accelerated removal orders, including in cases involving alleged human trafficking and threats of violence.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News.

In the suit, the groups said that U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has changed practices through a series of recent policy shifts that include reducing notice times for asylum interviews -- in some cases proving less than 24 hours' notice.

In the complaint, the groups also said that the Department of Justice has instructed immigration judges to complete all removal proceedings for detained unaccompanied children by Jan. 31, 2027. To meet the deadline, the groups allege that immigration judges are refusing to grant continuances of longer than three weeks.

"This push isn't coming from just one agency. It's a coordinated whole-of-government operation that abandons due process and child safety in service of faster removals," said Jason Boyd, vice president for federal policy at the advocacy group Kids in Need of Defense.

The suit comes two days after the Department of Homeland Security announced it was offering unaccompanied migrant children $3,000 to self-deport, a $500 increase over last year's incentive.

Earlier this month, the federal government quietly assembled a team of government attorneys to represent migrant children in court after the administration cut ties with a number of immigration advocacy groups that had previously provided those services.

text:
(CNN) — The search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, DC, home by federal law enfo…
