(CNN) — Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar is fighting back against the Trump administration’s search of her home earlier this week – disputing its legality and demanding the return of her property seized by federal agents.

Omar’s attorneys sent a letter Friday, obtained by CNN, to prosecutors at the Justice Department, saying, “This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the President’s chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar’s constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers.”

The administration pushed for an unusually aggressive search of Omar’s Washington, DC-area house in an immigration fraud probe that targets the congresswoman, possible false statements made on government documents, and a potential conspiracy, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation. Federal officers executed a search warrant early Monday after a federal magistrate judge signed off on the warrant, while limiting how the Justice Department could access her documents. Omar has been the persistent target of ire from President Donald Trump’s administration.

Omar sought to dismantle the basis of the probe, saying she became a lawfully naturalized citizen in 2000 after fleeing Somalia in 1995.

“There is no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status,” Omar’s attorneys, Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, wrote in the letter to federal prosecutors. They also demanded that all video and audio recordings made by federal agents during the search be preserved.

A Justice Department spokesperson told CNN in a statement that the letter from Omar’s attorneys was “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies.”

“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” the spokesperson said in the statement to CNN. “Leaking a letter to the press right after sending it is not good faith. It is a publicity play.”

Omar’s attorneys pointed out a number of issues with how the search of Omar’s home was conducted. They said the House of Representatives’ Office of General Counsel was not notified about the search until after it was publicly reported. The judge in Washington had mandated special procedures about giving notice to the House and to Omar and her attorneys about her Constitutional protections as a member of Congress, the letter said. Omar’s defense attorneys indicated the investigators may have infringed on the congresswoman’s rights by not following the judge’s parameters.

There also was no one from the US attorney’s office or the Justice Department at the search to read Omar her privileges under the Speech or Debate Clause, according to the letter, and instead Omar was presented with a waiver that she did not sign. Omar’s attorneys also alleged they did not have the opportunity to identify or segregate materials that were protected under the clause.

The search “arose from a years-old, tired conspiracy theory,” Omar’s attorneys wrote, also pointing out the search was conducted less than three weeks before Election Day.

“Historically, the Department has refrained from this type of investigative activity so close to an election, so as to avoid even the appearance of politically motivated law enforcement actions. But the political motivations behind this pre-election investigation and search are clear as day. For the reasons given above, this search was neither justified nor lawful,” they wrote in the letter, first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

Jeffress and Matz noted that Omar was repeatedly referred to by her first name in the search warrant paperwork and called on the agents to respect the congresswoman with her proper title going forward.

Katelyn Polantz contributed to this report.

This story has been updated.

text:
Legal organizations in Texas are asking a federal judge to order improvements to living conditions at Camp East Montana, Immigration and Customs Enforcement's largest immigration detention facility.

Attorneys representing detainees at Camp East Montana filed a motion for a preliminary injunction on Thursday, asking U.S. District Judge Leon Schydlower of El Paso to order the Trump administration to provide adequate medical care, access to food, and other improvements.

"Conditions at the encampment remain dangerous and inhumane. Plaintiffs therefore urgently request that the Court issue a preliminary injunction, in line with courts across the country, to protect the health and safety of all who are or will be detained at Camp East Montana," the motion states.

Speaking to KFOX14/CBS4 on Friday, senior supervising attorney for the Texas Civil Rights Project, Daniel Hatoum, said the motion seeks to order the government to act now, adding that "the detention facility has to change so that people inside no longer suffer a form of punishment because they are in immigration detention."

"It seeks an order near the beginning of a lawsuit that requires the entity that's being sued to follow the law while the lawsuit is going on. And basically the point here is that right now when we look at Camp East Montana, people are dying. People have died from neglect, but also the intentional abuse by guards. And that's just like the beginning of what's wrong... We cannot wait the length of an entire lawsuit for any type of relief in this litigation," Hatoum said.

According to the filed motion, "irreparable injury is likely" if the court does not grant the request, as the filing cites more than 40 declarations alleging medical neglect, inadequate food, unsanitary conditions and violence by guards.

"Next, the record amply demonstrates that “irreparable injury is likely in the absence of an injunction,”" the injunction states.

Hatoum said this would mean detainees will continue to face suffering and "likely die."

"The evidence is there that shows that these problems are ongoing and that they're happening now and that more people will likely die and face suffering if we don't act accordingly. We have been meeting with detainees for months at Camp East Montana. We've been asking about their stories. And the fact that there are 40 demonstrates and goes to the credibility of those detainee. This is not one person complaining about conditions at the center. This is a group of people all with a consistent story talking about the abuse that they suffer and why this is one of the most notorious immigration detention facilities in the country," Hatoum said.

In a press release from the Texas Civil Rights Project, named plaintiff Gerald Akari Angye called for immediate action, adding that conditions seem to be only getting worse.

“Urgent protection is desperately needed at Camp East Montana,” Angye said. “Today, people are still being detained in this windowless camp with inadequate food, water, medicine, and recreation. People with health issues do not receive the care they need. This case remains important to me because I am a voice for those harmed by this regime. I will never be the same after the violence I experienced by guards at Camp East Montana. Many others are still being held in those horrible conditions. The United States preaches democracy and human rights, but it is separating families and torturing people who are seeking safety. The world is watching. The inhumane conditions at Camp East Montana seem to be getting worse. No one of good conscience can support what is happening there. I plead with the court to give relief to people held in the horrible Camp East Montana.”

When reached for comment regarding the preliminary injunction, an ICE spokesperson said it "does not comment on pending litigation."

As of the latest update, the government had not filed a response to the injunction request, and the judge had not ruled.

READ THE MOTION:

The injunction comes as allegations and concerns of abuse, inhumane conditions, medical neglect, and use of force have continued to be raised at Camp East Montana, which opened in August 2025 as part of a broader federal effort to expand immigration detention capacity following increased enforcement actions.

In May, a federal lawsuit was filed by a coalition of civil rights organizations, including the ACLU and Human Rights Watch, against ICE, alleging widespread abuse, medical neglect, and unconstitutional conditions at Camp East Montana.

Attorneys representing detainees describe Camp East Montana as a humanitarian crisis, citing allegations of severe medical neglect, excessive use of force by guards, arbitrary solitary confinement, unsanitary living conditions, and inadequate food. The lawsuit argues that conditions at the facility violate detainees' Fifth Amendment due process rights and federal administrative law.

The organizations say the motion also comes as ICE is on track to have its deadliest year on record, saying deaths in detention centers have nearly doubled since last fall.

RELATED:Report: Dozens allege abuse and medical neglect at Camp East Montana

Additionally, since mid-December, three people have died at Camp East Montana, which was built last year to house thousands of immigrants.

According to ICE, 48-year-old Francisco Gaspar-Andres died from natural causes. An autopsy obtained by KFOX14/CBS4 states that Gaspar-Andres died from complications of liver disease. He was the first migrant who died at Camp East Montana.

Geraldo Lunas Campos, 55, originally from Cuba, was the second migrant who died on Jan. 3. His death was later ruled a homicide by “asphyxia due to neck and torso compression,” according to an autopsy report obtained by KFOX14/CBS4.

Eleven days after Lunas Campos’ death, Victor Manuel Diaz marked the third death at the detention facility. The 36-year-old Nicaraguan man was found unresponsive in his room. On-site medical staff and responding El Paso EMS performed life-saving measures but were unsuccessful.

While DHS has continued to deny allegations of abuse and inhumane conditions, ICE has also conducted its own internal review of the detention center, finding similar conditions, and hired a new contractor, who promised that conditions in the facility would improve.

In April, an internal ICE inspection found 49 deficiencies across the facility, including issues involving security, medical care, and how staff documented use of force.

The inspection was conducted Feb. 10 through 12 by ICE’s Office of Professional Responsibility.

While the report found no deficiencies in food service, saying meals met federal nutrition standards, the report found problems with how staff documented use-of-force incidents, including missing reports, a lack of documented medical checks, and failures in how those incidents were reviewed, including video not being properly documented.

Those findings came weeks before ICE moved in March to end its contract with the company operating the facility, Acquisition Logistics, and bring in a new contractor, Amentum Services Incorporated.

text:
A federal judge in Baltimore has dismissed Maryland’s lawsuit seeking records on conditions in the immigration holding rooms at the George H. Fallon Federal Building, in a ruling made public on Friday. The judge found that the state’s subpoena, a legal order to hand over records, relied on a state law that does not apply to the federal government.

Judge Julie R. Rubin of the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland ruled that the state had no legal right to sue U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, and the Department of Homeland Security because its subpoena was invalid from the start. She wrote that the court could not enforce it.

She did not rule on whether conditions in the holding rooms are lawful.

The subpoena, issued by the office of Attorney General Anthony Brown, cited a state law which authorizes investigations of civil rights violations. The law applies to any “person.” Maryland defines that word to include individuals and companies but not the federal government, Rubin wrote.

She also left open whether the law could be used to investigate a private contractor working for the federal government.

Whether state law applies to federal agencies is likely to come up more often as ICE moves to own more of the places where it holds people. ICE’s draft contract terms for new detention centers say state and local laws would not apply to them. On an earnings call this year, George Zoley, chief executive of the private prison company GEO Group, was asked why ICE would want to own facilities rather than contract for them. He said federal ownership brings protection from what he called “unwarranted litigation” and is the logical response to states considering more oversight.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has bought 11 warehouses for a combined $1.04 billion to turn into detention centers. It has also bought five detention centers from private prison companies, four from CoreCivic and one from GEO Group. The companies have said they will keep running the sites. A separate ICE plan calls for contractors to run new detention centers near Denver, Miami, Seattle, and State College, Pa.

Another Maryland law lets the attorney general challenge federal actions that threaten residents, including on immigration. The state cited that law in a cover letter but not in the subpoena itself. The judge said only the law named in the subpoena counted.

Brown’s office delivered the subpoena to ICE and the Department of Homeland Security on Jan. 30, asking for nine kinds of records from the previous year. The requests included detainee complaints, medical records, reports on the use of force, contracts for services, and detention logs.

The Fallon building has five holding rooms with a combined capacity of 56 people. They are meant for stays of up to about 12 hours and are not set up for medical care, hygiene, or sleeping. A video showing conditions inside led Brown’s office to open an investigation early this year.

The state alleged overcrowding, long detentions, too little food and water, unsanitary conditions, and denial of access to lawyers. Its lawsuit cited a former worker at ICE’s Baltimore office who told WUSA9 in February that blankets were soiled and that women were denied menstrual products.

ICE denied the subpoena on Feb. 25. The agency said the requests were too broad, too burdensome, and duplicated records it had already turned over in a separate lawsuit by detainees over the same rooms. The state replied that a court order in that case limits its access to those records. In March, the agency asked for another month to respond.

The state sued on March 10, arguing that the refusal was unlawful and arbitrary and that the agency had taken too long to respond.

In later court filings, the state said it was also investigating a private contractor it linked to conditions in the rooms. Rubin rejected that argument because the state’s lawsuit named only ICE and the Department of Homeland Security as targets of the investigation. She wrote that a party cannot add new claims in a later filing.

Rubin also oversees a separate lawsuit by people held in the same rooms. Earlier this year, she issued a temporary court order in their favor.

The judge dismissed the case without prejudice, which means the state can file it again. As of publication, the state had not filed an appeal.

PHOENIX, Ariz. – During the week of enforcement operations from Oct. 10 through Oct. 16, 2026, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Arizona brought immigration-related criminal charges against 279 individuals. Specifically, the United States filed 136 cases in which aliens illegally re-entered the United States, and the United States also charged 123 aliens for illegally entering the United States. In its ongoing effort to deter unlawful immigration, the United States filed 17 cases against 20 individuals responsible for smuggling illegal aliens into and within the District of Arizona.

These cases were referred or supported by federal law enforcement partners, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations (ICE-ERO), ICE- Homeland Security Investigations (ICE-HSI), U.S. Border Patrol, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the FBI, the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS), and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF).

Recent matters of interest include:

United States v. Calixtro-Rodriguez et al. Jesus Manuel Calixtro-Rodriguez and Julio Cesar Ramos-Mendez were charged by criminal complaint on Oct. 13, 2026, with Conspiracy to Transport an Illegal Alien for Profit. Ramos-Mendez was also charged in the complaint with Reentry of Removed Alien. On Oct. 10, 2026, Border Patrol cameras observed a driver in a Dodge Ram traveling south on Federal Route 15 on the Tohono O'odham Nation. The driver, later identified as Calixtro-Rodriguez, performed a u-turn and parked on the side of the road near mile marker 5, a known pick-up spot for illegal aliens. Multiple subjects were observed entering the Dodge Ram. Calixtro-Rodriguez then traveled northbound. Border Patrol Agents (BPAs) attempted to stop him to conduct an immigration inspection, but Calixtro-Rodriguez failed to yield. BPAs then deployed a tire deflation device which disabled the vehicle. All of the subjects bailed from the vehicle and ran away. BPAs were able to apprehend Calixtro-Rodriguez and three passengers, including Ramos-Mendez, who were determined to be citizens of Mexico, unlawfully present in the United States. BPAs learned that Ramos-Mendez was the group's foot guide. Records checks revealed that Ramos-Mendez had been previously removed from the United States and did not have authorization to return. [Case Number: 26-MJ-04143]

United States v. Christopher Paul Lopez. On Oct. 9, 2026, Christopher Paul Lopez was charged by criminal complaint with Transportation of an Illegal Alien. On Oct. 8, an Arizona Department of Public Safety Trooper performed a traffic stop on a Land Rover driving on the I-10. The Trooper observed Lopez lying in the rear of the vehicle during the traffic stop. Lopez began reaching for a black bag, prompting the Trooper to ask if the bag contained a firearm, which Lopez confirmed. The Trooper removed the bag and recovered a loaded Glock 19 handgun from inside. The Trooper directed Lopez to exit the vehicle to speak with them. Their conversation led the Trooper to believe Lopez and the driver were involved in human smuggling. BPAs responded to the scene and determined that the driver was a citizen of Mexico, unlawfully present in the United States. BPAs also learned that Lopez had been paid to accompany the driver from Tucson to Phoenix. [Case Number: 26-MJ-8411]

United States v. Jose Avendano-Soto. On Oct. 13, 2026, Jose Avendano-Soto was charged by criminal complaint with Transportation of an Illegal Alien. On Oct. 8, 2026, a Border Patrol Agent (BPA) observed an SUV driving directly alongside the US-Mexico border wall before stopping. Seven individuals exited the vehicle and deployed a rope ladder to climb over the wall. Five members of the group continued walking north into the United States. The two remaining individuals covered the group's footprints and returned to Mexico. BPAs found the five individuals later, hiding among vegetation wearing camouflage clothing. BPAs determined four were citizens of Guatemala and that one was a citizen of Mexico, and that all were unlawfully present in the United States. BPAs also learned that one of them, Avendano-Soto, was serving as the group’s foot guide into the United States. [Case Number: 26-MJ-1825]

A criminal complaint is a formal accusation of criminal conduct. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

text:
Editor’s note: This two-part series outlines the priorities and visions of Jena Griswold and Michael Allen, who are vying for the position of Colorado attorney general. Read about Michael Allen here.

Secretary of State Jena Griswold said she would continue the legal battles with the Trump administration if elected as attorney general, arguing Colorado needs a leader willing to challenge federal actions she considers unlawful rather than compromise.

Recommended Stories

▶

Griswold, a Democrat seeking to succeed term-limited Attorney General Phil Weiser, also promised to hold federal immigration agents accountable for alleged crimes and defend Colorado’s election laws.

She additionally outlined priorities involving water rights, consumer protection, artificial intelligence and the rising cost of living in a recent interview with Colorado Politics.

Griswold, term-limited as secretary of state, faces Republican Michael Allen, the current district attorney for El Paso and Teller counties, in the Nov. 3 general election.

“My first job right now is Secretary of State, and that’s what I’m immensely focused on,” Griswold said.

Griswold said her office has spent the past year and a half preparing for potential election disruptions, including a contingency plan for a scenario in which the U.S. Postal Service stops delivering mail ballots. She said she added a position to her office and hired someone formerly with the U.S. Department of Justice to strengthen contingency planning.

The prospect of disrupted mail delivery has already become a legal issue, she said, adding that her office’s first response under its contingency plan is to challenge such action in court.

Griswold said she would continue Weiser’s legal strategy of challenging the Trump administration, citing lawsuits involving federal funding for rural schools, anti-terrorism grants and energy and infrastructure projects.

Weiser has filed 87 lawsuits against the federal administration — cases that Griswold insisted are necessary to protect Colorado from “unlawful federal actions.”

“My opponent has already said that he believes these lawsuits are politically motivated and that he would move to dismiss most of them,” she said.

In an interview with Colorado Politics, Allen said if elected, he would review all 87 lawsuits and decide which ones were politically motivated and continue to fight those that benefit Colorado residents. Allen has criticized Griswold for focusing on the Trump administration in Washington rather than Colorado needs.

Asked whether an attorney general should seek compromise with a federal administration even when the two sides disagree, Griswold rejected making concessions in exchange for federal funding or other benefits.

In particular, Griswold pointed to — and criticized — Gov. Jared Polis for granting clemency to former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters, who was convicted in connection with a breach of election equipment in 2021.

Griswold, Weiser and other Democrats spoke against Polis’ decision to release Peters. The Colorado governor had always maintained that neither pressure from Trump nor the criticism from his party mates influenced his decision to commute Peters’ sentence. Instead, he said, his decision was solely based on his belief that her sentence had been too harsh. The governor noted the sentence for former Sen. Sonya Jaquez Lewis, D-Lafayette, who was convicted of four felonies, including attempting to influence a public official, the same charge Peters faced.

“It is not lost on me that she was convicted of the exact same felony charge as Tina Peters — attempting to influence a public official — and yet Tina Peters, as a non-violent first time offender got a nine year sentence,” Polis earlier defended his commutation of Peters’ sentence. “Justice in Colorado and America needs to be applied evenly.”

When asked whether she would consider compromising and working with the Trump administration in cases that benefit Colorado, Griswold said no.

“No, you don’t compromise on a case like that where the president is illegally and unconstitutionally retaliating against the state,” she said.

Griswold said Peters’ punishment was a matter for the courts and a jury to determine and argued that Colorado should not abandon its legal principles in response to federal pressure. Some have inferred that releases of some federal funds to Colorado were the result of Polis commuting Peters’ sentence.

Immigration enforcement and consumer protections

Griswold said she hold federal immigration officials accountable and oppose the expansion of immigration detention facilities in Colorado.

She pledged to maintain a tool Weiser launched that lets Coloradans report incidents involving federal officials to the attorney general’s office.

Griswold said she would enforce state restrictions on cooperation between state and local officials and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Colorado has adopted “sanctuary laws” that inhibit or directly bar cooperation with federal authorities on immigration enforcement.

Her campaign platform also includes protecting abortion rights, as well as fertility treatment and birth control.

Griswold said her background as the daughter of a working-class family informs her approach to consumer protection and affordability. During her tenure as secretary of state, her office has taken action against more than 30,000 fraudulent businesses listed in the state’s business registry, she said.

As attorney general, Griswold said, she would pursue illegal price gouging, challenge corporate landlords that illegally raise rents and oppose grocery store mergers that could reduce competition and affect food prices.

She also pledged to scrutinize large technology companies and utility providers as Colorado confronts the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Protecting Colorado water rights

Griswold said protecting Colorado’s water supplies would be a major responsibility for the next attorney general, particularly as Colorado and other Western states confront drought and negotiate the future of the Colorado River system.

Griswold, like Allen, agreed that Weiser has done a good job as attorney general in creating a department specifically focused on water rights. Both candidates have said that, if elected, they would follow Weiser’s lead.

Growing up in the Big Thompson Canyon between Drake and Estes Park gave Griswold firsthand experience of how important water is to Colorado communities, she said.

Griswold called for proactive conservation policies, protection of existing water rights and negotiations toward a fair agreement among the seven Colorado River Basin states.

She said any agreement should recognize the Upper Basin states’ historical underuse of their allocated water and avoid years of litigation and uncertainty.

If negotiations failed, Griswold said she would defend Colorado’s water rights, including in the ongoing dispute with Nebraska.

Artificial intelligence regulations

Griswold also said the attorney general should play a significant role in regulating artificial intelligence through consumer protection laws and safeguards against potential harms.

Griswold pointed to the risk of increasingly sophisticated scams targeting older adults and other consumers, as well as broader worries about the technology’s risks.

She said she would advocate for stronger AI safeguards while scrutinizing the effects of large data centers on Colorado’s water supplies and electricity costs.

“I will stand up to the monopoly utility and tech companies to protect our water and fight to make sure that data centers pay their own way,” she said, arguing that Colorado families and small businesses should not bear the costs of expanding AI infrastructure.

Griswold said her broader goal as attorney general would be to protect Coloradans from corporate misconduct while defending the state’s authority against what she views as unlawful federal interference.

The general election is on Nov. 3.

Mayor Karen Bass Friday joined immigrant rights advocates and community organizations in a promise to protect families amid reports the Trump administration has launched a 45-day immigration enforcement surge in California.

Bass reaffirmed that Los Angeles will continue to defend immigrant rights and ensure all residents know their rights and have access to trusted resources and support.

“No family should have to live in fear or face these challenges alone,” Bass said in a statement. “Los Angeles will continue to stand with and protect our immigrant communities, defend their rights, and make sure families know where to turn for help. We are not powerless. We will not abandon our neighbors or let fear divide us. We will continue working with our community partners to protect our people.”

Federal officials have described the enforcement operations as targeting the “worst of the worst.” However, the announcement has raised concerns about arrests of undocumented immigrants with no criminal record and potential racial profiling, echoing concerns from the federal immigration raids that began in Los Angeles in June 2025.

The announcement has left immigrant families, workers and small business owners worried about what comes next, according to Bass, who appeared with representatives of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights and the Los Angeles Rapid Response Network at a news conference Friday.

Across Los Angeles, entire communities are living in fear, with parents and workers worried they may not be able to go to work, take their children to school, or carry out daily routines without knowing whether they will make it home to their families, she said.

“Families should never have to live in fear because of their immigration status,” City Councilman Hugo Soto-Martínez said. “As federal enforcement increases, our responsibility is to make sure our communities have the information, resources and support they need to protect themselves and their loved ones. We must stand together, look out for our neighbors and make clear that Los Angeles will not turn its back on immigrant families.”

MENDOTA, Calif. (KFSN) -- Local, state and federal leaders, along with farmers and school administrators, gathered Friday at the Mendota City Council Chambers to discuss concerns about increased Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity and its impact on Central Valley families.

"No family should have to live in fear. No family should have to wonder whether their family will come home in the evening," Mendota Mayor Victor Martinez said.

Officials said many of the families they represent are worried about reported detentions and enforcement activity.

"Since October 5th increased ICE activity and reports of resident detentions have raised serious concerns among families and local leaders," Congressman Adam Gray said.

During the meeting, speakers described the effects those concerns are having on residents. Grower Don Cameron recounted a conversation with a 10-year-old girl.

"When we were talking about the ice raids, fear that her parents might not come home," Cameron said.

Martinez said he has also heard from farmers concerned about the impact on their workforce.

"From Bosque, he said 'hey, what's going on in Mendota right now? A whole crew didn't show up to work,'" Martinez said.

The leaders who spoke Friday called for immigration reform and an approach to enforcement that treats people with dignity.

"Federal immigration law must be enforced but how we enforce those laws matters. We can enforce the law, protect public safety and respect people's rights," Gray said.

Gray said he has contacted ICE with questions, including why the operations are taking place and where people are being taken. Action News said it has asked similar questions and received a repeated response that ICE cannot discuss its law enforcement operations and that the Department of Homeland Security enforces the nation's laws every day.

Martinez said the Mendota community is coming together in response to the concerns. He said volunteers are helping deliver groceries to people who do not want to leave their homes.

With only weeks left for the Nov. 3 election, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries made a surprise campaign stop in Miami-Dade County on Friday to boost Democrat Eliott Rodriguez’s bid to unseat three-term Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar in Florida’s 27th Congressional District.

The visit — coming just two and a half weeks before Election Day —underscores national Democrats' strategy to challenge Republicans even in traditionally conservative strongholds like Miami-Dade. Early voting begins Monday in Miami-Dade.

"Eliott Rodriguez is an incredibly compelling candidate," Jeffries told NBC News following a campaign stop with Rodriguez at CAO Bakery & Cafe in Pinecrest. "He’s a trusted voice here in South Florida. He’s articulated a set of values and a vision for making life more affordable for the people here in Miami-Dade County and beyond."

"Donald Trump and Republican policies have failed this community, and it is a real opportunity to flip this seat," Jeffries said.

Salazar's campaign did not issue any public statements about Jeffries visit, but on Thursday she appeared at a Community Newspapers breakfast event in Miami where she promoted her record to reform immigration reform and make life more affordable.

READ MORE: Two former news anchors, one seat: Inside the tightening race for Florida’s 27th District

Florida’s 27th District — which includes parts of downtown Miami, Little Havana, Coral Gables, and South Miami — is nearly 75% Hispanic, making it one of the most heavily Hispanic districts in the nation.

Trump carried the district by nearly 15 percentage points two years ago, and both the NBC News Decision Desk and Cook Political Report rate the current congressional race as "lean Republican". Only a few months ago it was considered a safe GOP seat.

In a statement to NBC News, National Republican Congressional Committee spokeswoman Maureen O’Toole said Republicans are confident Salazar will keep her seat.

"Democrats are on defense across the state of Florida, as voters have no interest in their toxic, socialist agenda," O'Toole said. "South Florida families know that Maria Salazar fights tirelessly for them in Washington, and they’ll proudly reelect her in November and reject out of touch radical Eliott Rodriguez."

Earlier this month, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added Rodriguez to the committee’s highly competitive ‘Red to Blue’ program, signaling that the DCCC is investing in his campaign with resources and fundraising support.

Addressing supporters inside CAO Bakery, Jeffries and Rodriguez talked about economic concerns and immigration policy. Jeffries criticized the Trump administration's recent immigration enforcement measures, calling them an "out of control" system that strays from protecting border security.

"We’re committed to making sure that in this great country of ours — a nation of hardworking immigrants who come here to pursue the American dream — immigration enforcement should be fair, it should be just, and it should be humane," Jeffries said with Rodriguez at his side.

Said Rodriguez: "People did not vote for this economy. People did not vote for this immigration policy. And people certainly did not vote for this corruption we are seeing in this country right now."\

"We’re going to relentlessly focus on making life more affordable for everyday Americans, lowering the high costs of groceries, gas and housing, while at the same time fighting to make healthcare affordable for every single American," Jeffries said.

Beyond South Florida, Jeffries’ campaign trail includes stops in battleground districts across Michigan, Ohio, and Pennsylvania as Democrats target the 218 seats required — a net gain of three seats — to secure the majority.

title: The Expansion of AI-Driven Biometric Systems in Immigration Enforcement
description:

text:
A PDF of this resource is available here.

Introduction

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is increasingly relying upon an extensive biometric data[1] and artificial intelligence (AI)[2] infrastructure in conducting operations. What began as a modest set of legacy identification tools has grown, through a rapid sequence of contracts and pilot programs between 2025 and 2026, into an interconnected system spanning facial recognition, iris scanning, real-time field surveillance, and AI-assisted targeting. In a short period, the population touched by this infrastructure has widened considerably. It now extends from individuals in active removal proceedings, to their family members and neighbors whose addresses appear in the same records, to protesters photographed at demonstrations, to the roughly one-third of American adults whose driver’s license photos are searchable by federal agents through existing data-sharing networks. This expansion is not simply a matter of more tools doing the same job faster. As this paper details, AI-driven platforms like ImmigrationOS and ELITE consolidate case data, government records, and biometric identifiers that previously existed in separate systems into single, continuously updated profiles, extending well beyond the population of noncitizens with pending immigration matters. At the same time, federal laws and regulations are limited in addressing how these AI tools collect, retain, or share this data, leaving agencies substantial discretion over deployment even as they touch citizens and noncitizens alike.

This paper traces that expansion in four parts. It first describes the legacy biometric and case-management infrastructure that predates the current AI buildout, including DHS’s Homeland Advanced Recognition Technology (HART) database and ICE’s longstanding use of state driver’s license records. It then examines three tools introduced or expanded since 2025: ImmigrationOS, a case-management and targeting platform; Mobile Fortify, ICE’s field-deployed facial recognition app; and ELITE, a related targeting tool built on public-benefits and government address data. Finally, it considers what this buildout means for individuals well outside ICE’s traditional enforcement population and examines the legal and regulatory gaps that currently leave these systems largely self-governed by the agencies that operate them.

Legacy Biometric Infrastructure

Before the recent expansion of AI-driven tools, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) had already built a substantial biometric infrastructure to support identification and case management across its component agencies. Between 2008 and 2021, ICE spent nearly $3 billion to expand surveillance, data collection, and data-sharing initiatives. DHS’s Automated Biometric Identification System (IDENT), which was first developed in 1994, holds face, iris, fingerprint, and DNA records on more than 320 million people. Many DHS agencies also rely heavily on the Investigative Case Management (ICM) system, which ICE has used since 2014 to organize records, track investigations, and support enforcement operations. ICM has served as the backbone for various ICE activities over the past decade, notably including prior enforcement operations. Additionally, the Homeland Advanced Recognition Technology (HART) system, developed in 2015, serves as a central database linking iris scans, fingerprints, and facial images, allowing different DHS components—including ICE, CBP, and USCIS—to query the same biometric profiles for identity verification.

DHS’s biometric infrastructure supports immigration enforcement by helping officers establish a person’s identity, identify the use of aliases, and connect an individual to relevant immigration and criminal records. For example, IDENT can alert officers when the same fingerprints are associated with different identities or when a person has previously been ordered removed, allowing ICE to pursue enforcement actions based on a more complete and accurate record. DHS has also used this biometric infrastructure for purposes beyond immigration enforcement. During the 2021 evacuation from Afghanistan, authorities checked evacuees’ fingerprints against IDENT and other federal records to verify identities and identify potential security concerns. By the end of fiscal year 2021, USCIS had submitted more than 8,400 biometric records to IDENT through the Afghan Special Immigrant Visa process.

Facial Recognition

Facial recognition capabilities also predate the current AI buildout. Research has documented ICE’s longstanding use of state driver’s license databases for facial recognition searches, a practice that draws on records collected for licensing purposes rather than law enforcement or immigration matters. Each state’s department of motor vehicles (DMV) independently maintains its own driver’s license and ID records, including photos, addresses, and physical descriptors. States are not automatically required to give federal agencies like DHS or ICE direct access to this data, and some states, like New York, have laws specifically blocking such sharing, but the REAL ID Act does require states to make certain license and ID data electronically accessible to other states through a shared verification network.

In practice, most states share DMV data through Nlets, an information exchange “switchboard” originally established in 1967 as the National Law Enforcement Telecommunications System. Nlets is a self-funded, nonprofit corporation governed by state law enforcement agencies that gives roughly 18,000 federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial law enforcement agencies real-time query access to all 50 states’ DMV records. Individual states retain some control over what they share and with whom, but, absent state-level restrictions, the data is generally available to any Nlets-connected agency without additional court authorization. Police or immigration enforcement officers can compare a person’s photo collected in the field against DMV images obtained through Nlets, allowing agents to identify someone even without an independent tip or an existing record. DMV databases are of particular value to ICE because some states allow residents to obtain a driver’s license regardless of immigration status. DHS and its component agencies are able to access Nlets as an authorized federal member for criminal justice purposes.

In an Nlets search, a single query is automatically routed to all states that permit multistate connections, and Nlets consolidates their responses into a single reply. The reply can include a driver’s name, address, date of birth, physical description, Social Security number, license type, restrictions, license status, and license number, and–where the responding state permits it–a photo. While ICE cannot use a Nlets query to directly flag someone as undocumented, it can be used to confirm the identity of someone already under investigation. Agents can use Nlets to identify individuals based on DMV photos or addresses, their license plates, or photographs of people’s faces taken in the field, checking Nlets to locate matches of known license holders. Because of the “switchboard” design, ICE cannot use Nlets to pull the records of everyone who obtained a license without proof of immigration status. Nlets queries must contain individualized information, so ICE can make a targeted request using an individual’s name, date of birth, and sex, or a license number. In the twelve months ending October 2025, ICE alone submitted more than 292,000 queries through Nlets.

ImmigrationOS

Building on these legacy systems, the second Trump administration has accelerated the adoption of AI-enabled technologies for immigration enforcement. In April 2025, ICE contracted with a technology firm to build the “Immigration Lifecycle Operating System,” known as ImmigrationOS, a software platform that ICE agents use to look up information on individuals and generate lists of enforcement targets. ImmigrationOS functions as an analytical layer sitting on top of ICE’s existing records, using algorithms to sort through that data and surface individuals or patterns that match criteria set by ICE. According to government documents, the platform was designed around three functions: 1) targeting and prioritization, 2) self-deportation tracking, and 3) immigration lifecycle management.

The targeting and prioritization function cross-references records to generate ranked lists of individuals ICE should prioritize for arrest. ImmigrationOS uses AI to sift through immigration records, criminal histories, known affiliations, and prior infractions. Government documents have asserted that “violent criminals” and people who have overstayed a visa are priority categories, although the agency has not disclosed the specific weighting or thresholds the algorithm uses to rank one person above another. The self-deportation tracking function monitors travel, reportedly using passport records among other data, to flag when someone appears to have left the country voluntarily. This gives ICE near real-time visibility into compliance without requiring a formal removal order. The immigration lifecycle management function is designed to streamline the deportation process from initial identification through eventual removal, consolidating case data that previously may have existed in separate files into one continuously updated profile.

Of note, the lifecycle function draws on DHS’s existing ICM platform, which ICE and HSI have historically used for civil and criminal enforcement matters. ICM documentation notes that U.S. citizens remain subject to criminal prosecution and are therefore included in the system, indicating that its case coverage extends beyond noncitizens in civil immigration proceedings. Public reporting has not confirmed whether Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) immigration court records are directly integrated into the ICM platform. Sources that have been confirmed are considerably broader, including passport and travel records, Social Security and IRS data, FBI, DEA, ATF, and SEVIS records, HHS and USCIS files, license plate reader data, and commercial data broker products such as CLEAR. Rather than requiring an ICE agent to manually search each of these separate databases one at a time, the system runs combined queries across these databases and then applies machine-learning models to reconcile mismatched identity records and flag individuals meeting enforcement or risk criteria. A working prototype was expected by September 2025, with the overall contract term running through September 2027. DHS officials confirmed they had started using the system in January 2026.

Mobile Fortify

ICE initially launched a mobile application called Mobile Fortify in spring 2025. The application allows authorized ICE agents and certain CBP officers to submit facial images, fingerprints, and photographs of identity documents from government-issued smartphones for comparison against biometric and immigration records maintained by DHS. Facial images are routed through CBP’s Traveler Verification Service, while fingerprints can be checked against IDENT through the Automated Targeting System. When the system identifies a potential match, it may return limited biographical and immigration information, such as a name, date of birth, citizenship status, alien registration number, previous immigration encounters, or possible visa-overstay status. DHS presents Mobile Fortify as a tool for improving the speed and accuracy of identity and immigration-status checks during enforcement operations. Mobile biometric matching can help officers quickly generate an identity lead when a person lacks identification, presents potentially unreliable documents, uses an alias, or cannot otherwise be identified through biographical information alone. Previously, officers might have needed to transport a person to an ICE facility for fingerprinting and additional record checks. By making an initial comparison available in the field, Mobile Fortify could reduce those delays, help officers connect a person to an existing immigration record, and potentially avoid prolonged detention when subsequent verification shows that the person encountered is not the intended target. DHS describes the application as a lawful enforcement tool that queries limited CBP immigration datasets and operates with a deliberately high threshold for confirming a match.

At the same time, DHS does not represent a Mobile Fortify facial-recognition result as conclusive proof of identity. In its AI Use Case Inventory, DHS acknowledges that even a facial-matching algorithm that has performed well in National Institute of Standards and Technology testing may return an incorrect candidate. DHS standard operating procedures and required training instruct officers to treat results only as potential matches, prohibit using a match as the sole basis for enforcement action, and require confirmation through established identity-verification procedures. These safeguards are important because they recognize the technology’s proper role as a lead-generation and decision-support tool, rather than a substitute for an officer’s investigation or independent evidence.

Nevertheless, questions remain about whether Mobile Fortify is being used in the field consistently with those stated limitations. Facial-recognition systems perform less reliably when photographs are captured under uncontrolled conditions involving poor lighting, motion, or unusual camera angles. Unlike fingerprints, a facial-recognition result generally identifies a possible candidate rather than establishing a definitive identity.

Despite DHS’s stated safeguards, privacy advocates have raised concerns about whose photographs Mobile Fortify may collect, how long the government retains them, and whether records of people who are not subject to immigration enforcement are subsequently deleted. DHS’s Privacy Threshold Analysis states that ICE does not provide individuals an opportunity to decline or consent to the collection and use of their photographs. It also acknowledges that officers could photograph someone who is not removable, including a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident. CBP may retain photographs submitted through the application for as long as 15 years, including photographs that do not produce a correct match, and information shared with another agency may be subject to that agency’s separate retention rules. Critics therefore argue that the tool could create lasting biometric records of citizens, lawful permanent residents, protesters, observers, and other people who are not ultimately shown to be subject to immigration enforcement.

Reported errors in Mobile Fortify’s deployment also raise questions about whether field practices conform to DHS’s requirement for independent confirmation. In one documented Oregon case, two photographs of the same detained woman returned different candidate identities, and the agent testified that the application did not display a confidence score. In another incident, ICE detained a U.S. citizen after Mobile Fortify associated him with a noncitizen record and released him only after additional investigation. These incidents do not establish the application’s overall accuracy, but they illustrate the importance of treating facial-recognition results as investigative leads that require corroboration rather than as definitive identifications.

Separate concerns involve the privacy review completed before Mobile Fortify’s deployment. ICE and CBP deployed the application without publishing a PIA specifically addressing Mobile Fortify, even though DHS classified it as a “high-impact” use in its AI Use Case Inventory. The application’s Privacy Threshold Analysis concluded that the program was privacy-sensitive and required PIA and System of Records Notice coverage. ICE and CBP privacy officers nevertheless determined that existing documentation was sufficient, but critics contend that these earlier documents do not adequately assess the distinct privacy risks created by collecting facial images through a mobile application during interior enforcement encounters.

ELITE

As ImmigrationOS moved toward its September prototype deadline, a company supplier for ICE simultaneously built a related, but distinct, AI-based targeting tool known as Enhanced Leads Identification & Targeting for Enforcement (ELITE). According to court testimony and internal reporting, ELITE populates a map with potential deportation targets, generates a dossier on each individual, and assigns a “confidence score” reflecting the likelihood that a given address is accurate and current. As one ICE officer testified in court, the tool “tells you how many people are living in this area and what’s the likelihood of them actually being there,” allowing agents to identify not just a single target but a cluster of people at a given location whom ICE may wish to target.

The tool searches address data from a range of government sources, including the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and USCIS, to “improve capabilities for identifying and prioritizing high-value targets through advanced analytics,” according to an ICE internal user guide. In practice, the HHS data at issue is drawn from Medicaid enrollment records, which include home addresses, dates of birth, and immigration status, and which ICE has used specifically to locate where a targeted individual is likely living, rather than to independently identify new targets on the basis of health information itself. ELITE’s use became public through court testimony in Oregon, where law enforcement agents described relying on the tool during a field enforcement operation to identify addresses where multiple people have had “contact with immigration officials, which could include a naturalized US citizen.” In some instances, addresses that individuals had provided to enroll in Medicaid were used to locate them for enforcement purposes.

Privacy advocates raised concerns that the system’s reliance on Medicaid and other public-benefits data represents a secondary use that health and social-service data were never intended for: Individuals share this information specifically to obtain benefits Congress has made them legally eligible to receive, and such data has not been historically shared outside of the agency other than to investigate waste, fraud or abuse of the program. While immigrant eligibility for many public benefits is limited, experts note that immigrant families—including those with U.S.-citizen children who remain eligible for Medicaid—may be chilled from obtaining benefits to which they or their family members are qualified.

AI Adoption Under the Second Trump Administration

Currently, AI-powered technologies such as ImmigrationOS and ELITE function less as autonomous decisionmakers and more as decision-support systems. The software analyzes records and generates a ranked list of leads or an address with a confidence score, while a human agent retains final authority over whether to act on that lead. An ICE official described this distinction directly, stating that the tools are “not telling us who to arrest, but they are giving us leads and saying, ‘hey, here’s all the information about this person.’” From ICE’s perspective, these systems allow agents to process large quantities of information more quickly, prioritize cases based on agency enforcement objectives, and devote fewer resources to outdated addresses or leads that cannot be verified. In 2026, ICE reported working on more than 40 AI use cases. An agency official also reported that ELITE produced a successful result approximately 80 percent of the time, compared with 30 percent for ICE’s previous internally developed system. If sustained across operations, more accurate address information could reduce unsuccessful visits, limit encounters with uninvolved residents at outdated addresses, and allow agents to focus on cases that are more likely to result in locating the intended individual.

DHS’s AI Use Case Inventory identifies similar efficiency benefits for facial recognition used in Homeland Security Investigations criminal cases. According to DHS, the technology reduces the time investigators spend manually searching online for images and can identify potentially relevant photographs or profiles that investigators might otherwise miss. DHS maintains that these capabilities can improve the speed and effectiveness of investigations into complex criminal and transnational networks while allowing investigators to devote more attention to corroborating evidence, analyzing relationships, and building cases.

DHS has also reported that HSI’s more limited use of facial recognition in child sexual-exploitation investigations has contributed to identifying victims, rescuing children, and arresting suspected perpetrators, including in previously unresolved cases. In so doing, it emphasizes that these facial-recognition results are investigative leads rather than confirmed identifications. DHS states that no law-enforcement action may be based solely on a facial-recognition lead; unsuccessful or unverified results are not entered into the investigative record, and trained personnel must document and vet the technology’s use under established investigative procedures. This requirement of follow-up verification reflects the government’s position that AI can make investigations faster and more comprehensive without transferring final investigative or enforcement authority from trained personnel to an automated system.

Concerns Regarding Expanded Use of Facial Recognition Technologies

Under the second Trump administration, AI-powered facial recognition tools have been increasingly deployed by immigration enforcement to identify removable noncitizens. Legal experts describe a “drastic shift” from DHS’s use of facial recognition technology, which was historically limited largely to investigations and ports of entry and exit. Advocates have characterized this pattern as “mission creep,” arguing that tools originally built and justified for immigration enforcement at the border are steadily being extended far from that original context. During enforcement operations in Minnesota in 2025, ICE reportedly used two separate facial recognition programs, including Mobile Fortify, to identify people who had been photographed at protests criticizing the agency’s operations. Multiple protestors and observers reported being intimidated by immigration agents using the technologies. In response, civil liberties groups argued the practice violated the First Amendment, representing monitoring and chilling of constitutionally-protected speech and assembly.

In early 2026, a lawsuit filed by the State of Illinois and the City of Chicago against DHS alleging widespread, “suspicionless” collection of biometric data of bystanders and protesters disclosed new details confirming how far Mobile Fortify’s use had already spread since its June 2025 launch. Court filings showed the app had been deployed more than 100,000 times nationwide during its first six months of operation, including “extensively during interior enforcement operations in Illinois.” The lawsuit also highlighted DHS’s own acknowledgment that the tool could photograph “someone other than an alien, including U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents,” since the app’s use is not limited to cases of individualized suspicion that someone is out of status or has engaged in criminal conduct and individuals have no ability to opt out of being scanned by a facial recognition technology. Critics, including privacy advocates involved in the litigation, have pointed to the absence of any disclosed retention limit for these images as the central risk. A U.S. citizen who is scanned by this technology and released within minutes can still end up embedded in a federal biometric database for over a decade, available for matching against future encounters, investigations, or other agencies’ systems, with no connection to any finding of wrongdoing. Once someone is scanned using these facial recognition tools, there is no public accounting of whether their photo is deleted, stored indefinitely, or shared with other agencies, regardless of whether the initial use of the technology on that person ever led to an arrest.

It was reported in June 2026 that DHS has outlined plans to extend AI-powered facial recognition capability, as described above, to local law enforcement agencies participating in the 287(g) program through a mobile app called the ICE Task Force Module. With more than 1,300 departments across 32 states now part of the 287(g) program, widespread implementation of the ICE Task Force Module to these jurisdictions could greatly increase the reach of these tools, scanning thousands of U.S. citizen faces and checking them against massive federal databases, including in non-immigration enforcement contexts. With the effort still in the planning stages, it is unclear whether the technology would be utilized for routine law enforcement encounters like traffic stops or on a more limited basis. But because the tool was designed specifically to help deputized local law enforcement officers assess whether the removability of people they encounter under immigration law, the implementation of this plan carries a real risk of further undermining community trust from immigrant communities and others concerned about being swept up by these enforcement efforts.

Governance Gaps in AI-Driven Immigration Enforcement

The technologies outlined above point to several recurring gaps in how such systems are governed. As the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights (USCCR) has observed, federal laws or regulations are limited in how they specifically address the use of facial recognition technology by the federal government. This does not mean existing law is entirely silent on the underlying conduct – several general-purpose statutes may apply in a limited or indirect fashion. The Privacy Act of 1974, for example, establishes controls on how federal agencies collect, maintain, and disclose personal information held in “systems of records,” and USCCR’s report notes that the Privacy Act may constrain or limit agency use of facial recognition technology and related data practices. But the law predates modern AI and biometric technology by decades and is not a clear fit for all aspects related to facial recognition or AI-driven immigration enforcement tools.

Additionally, retention periods and access limits for biometric data also remain largely unspecified across the tools examined. The Privacy Act requires that agencies publish notice of their systems of records and limits disclosure absent an individual’s consent or a statutory exception, and separately, the Federal Information Security Modernization Act requires agencies and their contractors to maintain adequate data security programs. Neither statute, however, sets a specific retention period for biometric data, and the USCCR’s review found no federal regulations imposing regular oversight requirements or clear data-handling standards for facial recognition technology. Given this gap, individual departments have taken inconsistent approaches. The Department of Justice’s (DOJ) interim facial recognition policy, adopted in December 2023, addresses data retention and requires that facial recognition results serve only as investigative leads rather than a sole basis for arrest, but this policy only applies to DOJ and does not bind DHS, ICE, or CBP.

Individual databases have limited surveillance power on their own but combining them into a single platform with probabilistic targeting creates capabilities far beyond prior database tools. Moreover, those capabilities do not stay confined to ICE’s intended targets. ELITE’s use of Medicaid and other public-benefits data to generate address confidence scores draws in household members, family contacts, and anyone else who shares an address or account with an enforcement target, including U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents who have no connection to the underlying investigation beyond living with or near someone under scrutiny. This spillover is structural, not incidental: ICE’s data-sharing agreement with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services reportedly grants it access to records on nearly 80 million Medicaid enrollees, and health-policy researchers have noted that immigration status cannot reliably be isolated within that dataset, meaning citizens and lawfully present immigrants are swept into the same enforcement pipeline as undocumented individuals.

The same logic extends beyond ICE itself. Once biometric and household-linkage data are consolidated into a searchable, cross-referenced system, nothing in current law limits which other agencies could access it for purposes having nothing to do with immigration enforcement, raising a number of concerns including undue legal scrutiny on citizens and legal residents. While a conventional, non-AI database-matching tool drawing on the same combination of government records could theoretically generate comparable address and household linkages, the risks of abuses are heightened by incorporating AI into such a system. What AI adds is the scale and speed at which previously siloed, sensitive records, Medicaid enrollment, DMV files, utility accounts, biometric scans, can now be fused, cross-referenced, and scored automatically, turning a theoretical vulnerability into an operational one.

The result is a set of privacy risks that are genuinely new in degree, if not in kind: citizens, lawful permanent residents, and immigrants alike are now discoverable, linkable, and trackable through their ordinary interactions with government and commercial systems, entirely independent of their own immigration status or any individualized suspicion of wrongdoing. Absent binding, government-wide limits on retention, access, and downstream use, the risk is that these capabilities will keep expanding faster than the legal framework meant to constrain them. Used responsibly and paired with meaningful oversight, that capability could support more precise, better-targeted enforcement. Deployed without clear limits on data retention, access, and use, however it instead exposes citizens and noncitizens alike to expanded surveillance risk regardless of their own immigration statuses.

[1] “A measurable physical characteristic or personal behavioral trait used to recognize the identity, or verify the claimed identity, of an applicant. Facial images, fingerprints, and iris scan samples are all examples of biometrics.” National Institute of Standards and Technology, “Biometrics,” Computer Security Resource Center, accessed July 21, 2026, https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/biometrics

text:
Federal

Trump Administration Slashes Refugees’ Window to Contest Status Termination From 30 Days to 10

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued an interim final rule on October 14 reducing the time refugees have to respond when U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) initiates the termination of their refugee status. The rule took effect immediately, shortening the response period from 30 days to 10 calendar days while retaining the opportunity to submit written evidence, request an interview, or both before USCIS makes a final decision. The rule applies to individuals who remain in refugee status and have not adjusted to lawful permanent residence. DHS says the shorter period will allow it to act more quickly on eligibility concerns, citing alleged deficiencies in screening during the Biden administration, a characterization refugee resettlement organizations dispute.

The change comes amid the administration’s broader review of refugees admitted during the Biden administration and a hold on affected pending green card applications. DHS identified approximately 186,000 refugees admitted during fiscal years 2015 through 2025 who had not become permanent residents as the maximum population potentially subject to the measure, not an estimate of how many will receive termination notices or lose their status. Advocates warn that the shortened deadline could deny refugees a meaningful opportunity to obtain counsel, gather records, translate documents and contest the government’s determination. Termination ends employment authorization associated with refugee status and can lead to removal proceedings, although it is not itself a deportation order. There is no administrative appeal of USCIS’s termination decision, but individuals may seek available protections in immigration court. DHS is accepting public comments through November 13 while the shorter response period remains in effect.

DHS Finalizes Rule Ending Automatic Extensions for Immigrant Work Permits

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) finalized a rule October 14 eliminating automatic extensions of up to 540 days for certain immigrants whose work permit renewal applications remain pending. The rule makes permanent, without changes, an interim policy that took effect October 30, 2025, rather than imposing a new restriction on renewal applications. Affected categories include asylum applicants, applicants for lawful permanent residence, and certain H-4 spouses of H-1B workers. Unless they have another basis for employment authorization, affected applicants must stop working when their Employment Authorization Documents (EADs) expire and cannot resume until U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) approves their renewals. The rule preserves qualifying automatic extensions associated with applications filed before October 30, 2025. DHS says the change allows more frequent vetting of applicants.

The automatic extension was intended to prevent workers from losing employment because of government processing delays. As of June 30, more than 432,000 work permit renewal applications had been pending at USCIS for at least six months, including more than 91,000 pending for over 18 months, even though applicants generally cannot file renewals more than 180 days before their permits expire. The policy leaves affected workers and employers facing potential employment interruptions despite timely renewal filings. The final rule also comes amid broader administration efforts to restrict employment pathways for H-1B families, including a separate proposal that could eliminate work authorization eligibility for certain H-4 spouses. That proposal remains under review and is distinct from the rule ending automatic extensions.

DHS Rebuffs Watchdog Call for ICE to Use Auto-Activated Body Cameras

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) rejected a Government Accountability Office (GAO) recommendation that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) adopt safeguards, including automatic activation technology, to ensure officers record enforcement encounters when required. An October 14 report found that ICE does not use technology that activates cameras when officers draw weapons or stand near colleagues whose cameras are recording, unlike U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), which already uses automatic activation. ICE policy requires officers to record arrests, searches, brief detentions and other activities, but personnel at six of the 10 locations GAO reviewed across both agencies expressed uncertainty about when recording was required. DHS argued that automatic activation could inadvertently record sensitive interactions with informants or victims, or bystanders engaged in protected First Amendment activities. GAO countered that DHS had not proposed alternative safeguards to prevent critical encounters from going unrecorded.

The findings come amid bipartisan scrutiny of missing body-camera footage following ICE shootings, including fatal incidents in Houston and Biddeford, Maine, in July. GAO found broader weaknesses in both agencies’ camera programs, including outdated deployment plans and uncertainty about operating newer equipment. DHS accepted the report’s six other recommendations and said ICE had acquired enough cameras to equip all officers and agents nationwide, with training ongoing. Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Mississippi), the ranking member of the House Homeland Security Committee, called ICE’s rejection of automatic activation unacceptable and said he planned to introduce legislation requiring it.

Legal

Federal Judge Orders Trump Administration to Reinstate 2027 Diversity Visa Lottery

On October 14, a federal judge in California ordered the State Department to reinstate the fiscal year 2027 Diversity Immigrant Visa lottery after the administration failed to open registration on schedule. The judge granted a preliminary injunction in a lawsuit brought by immigration law firm Red Eagle Law, finding that the firm was likely to succeed on its claim that the department’s inaction amounted to “arbitrary and capricious government action.” The administration argued that opening registration after the normal timetable had passed would conflict with federal regulations. The judge rejected that argument, finding that enforcing the timetable under those circumstances would prevent the lottery from taking place altogether. The order requires the department to announce a registration period, accept eligible entries and resume the selection and application process for the 2027 program.

Created by Congress in 1990, the Diversity Visa program makes up to 55,000 immigrant visas available annually to people from countries with historically low levels of immigration to the United States. Selection in the lottery does not guarantee a green card, as applicants must still satisfy eligibility, documentation and other immigration requirements. The administration suspended the program in December 2025 and subsequently introduced a passport requirement for applicants. The injunction requires registration to remain open for at least 30 days and directs the department to process selected applicants under its usual procedures until available visas are issued or the fiscal year ends on September 30, 2027.

Family of Renee Good Files Suit as ICE Shootings Continue Nationwide

The family of Renee Good, a 37-year-old U.S. citizen fatally shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Minneapolis, filed two federal lawsuits October 1 seeking damages and accountability for her death. Good’s partner, Becca Good, and brother, Brent Ganger, allege that officer Jonathan Ross used excessive force when he shot her in her vehicle during a January 7 immigration operation. One lawsuit seeks damages for wrongful death under the Federal Tort Claims Act. The other invokes the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, alleging that Ross and senior administration officials participated in a coordinated campaign to violate the civil rights of Somali and Hispanic communities and intimidate people observing enforcement operations. Federal officials initially said Ross acted in self-defense, while the family argues that video shows Good steering away from him. The White House called the lawsuits “baseless” and said it would vigorously defend them.

The lawsuits come amid continued immigration-enforcement shootings and heightened federal focus on Minnesota’s Somali community. A review updated October 12 identified at least 30 shootings by federal immigration officers during the second Trump administration, leaving nine people dead and 13 injured. Separately, federal agents searched the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minnesota), seized her phone and issued subpoenas to relatives as part of an investigation into potential immigration-related crimes involving her family’s history.

Judge Orders Return of Egyptian Man Wrongly Deported to Equatorial Guinea

A federal judge in Arizona ordered the Trump administration on October 6 to facilitate the release and return of Ahmed Soliman, an Egyptian man deported to Equatorial Guinea despite having no ties to the country. The judge, a Trump appointee, found that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) violated Soliman’s Fifth Amendment due process rights when it removed him to the Central African nation. Soliman, who is gay, had previously received protection from deportation to Egypt because he would likely face torture there. The judge cited accounts that Soliman had been held under armed guard, threatened at gunpoint, beaten and held incommunicado in Equatorial Guinea. On October 9, the administration said it had begun working with his attorneys to locate him and facilitate his return. DHS said it would comply with lawful court orders but maintained that Soliman would not ultimately remain in the United States.

The ruling comes as the administration continues expanding third-country deportations, sending people to countries other than their own, sometimes despite protections against removal to their home countries. Observers documented 536 people deported to African countries where they held neither citizenship nor habitual residence between January 2025 and August 2026. Separately, the United States sent 22 non-Jamaican adults to Jamaica on October 13 under a June agreement establishing the island as a temporary transit point before onward transfers. Jamaican officials said they expect to receive approximately 25 people every two weeks and would not accept individuals with criminal histories under the arrangement. The transfers are proceeding while the Supreme Court allows third-country deportations to continue pending further review, with arguments scheduled for December.

State and Local

ICE Launches “Operation Safe California”

A recent surge in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) presence in Central California, a predominantly agricultural region, has raised concerns among residents and advocates amid reports of what the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is calling “Operation Safe California.” San Joaquin Valley residents described a sudden increase in enforcement activity, and advocates said at least 100 people had been detained over three days in October. ICE, however, declined to confirm a change in activity, citing officer safety and operational security. The reported surge follows record-high arrests nationwide.

Across California, reports of people being pulled over, stopped or detained have heightened fears in immigrant communities. In small agricultural towns, residents described fewer people leaving their homes, with some calling their communities “ghost towns.” In response, California lawmakers sent letters demanding transparency about the operation’s purpose and scope. “Federal immigration laws must be enforced, but how that happens matters. We need answers about what’s taking place, who is being targeted and whether people’s rights are being protected,” they wrote. DHS maintains that enforcement is focused on people with active warrants and known criminal histories, but local attorneys and advocates say the activity they are seeing extends beyond those groups.
