text:
CHICAGO (WLS) -- The decision from a looming U.S. Supreme Court case could impact millions of undocumented families across the country, many in Chicago.

It's a crucial beam holding up President Trump's deportation agenda: Mandatory detention for all undocumented immigrants detained, regardless of if they have a criminal history.

But as the ABC7 I-Team has reported over the past year, many have successfully challenged the policy in court, earning a temporary freedom.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

Now, the U.S. Supreme Court has agreed to take on a case weighing whether the administration's policy shift is lawful.

Over the last year, the I-Team was there to capture moments some parents feared they wouldn't see when they were reunited with their families back in Chicago after they were arrested by federal immigration agents.

"Every day felt like an eternity for me being in there," said Josue Pire-Hidalgo, a Chicago Public Schools custodian that was released after 42 days in custody.

"All I wanted to do was cry with happiness," said Ramiro Cabrera, a father who spent 41 days in ICE custody.

Cabrera, Pire-Hidalgo, and thousands more were held in ICE detention after the Trump administration reversed decades of precedent, imposing a mandatory detention policy for all undocumented immigrants.

The Administration argued it was closing "loopholes" that previous administrations used to allow immigrants to remain free.

But these men, and many more, successfully challenged that policy in court.

"They were in very, very large numbers... challenging the lawfulness or the constitutionality of that detention," said Eva Saltzman, a former Chicago immigration judge.

For ten years, Saltzman determined whether a person was eligible for release while their deportation or removal cases proceeded.

She says the policy shift last year led many people to choose deportation over detention.

"People who would otherwise be seeking relief, who may be eligible for asylum or cancellation of removal, are increasingly going to forgo, forego that application, and forgo that opportunity simply so that they're released from custody as quickly as possible," Saltzman said.

After the policy shift, Saltzman said she continued to review cases based on their merits.

In the case of Ruben Torres-Maldonado, he was arrested by ICE a year ago but asked to be released to spend time with his daughter who was dying of cancer.

Despite the administration's new policy, Saltzman granted the father's release.

Then, this past July, Saltzman said her career in immigration court ended abruptly.

"I was fired or terminated without cause, so I don't know the official reason for my termination. I did handle a number of very high profile cases," Saltzman said.

Saltzman told the I-Team, "I do have concerns for what due process looks like in our immigration courts.

The Trump Administration's efforts to make its "mandatory detention" policy permanent have now reached the U.S. Supreme Court.

On Oct. 1, the Supreme Court announced it had agreed to hear the case of Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, a case centered around a Brazilian citizen with no criminal record who had applied for asylum, but was placed in mandatory detention after he was arrested by agents last year.

Federal judges across the country have delivered more than 9,300 rulings against the administration's mandatory detention policy, according to a Politico analysis.

Two Appeals Courts sided with the Trump Administration, asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.

The Supreme Court will hear the case early next year.

Saltzman said the Justices' decision will be consequential.

"You suddenly have a new situation where millions of people in the United States could be immediately subject to mandatory detention, and that would be a very, very significant change," Saltzman said.

text:
Any non-citizen who illegally votes in American elections will be arrested and held accountable

WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released the following statement after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) arrested Mukeshkumar Somabhai Chaudhari, a non-citizen, for knowingly making a false claim of United States citizenship to vote in the 2024 general election.

On September 10, a federal grand jury in the District of Minnesota returned the two-count indictment charging Chaudhari with allegedly making the false citizenship claim. According to the indictment, on or about November 5, 2024, Chaudhari signed the voter signature certificate required by Minnesota law to vote in the general election. The certificate required him to swear or affirm that he was a citizen of the United States. The indictment alleges Chaudhari was not a U.S. citizen and knowingly made the false citizenship statement in order to vote.

Image

Mukeshkumar Somabhai Chaudhari

“Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences, including criminal charges and deportation,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “Under President Trump’s leadership, this administration will never allow the votes of American citizens to be cancelled out by non-citizens illegally voting in our elections. Only American citizens should be electing American leaders.”

“Voting is reserved for U.S. citizens, and falsely claiming citizenship to cast a ballot is a serious crime,” said HSI St. Paul Special Agent in Charge Travis Pickard. “HSI has the experience and authority to investigate these cases, and we take that responsibility seriously. We will continue working with our law enforcement partners to protect the integrity of our election systems.”

Chaudhari is charged with one count of false information in voting and one count of making a false claim of citizenship in order to register to vote or vote. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on each count.

text:
The Department of Justice’s demand that California investigate and block ballots from 20,000 people it alleges could be noncitizens may violate a court order barring the department from unilaterally attempting to shape state voter rolls and keep voters from the ballot, a pro-voting group told a federal judge.

Common Cause, which successfully challenged the administration’s broad effort to obtain Americans’ confidential voter information and compare that against federal immigration data to cull state voter rolls, is asking the court to hold a status conference on the matter.

The DOJ sued Thursday to stop California from counting ballots sent to more than 20,000 registered voters it alleges are “likely noncitizens” until their citizenship status is confirmed.

The lawsuit, a major escalation in the Trump administration’s effort to exert more federal control over elections, came after the department sent letters to California election officials with a slim 48-hour deadline to comb through and vet a thumb drive with names the government suspects may be noncitizens.

“By attempting to superintend voter roll list maintenance and prohibit registered voters from exercising the franchise without adequate consideration of the reliability of the underlying data, DOJ’s October 13 letters and the actions described in the California Complaint appear to implicate—and perhaps outright violate—the Court’s October 9 Vacatur Order,” Common Cause wrote in its filing overnight.

In the Oct. 9 order, U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan vacated what the DOJ internally deemed its “list maintenance project.” Her broad decision said the administration unlawfully exceeded its authority and violated privacy laws. She also asserted the administration downplayed the risk that eligible voters could be mistakenly flagged as noncitizens through flawed federal databases.

Common Cause said it immediately contacted counsel for the DOJ with questions about how the department identified the alleged noncitizens in California and its data sources. It said the DOJ’s response adopted “an exceedingly narrow view” of Sooknanan’s order as only applying to the controversial SAVE database, which is used to verify immigration status.

The administration said it didn’t use that database in its review for California. Instead, it said the Department of Homeland Security used other data sets across several agencies, including the State Department and Social Security Administration, to gather and compare federal data to publicly available records.

The DOJ on Friday appealed Sooknanan’s decision to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals.

Common Cause isn’t the only one questioning whether the DOJ is disobeying Sooknanan’s order.

“In that order, the court vacated the DOJ’s policy of, among other things, comparing state voter roll information ‘against a federal database to identify purportedly ineligible voters,’ in collaboration with DHS, ‘and demanding that states remove voters from their rolls based on the results of those comparisons.’ It appears that your letter may utilize a policy that a federal court has already deemed unlawful,” California Secretary of State Shirley Weber (D) wrote in a response letter to the administration this week.

Services, Immigrant Rights and Education Network (SIREN) and Mi Familia en Acción (MFA) also cited Sooknanan’s order in their motion to intervene in the DOJ lawsuit in California’s defense.

“Just last week, a federal court in D.C. went further and vacated the policy at the heart of DOJ’s unlawful campaign,” the groups* wrote in a filing overnight. They added that the order “emphasized that DOJ’s efforts to target purported noncitizens have already resulted in the ‘remov[al of] citizens from the voter rolls in their home states and risks disenfranchising many more.’”

SIREN and MFA argued more broadly that the DOJ’s entire scheme in California is “lawless.”

“No federal law authorizes DOJ’s extraordinary demand, which would upend California’s elections and would result in an unprecedented intrusion of the federal government into state-run election administration,” the groups wrote.

*The Elias Law Group (ELG) represents the intervenors in this case. ELG Firm Chair Marc Elias is the founder of Democracy Docket.

text:
Immigrant advocacy groups representing migrant children have sued the Trump administration to stop what they call a "cruel and unlawful scheme" to fast-track migrant children's asylum cases.

In a complaint filed Thursday night, the groups allege that new government policies have transformed the asylum process for migrant children into a "deportation assembly line depriving them of their rights."

The lawsuit comes as immigration attorneys and advocates say unaccompanied migrant children are being rushed through the immigration system and that their deportations have been accelerated as part of the Trump administration's aggressive immigration crackdown.

"A system that moves faster and that is by design made so that children are unable to access lawyers and are railroaded into deportation orders is not justice. It's assembly line deportation of the most vulnerable among us," said Lindsay Toczylowski, co-founder of the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, during a press call.

The groups said unaccompanied children are facing rushed hearings, difficulty finding lawyers, and accelerated removal orders, including in cases involving alleged human trafficking and threats of violence.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News.

In the suit, the groups said that U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has changed practices through a series of recent policy shifts that include reducing notice times for asylum interviews -- in some cases proving less than 24 hours' notice.

In the complaint, the groups also said that the Department of Justice has instructed immigration judges to complete all removal proceedings for detained unaccompanied children by Jan. 31, 2027. To meet the deadline, the groups allege that immigration judges are refusing to grant continuances of longer than three weeks.

"This push isn't coming from just one agency. It's a coordinated whole-of-government operation that abandons due process and child safety in service of faster removals," said Jason Boyd, vice president for federal policy at the advocacy group Kids in Need of Defense.

The suit comes two days after the Department of Homeland Security announced it was offering unaccompanied migrant children $3,000 to self-deport, a $500 increase over last year's incentive.

Earlier this month, the federal government quietly assembled a team of government attorneys to represent migrant children in court after the administration cut ties with a number of immigration advocacy groups that had previously provided those services.

Burlington, Mass. — U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) led the entire Massachusetts delegation in sending a letter to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security Office of the Inspector General (DHS OIG) requesting an independent inspection of the Burlington ICE facility.

Joining Senator Warren in sending the letter are Senator Ed Markey (D-Mass.) and Representatives Richard Neal (D-Mass.), Lori Trahan (D-Mass.), Jake Auchincloss (D-Mass.), Katherine Clark (D-Mass.), Seth Moulton (D-Mass.), Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.), William Keating (D-Mass.), and James McGovern (D-Mass.).

Over the past year, reports and evidence from advocates and attorneys show that ICE appears to have transformed the short-term administrative processing center into a de facto detention site—holding people for days and weeks in conditions that threaten their health, safety, and due process rights.

The lawmakers wrote to ICE in June 2025 following alarming reports that ICE was detaining people for days at a time despite the Burlington facility not being designed for overnight detention. ICE denied that it was violating its policies and instead pointed to their own self-inspection completed in March 2025. Members of the Massachusetts delegation have continued to exercise their constitutional responsibilities, making unannounced visits and inspecting the facility. Most recently, on September 8, 2026, Senator Warren and Representative Trahan conducted an unannounced visit to the Burlington facility.

“Days later, we learned via public reports that on the very same day that they visited, a federal judge ordered that ICE release a woman who had spent approximately four days at the facility. That woman, as described above, had recently miscarried and was denied adequate care during her multiday detention. Just one month prior, a 52-year-old woman was reportedly held at Burlington for 20 days,” the lawmakers wrote.

“Congress and the public deserve immediate transparency about ICE’s practices and the secretive use of this Massachusetts building as an unmonitored detention site. Congress has tasked DHS OIG under the 2024 Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act to conduct unannounced inspections of ICE detention facilities—including field offices and holding facilities—to ensure compliance with detention standards. Accordingly, we request that the DHS OIG conduct an inspection of the ICE and ERO Boston Field Office, headquartered in Burlington, Massachusetts and share its findings with Congress,” the lawmakers concluded.

text:
Poland’s interior ministry has withdrawn a proposal to make it a criminal offence, punishable by up to three years in prison, to provide support to migrants who are in the country illegally. The idea had prompted criticism from human rights groups and even opposition from within the government.

The interior ministry said the amendment had been intended to clamp down on migrant smuggling. But activists feared it would criminalise humanitarian aid, such as that provided to migrants who have irregularly crossed the border from Belarus.

Under current Polish law, anyone who facilitates the illegal stay of a person in Poland in exchange for financial or personal benefit can be jailed for up to five years.

However, this week, the interior ministry proposed an amendment that would also have penalised anyone who knowingly “enabled or facilitated” the illegal stay of someone in Poland, even if not for financial or personal benefit. The offence would have been punishable by up to three years in prison.

“Currently, this behavior is not criminalised, creating a loophole for those who exploit such situations and, under the pretext of helping migrants, aid them in their illegal stay, thus serving as a springboard for further illegal migration,” wrote deputy interior minister Czesław Mroczek, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily.

That immediately prompted concern that the law could be used against volunteers and residents of border areas who provide aid – such as food, water, medical treatment, clothing or shelter – to migrants who have crossed illegally from Belarus.

Since 2021, tens of thousands of people, mainly from Asia and Africa, have tried to cross that border with the encouragement and support of the Belarusian authorities. They have sometimes used violence against Polish border officers.

Poland and the EU accuse Belarus of “weaponising” migration as part of the “hybrid warfare” being waged by Russia and its allies against European countries. They have implemented tough border protection measures to prevent crossings and facilitate “pushbacks” of those who cross.

However, many human rights and aid organisations argue that the migrants – over 100 of whom have died around the border since 2021 – are often victims of this process and need humanitarian support.

In response to the interior ministry’s proposal, 61 organisations, including Amnesty International, the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights and the Auschwitz-Birkenau Foundation, signed a joint statement condemning the plans, which they said “violate international standards binding Poland”.

The organisations warned that the proposed wording could expose medical staff treating migrants, lawyers providing legal assistance, facilities working with children, and organisations supporting victims of human trafficking to criminal liability.

“This measure is not aimed at smugglers, but rather at activists or residents of border areas who provide humanitarian aid to foreign nationals who have crossed the border illegally and are present in Poland,” attorney Radosław Baszuk told the Rzeczpospolita daily

Baszuk previously represented five Polish activists who were prosecuted for providing food, clothing and shelter to a group of Middle Eastern migrants who had entered Poland from Belarus in 2022.

They were acquitted last year, with the ruling made final in March this year after an appeal. But Baszuk told Rzeczpospolita that, under the interior ministry’s proposed amendment to the relevant law, his clients could been convicted.

On Wednesday, Poland’s commissioner for human rights, Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram, also wrote to the justice ministry to “express concern” that the proposed changes “could lead to criminal liability for charitable or humanitarian activities undertaken towards individuals whose residence status has not yet been regulated”.

Even a member of the government, the minister for family, labour and social policy, Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk, expressed her “firm opposition” to the plans on social media. She is from The Left (Lewica), one of the junior partners in Poland’s ruling coalition.

In response to the growing criticism, the interior ministry announced on Friday that it was withdrawing the proposal, saying it decided to do so “to eliminate any doubts and prevent the misinterpretation of regulations”.

“From the beginning, the ministry’s sole objective has been to tighten the system and target the organisers of this practice [of migrant smuggling],” said the ministry, quoted by Rzeczpospolita.

“Legal provisions must effectively protect the state’s borders against organised crime, while simultaneously fully safeguarding humanitarian values ​and life-saving activities.”

Both the former Polish government and the current one, which took power in December 2023, have regularly faced criticism from human rights groups over their response to the migration crisis on the Belarus border.

Earlier this year, the previous human rights commissioner, Marcin Wiącek, expressed concern over a ban on asylum claims introduced by the government in March 2025. He noted that the measures had been described as a temporary solution, but have remained in place ever since.

The government, however, argues that its measures have been effective in preventing the illegal trafficking of migrants. Its data show that attempted border crossings from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%.

It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally.

title: 'Unsafe' conditions at Texas ICE facility put immigrants at risk of injury or death, lawsuit says
description:
It was the first lawsuit relating to Camp East Montana, and was revealed by the Guardian at the time.
The class-action lawsuit filed against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) accuses the agency of “dire” conditions that severely violated the human and constitutional rights of those at the facility.
The latest severe warnings in the case are included in documents that ask the judge to find Camp East Montana’s conditions unlawful and require improvements, with an independent monitor enforcing compliance.
The move followed three deaths of Camp East Montana detainees in the custody of ICE.
Williams warned in testimony in the filing that “people at Camp East Montana are at risk of serious injury and death at the hands of guards”.
text:
Attorneys and experts are raising the alarm that immigrants at Camp East Montana, the sprawling desert detention camp on the Fort Bliss military base in west Texas, face a risk of serious injury or death because of ongoing, extreme health and safety hazards there, according to a fresh court filing, the Guardian can reveal.

The allegedly dangerous conditions persist at the tent jail, the largest immigration detention facility in the US, despite regular reports from inside and outside the federal government that it has violated dozens of official standards since it opened last year.

One correctional expert, who has run two state prison systems, Dean Williams, said in testimony as part of the new filing that conditions at Camp East Montana “shock the conscience” and were “far beyond those of the most secure prisons I have overseen”, even though it is a civil, not a criminal, detention facility and the vast majority of the men and women held there have no criminal records.

“Poor healthcare and unsafe conditions at Camp East Montana have resulted in preventable death and put all people at risk of harm, including serious injury and death,” said another expert, Jeffrey Keller, a doctor and administrator who has run the healthcare for detention centers in nine states, as part of the filing.

The new documents were filed in federal court in the western district of Texas, El Paso, on Thursday night as part of a lawsuit filed in May.

It was the first lawsuit relating to Camp East Montana, and was revealed by the Guardian at the time. The class-action lawsuit filed against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) accuses the agency of “dire” conditions that severely violated the human and constitutional rights of those at the facility.

The latest severe warnings in the case are included in documents that ask the judge to find Camp East Montana’s conditions unlawful and require improvements, with an independent monitor enforcing compliance.

The lawsuit was filed by the American Civil Liberties Union Foundation, the ACLU Foundation of Texas, the Texas Civil Rights Project, and the law firm Farella Braun + Martel LLP on behalf of detainees.

Their new request is a motion for preliminary injunction and comes as people detained there continue to describe alleged use of force and harassment from guards, lack of appropriate medical care, extremely limited access to hygiene products, exposure to serious contagious illnesses, not enough edible food and other concerns that raise alleged constitutional and statutory issues as well as ethical ones.

“All tell similar stories – of relentless physical and verbal abuse by guards; of going days or weeks without seeing the sun; of filthy, crowded living conditions with repeated outbreaks of measles, tuberculosis and other diseases; and of egregious medical neglect that has resulted in unnecessary suffering and death,” the new court filing says.

One unnamed male detainee is quoted as saying: “I am dying of hunger here. I throw up frequently after eating. I am a skeleton of the person I was before. Any day now, I think I will die here.”

The Trump administration swapped contractors at the privately run ICE facility to Amentum Services, Inc, a Virginia-based company, in March, from a different Virginia-based contractor. The move followed three deaths of Camp East Montana detainees in the custody of ICE.

The court filing on Thursday includes a description of how the daughter of one of those three men saw her father on a video call the day before he died and “[i]t was like he was drowning in his own blood”. His doctor told her that the detention staff “waited until the last minute to take him to the hospital”.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the parent agency of ICE, Amentum and the Pentagon have been approached for comment. The Pentagon referred the Guardian to DHS.

Camp East Montana has received “among the highest number of violations in a single report of any facility” inspected by the government watchdog, the Office of Detention Oversight, according to the non-profit newsroom Pogo Investigates.

And warnings of failing to meet official federal standards and other problems began almost as soon as the facility opened in August 2025 amid the second Trump administration’s crackdown on immigration, with ICE noticing medical service gaps, unsanitary conditions and a lost, loaded firearm, while the Pentagon flagged “at least 22 violations” around food services, safety and hygiene during the operation’s first week, according to the court filing.

Misconduct allegedly runs rampant among guards, who “regularly use unnecessary and excessive force against people”, including against one of the lawsuit’s named plaintiffs, Gerald Akari Angye, who suffered a fractured spine and wrist, attorneys wrote in the court document.

Guards have also allegedly called detainees slurs including “faggot”, “gay” and “fucker”, and in one instance, a guard revealed that a person in custody was HIV positive and then had others vote as to whether that person should be removed from the housing unit, the filing says.

Williams warned in testimony in the filing that “people at Camp East Montana are at risk of serious injury and death at the hands of guards”.

At the same time, people in custody who have sought out healthcare have sometimes allegedly undergone treatment in public hallways or had regular appointments in the middle of the night, when they should have been sleeping – if they received care at all. In one example, “a nurse told someone to harm himself, making him stop asking for help”, according to the attorneys filing the latest accusations.

More than a dozen people reportedly contracted measles in February and March, with hundreds more held in quarantine and isolation for the disease in May and June. Meanwhile, in November, someone with tuberculosis was allegedly housed within the facility’s general population.

The facility is accused of conditions where soap is widely unavailable, so detainees must ration containers of shampoo “the size of single-use ketchup packets, but even then [they] do not have enough to wash their hands after using the bathroom and before eating”, the attorneys alleged.

And without access to nail clippers in the housing units, guards have instead told people they can bite their nails, and, on their toenails, the guards have allegedly been heard to say: “If you can bite them, bite them,” according to the court filing.

“Rain, rocks, mice, and crickets infiltrate the living areas. Toilets clog and overflow and are not timely fixed. The foul smell of urine, feces, and body odor is ever-present,” the attorneys wrote in the latest filing.

They underscored that these conditions “serve no legitimate governmental purpose”.

text:
BROCKPORT, N.Y. — Students and union members gathered at SUNY Brockport on Thursday to support German Machado, a campus employee detained by federal immigration agents earlier this week.

RELATED:

Union leader speaks in support of SUNY Brockport employee detained by ICE

Students want answers after ICE detains SUNY Brockport employee, set to rally Thursday in support of him

News10NBC’s Garrett Chan was on campus for the rally, where participants handed out stickers, papers and signed a poster calling for Machado’s return. Alissa Karl, vice president of academics for United University Professions, said students and employees are worried about Machado’s detention.

“So not just employees, but students are really concerned about a fellow member of this campus who’s got every right to be in this country and work in this country and has been detained for no reason. And we we want him to have due process quickly, and we want him to come back to work and back home with his family,” Karl said.

Karl said the union worked with Machado’s wife to organize the event according to her wishes. The union said Machado had authorization to work in the United States until 2029. However, the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement said having work authorization or a pending application does not mean legal status in the U.S.

“This is part of the creating a climate of fear, right? That folks feel like, you know, even if they have, you know, kind of full status and they’re documented that they can be picked up off of the street. And that’s the opposite of what a higher ed institution like Brockport wants to provide, right? We want people to be secure and safe and, you know, kind of pursue their goals and dreams,” Karl said.

Some students said they did not know Machado personally but felt it was important to support a key member of the campus community. Shaun Victory, a SUNY Brockport student, said Machado’s work was essential.

“Talk to any staff member and any student here on campus, and they’ll tell you about the work that he did was invaluable. I mean, there’s online class, and the entire academic infrastructure is online. So people that do the work that he does are invaluable to the campus life,” Victory said.

Other students said seeing an ICE arrest happen locally made the situation feel more personal. Paix Day, a SUNY Brockport student, shared their perspective.

“I know what it’s like to come from a family of immigrants. So, you know, living my whole life hearing, whether my family was going to be, like, separated or not. It’s heartbreaking seeing members of the community like, being separated from their families, like, you know, left and right,” Day said.

Union members said they have been checking in with Machado’s wife to provide mental and emotional support and to ensure she has legal representation. DHS said Machado legally entered the U.S. in August 2016 and had until February 2017 to stay legally.

The rally concluded with calls for Machado’s return and support for his family as the campus community awaits further information.

description:
New York City successfully shut down the Trump administration’s lawsuit challenging the city’s decades-old policies that limit local law enforcement’s cooperation with federal immigration authorities.
A Brooklyn-based federal judge late Thursday dismissed the White House’s case, filed last year, that argued those policies — collectively known as the sanctuary city law — are unconstitutional and make it harder for federal immigration officers to do their jobs.
The Justice Department said those statutes are preempted by federal law.
A federal judge in Rochester, N.Y., dismissed a similar lawsuit against the Western New York municipality in September.
Direct Regulation The US contends the city’s rejection of congressionally authorized means of enforcing federal immigration law constituted an unlawful direct regulation of the federal government.
text:
New York City successfully shut down the Trump administration’s lawsuit challenging the city’s decades-old policies that limit local law enforcement’s cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

A Brooklyn-based federal judge late Thursday dismissed the White House’s case, filed last year, that argued those policies — collectively known as the sanctuary city law — are unconstitutional and make it harder for federal immigration officers to do their jobs. The Justice Department said those statutes are preempted by federal law.

The government’s preemption arguments “amount to nothing more than a backdoor around the Tenth Amendment,” Judge Ramon E. Reyes Jr. of the US District Court for the Eastern District of New York said in his ruling. That amendment’s anticommandeering doctrine, which prevents federal agencies from compelling state action, precludes relief for the US, the judge added.

Ruling in favor of the US government would allow city agencies and individual employees to decide for themselves whether they comply with state and local law as part of their work, making it impossible for the municipality to control those entities, Reyes said.

That kind of system, he continued, would direct “the expenditure of municipal resources and obviously violate federalism, contravene due process, and foreclose efficiencies available through the implementation of uniform processes.”

The decision adds to a string of losses the Trump administration has faced in its effort to take down similar laws in cities across the country and pave the way for the White House to carry out its deportation plans. A federal judge in Rochester, N.Y., dismissed a similar lawsuit against the Western New York municipality in September.

“This is a victory for New Yorkers and a rebuke to ICE’s deportation agenda,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) said in a press statement. “The federal government came to court seeking to force New York City to turn its public servants into deportation agents and divert our resources toward carrying out ICE’s cruel agenda.”

The city will continue to “use every tool at our disposal to protect New Yorkers from ICE’s abuses,” he said.

The US Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Failing Cases Elsewhere

The law at issue prevents local law enforcement from honoring a civil immigration detainer without a judicial warrant. One provision says that no city agency should use its resources or “subject its officers or employees to the direction and supervision of the secretary of homeland security primarily” for immigration enforcement purposes.

The administration’s July 2025 complaint said those laws violate the federal government’s “well-established, preeminent, and preemptive authority to regulate immigration.” The Justice Department argued the laws should be declared invalid for violating the Supremacy Clause.

New York City over the past several months has filed multiple letters with the court pointing to other sanctuary city suits that have been dismissed across the country, including those in Rochester, Los Angeles, Boston, New Jersey, Minnesota, and Colorado.

Reyes’ ruling cited a Massachusetts federal court’s decision earlier this year that dismissed the White House’s case against Boston. There, Judge Leo T. Sorokin said a court ruling can’t “lessen or alleviate” the federal government’s alleged injuries.

“Other actors, not this Court, hold the authority to grant the United States the redress it seeks,” Reyes said, building on Sorokin’s rationale. The relief the US seeks must come from the state or city legislature or Congress, all of which could enact laws that authorize law enforcement officers to conduct civil immigration arrests, he added.

Direct Regulation

The US contends the city’s rejection of congressionally authorized means of enforcing federal immigration law constituted an unlawful direct regulation of the federal government.

The Second Circuit — which maintains jurisdiction over federal courts in New York, Connecticut, and Vermont — hasn’t defined direct regulation, Reyes said, and he declined “to define the bounds” himself.

The judge concluded that the “challenged provisions cannot be classified as functionally regulating the United States.” Enjoining New York City’s policies “would result in the commandeering of state and local resources,” in violation of the US Constitution, he added.

Reyes also rejected the administration’s argument that it’s been harmed by the city’s policies, which prohibit local law enforcement officers from sharing with immigration officers information about a person who has been in local custody, and from executing an ICE detainer request to maintain custody of a non-citizen for 48 hours without a judicial warrant.

Federal immigration officers must now engage in dangerous efforts to re-arrest immigrants who were previously in local custody, the US said in its complaint.

US law bars local governments from preventing their agencies and officials from disclosing information about a person’s citizenship or immigration status, Reyes said. However, that information isn’t the same as the information the US is seeking about immigrants who have been released from local custody, he explained.

The administration’s assertion that information about custody release is the same as immigration or citizenship status “is contrary to law,” Reyes said.

title: New UW report shows how feds gather WA driver data to make ICE arrests - KUOW
description:
So far this year, UW researchers have documented 356 immigration-related detentions and arrests in Washington state where federal agencies have been provided records by state agencies.
When immigration enforcement makes a vehicle arrest, they use a variety of factors to identify someone to deport, including racial profiling.
When they think they’ve found someone they can arrest, they look up their license plate, accessing non-public records state agencies collect.
The UW report raises questions of transparency when data brokers re-sell driver records to others.
But contracts between ICE and data brokers like LexisNexis, which buys Washington state records, show that ICE is allowed to conduct all their searches of LexiNexis anonymously.
text:
So far this year, UW researchers have documented 356 immigration-related detentions and arrests in Washington state where federal agencies have been provided records by state agencies.

“ Those are just the ones where we were able to confirm it with ‘smoking-gun’ evidence connecting a given plate search to a known immigration arrest,” Angelina Godoy said.

Godoy is the director for the UW Center for Human Rights which recently published a report analyzing four different avenues that immigration enforcement have at their disposal to access driver and vehicle information – in violation of state laws.

State DMV records, like the Washington State Department of Licensing, where state driver and vehicle records are housed

Nlets or the National Law Enforcement Telecommunications Systems, an international public safety information network with nodes throughout all law enforcement, and entryways into state driver data

Data brokers, where states sell their Department of Licensing records to private businesses

Local and state agencies, a potential backchannel for feds attempting to access state records

Researchers analyzed how Washington, New York, Maryland, and Minnesota navigate shoring up priorities outlined in their state laws, so called “sanctuary” laws. They've found each currently has varying gaps in consistency, a result of selective enforcement and other supplemental laws that work to uphold the priorities laid out in each state.

Among the four states UW researchers focused on, Washington was the first to make it easy for undocumented immigrants to get a driver's license through its Department of Licensing.

But now immigration agents are using that same licensing data to arrest undocumented people who have Washington drivers licenses.

Guillermo Rivera is a community organizer who helped UW researchers put together this report showing Washington driver records have been used to make arrests, a practice he said goes directly against state law.

“ Communities are being hurt,” Rivera said, “whole communities all around the Washington state. This is unacceptable. This is inhuman, what is happening.”

He said the children of immigrants who are U.S. citizens have watched their phones in shock as the tracked locations of their parents show them being taken to the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma.

Others, he said, will look for the last location of their parents after not hearing from them, only to find a smashed window of a parent’s work vehicle. People are afraid to go to work, doctors appointments, and participate in daily life, Rivera said.

When immigration enforcement makes a vehicle arrest, they use a variety of factors to identify someone to deport, including racial profiling.

When they think they’ve found someone they can arrest, they look up their license plate, accessing non-public records state agencies collect. It’s a core component of mass deportation efforts that have in some cases ensnared U.S. citizens, and tattered many mixed immigration status communities.

Compared to those other states, Washington doesn’t require a judicial warrant for federal immigration enforcement to access state-held driver and vehicle data. But UW researchers say, given what is happening, the state should require warrants, along with a combination of other requirements.

Requiring judicial warrants is an avenue the Washington governor’s office is considering.

“As far as we know – no state requires judicial warrants for all federal inquiries involving driver data. However, as part of our ongoing effort to protect public safety and limit access to state data for civil immigration enforcement, our team is reviewing what other states have done, and what is lawful, to require judicial warrants for civil immigration-related requests,“ the governor’s office wrote to KUOW.

In so-called “sanctuary” states like Washington, federal immigration enforcement is barred from direct access to Department of Licensing records. The state’s Keep Washington Working Act prohibits state agencies from sharing data for civil immigration enforcement purposes. But federal agencies have found other avenues to access these records, like through Nlets.

“Where you cut off one pathway, you squeeze a balloon, and another bubbles out,” Godoy said.

Tracking this practice, researchers have been able to verify the use of Washington driving information in 356 arrests in 2026.

The National Law Enforcement Telecommunications Systems (Nlets), allows federal law enforcement to request information on a driver from a system Washington state uses called ACCESS, managed by Washington State Patrol. Nearly 20,000 other users across 500 agencies also use this platform, according to the report.

“Nlets allows law enforcement at all levels to query databases, such as a state’s driver and vehicle records, criminal records, and corrections records,” the governor's office wrote in a statement to KUOW.

“My team has worked to limit Customs and Border Protection access for immigration enforcement, while maintaining access necessary to protect public safety… to protect vulnerable Washingtonians,” Gov. Bob Ferguson wrote in the press statement.

It remains unclear the percentage of arrests in Washington using Nlets are of people with civil immigration violations as opposed to criminal charges. But nationwide an estimated 70% of people in immigrant lockup have no criminal history.

Through these systems researchers say federal immigration enforcement will make repeated requests for driver information, linked to a license plate number, until a successful search gets them what they’re looking for, resulting in an immigration arrest. The governor's office said they’ve blocked nearly 2,000 requests for information largely by Customs and Border Patrol, and banned 16 Originating Agency Identifiers because they’re for civil immigration enforcement, and therefore violate state law.

The researchers applaud the banning efforts, but Godoys said it doesn’t compare with the more than 1,000,000 successful searches by immigration enforcement they’ve found. The UW researchers have also found that if one agent’s account is banned, they’ll often switch to another agent to regain access to the system.

This game of whack-a-mole isn’t going to provide a complete resolution to the issue of protecting immigrants who live in sanctuary states, according to researchers.

“That's the reason why in our report we emphasize the need to tackle all four of the pathways,” Godoy said.

The UW report raises questions of transparency when data brokers re-sell driver records to others. Documents show that when these records are re-sold, Washington state requires that they not be allowed to be used for civil immigration enforcement. Private data brokers have their own accountability system to fulfill these requirements. But contracts between ICE and data brokers like LexisNexis, which buys Washington state records, show that ICE is allowed to conduct all their searches of LexiNexis anonymously.

“Such contract agreements hinder the ability of audits to ensure that recipients and subrecipients of DMV data are adhering to permissible use requirements and state laws,” the report says.

There’s also the fourth way researchers have identified that allows immigration enforcement to access drivers’ records, via local and state agencies, such as law enforcement.

“ We know that collaboration still happens,” Godoy said. “We need to envision it and tackle it if we are to cut down on this type of data sharing.”

For Rivera’s part, he wants the governor to act, and soon.

title: In 100th lawsuit against Trump, California challenges immigration arrests near courthouses
description:
California sued the Trump administration for the 100th time in under two years Thursday, challenging the practice of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting people for alleged civil immigration violations at or near state courthouses.
Gen. Xavier Becerra, a current gubernatorial candidate — sued the Trump administration more than 120 times over four years.
Although the lawsuit focused on immigration courthouses, the ruling also covered state criminal courthouses, restoring earlier restrictions that barred civil immigration arrests in or near courthouses except in limited circumstances.
The Trump administration is appealing the ruling.
Since then, California court officials have tracked arrests by federal agents and reported them to the Judicial Council of California.
text:
California sued the Trump administration for the 100th time in under two years Thursday, challenging the practice of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting people for alleged civil immigration violations at or near state courthouses.

California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said such arrests have long been barred because they are unconstitutional and deeply disruptive to the rule of law and the rights of victims, witnesses, defendants and other parties to court proceedings.

"We've seen serious criminal charges dropped and entire cases jeopardized because victims and witnesses are too scared to come to the courthouse to testify," Bonta said. "Our justice system cannot function this way."

Bonta said his office having to take the Trump administration to court 100 times in less than two years, often alongside other Democrat-led states, was a "sobering milestone" and a reflection not of political interference on California's part — as the president and his supporters have cast it — but of Trump's nearly unbridled lawlessness.

"It's very troubling when the most powerful person on the planet and the president of our country is the one trampling over the Constitution, breaking the law so blatantly and brazenly, so consistently, so frequently," Bonta said.

Independent legal experts said several factors have driven the wave of lawsuits.

Read more: With midterms underway, Justice Department presses California to withhold flagged voters' ballots

Presidents from both parties have increasingly flexed their executive power, and state attorneys general have increasingly sued in response. During Trump's first term in office, California — under the leadership of then-Atty. Gen. Xavier Becerra, a current gubernatorial candidate — sued the Trump administration more than 120 times over four years. Texas Atty. Gen. Ken Paxton — now a Republican candidate for Senate — sued the Biden administration just over 100 times in four years.

Trump in this term quickly began implementing an array of policies left over from his first term or outlined in the Project 2025 policy blueprint, many of which Bonta and other Democratic attorneys general were prepared to sue over, experts said.

Trump was also able to appoint a host of loyalists with the help of the Republican-controlled Congress, who helped advance policies that less loyal agency heads would have balked at, and which were sure to draw additional legal challenges, experts said.

Daniel Farber, a professor at UC Berkeley Law School and author of "Contested Ground: How to Understand the Limits of Presidential Power," said California's raft of lawsuits is a result of the current Trump administration "doing more aggressive things right off the starting block" — but also repeatedly targeting California specifically.

Bonta claimed in August that his lawsuits had saved California more than $200 billion, namely by reversing Trump cuts to federal funding meant for the state.

The White House has consistently derided Bonta's litigation against the administration as baseless and misguided. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis on Thursday said Bonta should stop bragging about "filing frivolous lawsuits" and "focus on addressing problems in his own state."

"The reality is, with well over 25 Supreme Court victories, the administration's policies have been consistently upheld as lawful, despite some lower courts issuing an unprecedented number of lawless injunctions," Bis said.

ICE, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment, has defended its arrests near courthouses as a "common sense" approach to apprehending offenders at times and locations where authorities know they will be.

The 100th case

Bonta's lawsuit argues that such arrests are arbitrary and capricious given the chilling effect they have on justice in the state. They violate the Immigration and Nationality Act as intended by Congress, and interfere with California's rights under the 10th Amendment to execute its "core sovereign judicial and police functions," Bonta's office said.

His arguments echo those made by other state officials in the past. During Trump's first term, for example, then-California Supreme Court Chief Justice Tani G. Cantil-Sakauye called the arrests "disruptive, shortsighted and counterproductive."

Arrests at or near courthouses began to rise again after Trump took office in January 2025. An ICE memo, issued in May 2025, said agents could conduct "civil immigration enforcement actions in or near courthouses when they have credible information that leads them to believe the targeted alien(s) is or will be present at a specific location."

Incidents quickly began cropping up. In June 2025, ICE agents arrested two women outside a Los Angeles County courthouse after a hearing in a local criminal case. The same unfolded across the state.

Alejandro Barraza, a criminal defense and immigration attorney, said he has witnessed the effect firsthand.

In October 2025, a client was arrested driving home from a hearing at the Riverside County Hall of Justice. In December, another client was arrested leaving the Rancho Cucamonga courthouse. And a third client chose to plead guilty in his criminal case rather than go to jury trial, despite Barraza's advice that the case was worth fighting, for fear of being arrested by ICE.

"The victims are losing," Barraza said. "Our clients are losing their rights to due process. Everyone is losing."

In June, U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts in San Francisco struck down ICE's expanded courthouse arrest policies nationwide. Although the lawsuit focused on immigration courthouses, the ruling also covered state criminal courthouses, restoring earlier restrictions that barred civil immigration arrests in or near courthouses except in limited circumstances. The Trump administration is appealing the ruling.

Since then, California court officials have tracked arrests by federal agents and reported them to the Judicial Council of California. Thirty people were taken into custody in June, 29 in July, 19 in August and 14 in September.

Read more: California leads lawsuit challenging Trump's rollback of fuel economy rules

State legislators have tried to push back. Last month, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law strengthening California's protections against civil arrests for people traveling to, attending or leaving courthouses for lawful purposes. The measure extends those protections to public ways within 1,000 feet of court facilities, while preserving an exception for arrests made under a valid judicial warrant.

Bonta said his lawsuit is necessary despite the new California law, in part because the Trump administration thinks that "no state law applies to them," and courts have in some cases agreed — including the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, which this week blocked a state law that would have required federal immigration agents to display identification while working in the state.

The wider legal battle

Bonta's office has had substantial success in halting some of the Trump administration's biggest policy moves — including its plans to end birthright citizenship for the U.S.-born children of immigrants, its worldwide tariffs, its deployment of National Guard troops in Los Angeles and other U.S. cities, and its withholding of billions of dollars in federal funding allocated to the state by Congress.

Michael McConnell, director of the Constitutional Law Center at Stanford Law School, said many of California's lawsuits have been "legally meritorious," as there is a "whole lot of legal error" coming out of the Trump administration — with a "lot of the overreach" having been "facilitated by the lack of internal checks" from loyal Trump agency heads.

However, he also said that as a California taxpayer, he doesn't "appreciate having government using my tax dollars for what essentially are in many cases ideological lawsuits, even if meritorious," because private litigants can and often do bring lawsuits of their own. He said he felt the same way about many of the lawsuits brought against the Biden administration by Republican states.

Bonta said he is proud of his team for challenging the Trump administration every time they believed it had broken the law and harmed California, despite Trump's intentional effort to make that difficult.

"It was a shock and awe," he said. "It was flood the zone. It was trying to overwhelm with speed and volume, and we kept pace every time."

What happens next, he said, will depend on Trump. If he keeps breaking the law in ways that hurt the state or its residents, Bonta said he'll keep getting sued by California.

text:
Professor Margaret Satterthwaite ’99, the United Nations special rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, has been selected as a recipient of the 2026 Eleanor Roosevelt Prize for Global Human Rights Advancement. Awarded by the American Bar Association (ABA) Center for Human Rights, the prize honors those whose work has advanced the principles set forth in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which was championed by Eleanor Roosevelt.

In its announcement of the prize, the ABA referred to Satterthwaite’s work as special rapporteur since her appointment by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022. In her reports to the council and to the General Assembly, Satterthwaite has identified emerging threats and issues related to judicial systems across the globe, including improper influence exerted on the judiciary by corporations and wealthy individuals; necessary safeguards to protect judges, lawyers, prosecutors, and community justice workers from intimidation and reprisal; and Indigenous peoples’ right to develop and maintain justice systems.

In her UN role, Satterthwaite has also spoken out against threats in the United States, such as executive branch actions targeting law firms, lawyers, and federal judges, and advocated for withdrawing sanctions on International Criminal Court judges and prosecutors. She collaborated with the special rapporteur on the human rights of migrants in documenting the federal government’s efforts to execute executive policy through US immigration courts.

Satterthwaite will receive the prize during a November 30 ceremony at the New York City Bar Association along with this year’s other recipient, Lawyers for Lawyers, a nonprofit based in the Netherlands. Since its inauguration in 2018, the prize has honored individuals and organizations such as Hillary Rodham Clinton, Dr. Anthony Fauci, Billie Jean King, the American Civil Liberties Union, Amnesty International, the Elton John AIDS Foundation, Human Rights Watch, Lambda Legal, and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund.

At NYU Law, Satterthwaite serves as faculty director of the Center for Human Rights and Global Justice and the Robert and Helen Bernstein Institute for Human Rights. In the Legal Empowerment and Judicial Independence Clinic, she gives her students the opportunity to participate in her work as special rapporteur. Previously, she directed the Global Justice Clinic.

Satterthwaite, the author or co-author of more than a dozen human rights reports and dozens of scholarly articles and book chapters, has focused her recent research on judicial independence, autocratization and the rule of law, legal empowerment, and wellbeing among human rights workers. After graduating from NYU Law, she clerked for Judge Betty Fletcher of the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and the judges of the International Court of Justice. Satterthwaite subsequently worked for human rights organizations including Amnesty International, Human Rights First, and the Commission Nationale de Vérité et de Justice in Haiti before joining the NYU Law faculty in 2006.

title: Trump administration sued over accelerated immigration process for migrant kids
description: (CNN) — A group of attorneys filed a lawsuit Thursday challenging the accelerated immigration process for unaccompanied migrant children, saying the Trump administration’s policies are unlawful.
text:
Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, is defending her legal back…

Ukraine attacked a Russian oil refinery, abandoning a brief truce involving ener…



Migrant children as young as two are showing up at immigration courts nationwide, many without attorneys, to make their case to stay in the US.





(CNN) — A group of attorneys filed a lawsuit Thursday challenging the accelerated immigration process for unaccompanied migrant children, saying the Trump administration’s policies are unlawful.

Under President Donald Trump, unaccompanied migrant children have been increasingly forced to navigate a complicated and accelerated immigration process with dwindling help after the administration ended a long-standing contract for legal services this summer — and as administration officials try to wrap their cases at an unprecedented pace.

“This is not the immigration process that Congress intended for unaccompanied children; it is a deportation assembly line depriving them of their rights,” the lawsuit states. Thursday’s lawsuit was filed by six legal service providers who work with unaccompanied migrant kids.

It focuses on unaccompanied migrant children who are residing with family in the US or are detained, either after recently crossing the US southern border or because their guardians were picked up by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Detained children are held in shelters operated by the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Refugee Resettlement, which is charged with their care.

CNN previously reported that children are contending with a fast-tracked immigration process, including abruptly rescheduled asylum interviews, sometimes with only a 24-hour notice — and increasingly without legal help. Migrant children as young as 2 are also showing up at immigration courts nationwide, many without attorneys, to make their case to stay in the US and avoid deportation.

Like adults, children must also go through immigration proceedings and present evidence to back up their asylum claim, and there’s no requirement for them to have legal representation throughout the process.

According to attorneys, asylum interviews have been abruptly pushed up.

“Since August 1, 2026, Plaintiffs have collectively received more than 600 notices of asylum interviews scheduled to take place in quick succession. Their attorneys are expected to represent children in multiple asylum interviews on the same day, sometimes at the same time, forcing them to forgo preparation and severely limiting their ability to effectively represent their unaccompanied child clients,” the lawsuit states.

“For these children, who risk being sent back to the countries they fled, the stakes could not be higher,” it continues.

The lawsuit calls for a return to the status quo — for example, when children were given at least 21 days notice prior to their asylum interview — and cites a federal law that’s been in place for nearly two decades, the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008, that’s supposed to provide protections for unaccompanied migrant children.

The lawsuit was filed in the US District Court for the District of Maryland.

The Trump administration has previously denied claims that cases are being fast-tracked, arguing that officials prioritize timely completion of cases. And in a statement to CNN last month, an HHS spokesperson said, “ORR will continue facilitating the ability of [unaccompanied alien children] in its custody to fully participate in immigration legal proceedings with representation by counsel, including hearings before EOIR immigration judges, who manage their own juvenile case dockets and schedules and make independent decisions on asylum claims under consideration.”

text:
SAN ANTONIO – Two days after the City of San Antonio sued to block the conversion of an East Side warehouse to a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention and processing facility, councilmembers indicated they want to explore ways to fight the agency moving into leased space at Brooks.

Councilmembers voted 9-2 Thursday approving a resolution to work and coordinate with community stakeholders on efforts to prevent or delay an ICE detention facility in the city’s urban core.

At Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones’ urging, the council first added language asking them to also take similar steps to block or delay the execution of recently reported, 15-year leases at a building at Brooks, which federal records show are linked to ICE and will reportedly be occupied by attorneys and support staff.

“I think we should take the opportunity to also communicate that we — for those of us up here that do — do not support the establishment of such a strong legal footprint. Which would again enable, I think, an even stronger presence and a type of facilitation network that would set up a larger presence here,” Jones said.

A majority of councilmembers have opposed the planned conversion of a 640,000-square-foot warehouse into a processing facility, with a planned daily population of up to 1,500 people.

On Tuesday, the city sued the Department of Homeland Security, ICE, and the heads of both agencies, arguing the government had not done a required environmental review process.

“ICE has gone rogue and at the very least, we must take action to protect all San Antonians from this threat,” Jalen McKee-Rodriguez (D2), who represents the area where the facility is planned, said at Thursday’s meeting.

Councilwoman Phyllis Viagran (D3) had pushed for Thursday’s original resolution, but she opposed the mayor’s amendment, noting “Preston Hollow holds the lease.”

“We cannot come in and say, ‘You, Preston Hollow, can’t lease out to these people.’ So that’s where it gets difficult, and that why I didn’t want to — if legally we can’t do it, I don’t want to vote for what it is,” Viagran said, though she noted she ultimately voted for the amended version.

Federal records show the leases are worth $42.5 million and $9.8 million for a combined $52.3 million.

Notice identification numbers on the documents link back to separate federal records indicating the leases were meant for ICE.

Preston Hollow Community Capital, which has a controlling interest in the WatersEdge office buildings, told KSAT the leases at WatersEdge II building on Inner Circle Drive are for administrative office space.

They said they have no involvement in the East Side detention facility.

“We recognize the community’s concerns about immigration detention facilities and want to be clear about the federal office leases at WatersEdge on the Brooks campus. These leases are for administrative office space and expressly prohibit detention facilities, holding cells, and the processing of individuals or families in custody.

We understand the space will consolidate existing San Antonio-based functions of the Department of Justice’s Executive Office for Immigration Review and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Office of the Principal Legal Advisor. The anticipated occupants are attorneys and support staff."

Preston Hollow Community Capital

The EOIR “conducts immigration court proceedings, appellate reviews, and administrative hearings,” according to its website, while OPLA represents DHS in immigration removal proceedings before the EOIR.

A DHS spokesperson told KSAT in an emailed statement that ICE would not confirm office locations, claiming a “coordinated campaign of violence” against its officers.

“Is it really news that when a federal agency hires more personnel that they need more space?” the emailed statement continues. “Thanks to the Big Beautiful Bill, we have an additional 12,000 ICE officers and agents on the ground across the country. That’s a 120% increase in our workforce.”

San Antonio’s two conservative council members, Misty Spears (D9) and Marc Whyte (D10), voted against Thursday’s resolution and have also opposed the lawsuit.

“This has nothing to do with environmental impacts. I mean, this is all ... fluff and cover and a pretext for wanting to send a certain message to people,” Whyte said.

text:
EL PASO, Texas – Legal organizations filed a motion for preliminary injunction today demanding ICE provide adequate healthcare and improve conditions for people detained at Camp East Montana, the nation’s largest immigration detention facility located on the Fort Bliss military base in El Paso, Texas.

The motion comes as ICE is on track to have its deadliest fiscal year on record, as deaths in detention have nearly doubled since last fall, including three deaths at Camp East Montana alone.

The motion, which was supported by more than 40 declarations from people currently or formerly detained at Camp East Montana, loved ones of people who have died, and correctional and medical experts, describes the government's systemic failure to provide adequate medical care and humane living conditions.

The conditions reported include medical neglect, unsanitary and unsafe conditions, confinement to windowless tents for 23 to 24 hours a day, barriers to legal counsel, and such little food that people experience substantial weight loss and other serious medical conditions. People detained at the facility also describe being physically beaten by guards and confined in extreme isolation as punishment for seeking help.

“The conditions reported in those declarations shock the conscience,” Dean Williams (he/him), a former state prison director who evaluated the conditions in Camp East Montana, wrote in support of the motion. “People describe degrading, unsafe, and unsanitary conditions, abuse by guards, and extreme restrictions and harsh treatment far beyond those of the most secure prisons I have overseen.”

In May of 2026, the American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of Texas, Texas Civil Rights Project, and Farella Braun + Martel LLP filed their lawsuit against ICE after the federal government began detaining thousands of people in a tent encampment on the Fort Bliss military base in the El Paso desert. The facility has repeatedly come under fire since its opening in August 2025 following rampant reports of abusive, inhumane, and deadly conditions.

Quotes from named plaintiffs in the lawsuit are as follows:

“Urgent protection is desperately needed at Camp East Montana,” said named plaintiff Gerald Akari Angye. “Today, people are still being detained in this windowless camp with inadequate food, water, medicine, and recreation. People with health issues do not receive the care they need. This case remains important to me because I am a voice for those harmed by this regime. I will never be the same after the violence I experienced by guards at Camp East Montana. Many others are still being held in those horrible conditions. The United States preaches democracy and human rights, but it is separating families and torturing people who are seeking safety. The world is watching. The inhumane conditions at Camp East Montana seem to be getting worse. No one of good conscience can support what is happening there. I plead with the court to give relief to people held in the horrible Camp East Montana.”

“It’s hard for outside observers to understand what people go through at Camp East Montana,” said named plaintiff Navdeep. “That’s why we are sharing our stories. I don’t want people to continue suffering and experiencing the terrible conditions I experienced there. We need the court to take action to immediately improve conditions at Camp East Montana and to prevent additional suffering.”

“Camp East Montana is not built to accommodate the basic needs of people,” said named plaintiff ZOR. “If the court fails to intervene, things may get even worse. If nothing is done, I worry it will be a signal that it is okay that for the law to continue being ignored at Camp East Montana. I believe the conditions at Camp East Montana are meant to break people down emotionally and to punish them so they become desperate to leave. It is unbearable to be mistreated every day and trapped in a dirty room with up to 72 people. Many of us are only able to endure it because of the strength we get from the thought of our families.”

Additional quotes from co-counsel are as follows:

"The need for court-ordered relief is urgent," said Savannah Kumar (she/they), staff attorney at the ACLU of Texas. “For the past year, the government has disappeared thousands of people into its desert camp that has been the site of beatings by guards, death, disease, and hunger. The situation has continued to deteriorate. People held inside tents describe the denial of desperately needed medical care, environmental hazards, and filthy conditions. These unbearable conditions violate U.S. law and erode the moral fabric of our country. A preliminary injunction is necessary to prevent additional death and abuses at the largest immigration detention camp in the country. All of us, no matter where we were born, are created equal and are entitled to dignity that is being systematically denied at this horrific tent camp.”

“We cannot wait any longer,” said Rita Lomio (she/her), Senior Counsel at the ACLU’s National Prison Project. “ICE and the Department of Defense have long known of the cruel and deadly conditions at the tent encampment on the Fort Bliss military base. They have demonstrated time and again that they cannot or will not act to end the abuse. Former prison and jail directors have found that conditions at Camp East Montana are unprecedented and make all who live and work at the encampment unsafe. While litigation continues, a preliminary injunction is needed to end the most egregious abuses before more people needlessly suffer and die.”

“State-sanctioned violence is occurring in and outside of facilities like Camp East Montana, and the blatant disregard for human life and access to basic health care should shock the conscience of every American,” said Rochelle Garza (she/her), President of the Texas Civil Rights Project. “If we, as a society, say nothing and go along with the notion that certain lives matter less than others, the government’s abuse and neglect will continue to be normalized. Our preliminary injunction is an effort to stop ICE, and the harm that has seeped into the walls of their detention facilities, from going unchecked.”

“Detention does not strip individuals of their fundamental rights to safety, dignity, and necessary medical care,” said Cynthia Castillo (she/her), partner at Farella Braun + Martel LLP. “The record in this case shows deeply troubling medical neglect, dangerous living conditions, and mistreatment that demand immediate action. A preliminary injunction is essential to prevent further irreparable harm and to ensure that individuals detained at Camp East Montana are treated humanely while their legal claims are heard.”
