That rate was even higher among demographics that may be key to the Republican Party’s prospects in November.

The poll, conducted in September, found that 60 percent of independent voters agreed with the idea that Trump’s immigration efforts have overreached. Two-thirds of Hispanic participants also agreed with the campaign having “gone too far”.

Experts say the political debate about immigration in the US has shifted since the last major election in 2024. At the time, the focus was largely on border security. But increasingly, attention has fallen on how enforcement operations are being conducted.

Cynthia Penaloza is among those questioning the Trump administration’s tactics.

In August, her sister, 23-year-old Joceline Penaloza Magana, was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Houston, Texas, during a traffic stop. Joceline remains in custody to this day.

“We’re always afraid. We’re uncertain of what’s going to happen, if she’s going to be sent back to Mexico, if we’re ever going to be together again or how this is going to change our lives forever,” Cynthia told Al Jazeera correspondent Phil Lavelle.

She rejects Trump’s assertion that his administration’s immigration enforcement operations have targeted “the worst of the worst”.

Joceline, according to the Penaloza family, was an honour roll student who does not have a criminal record. She was brought to the US as a young child, about five years old.

“She’s always been a good girl,” Cynthia told Lavelle.

A focus on ‘criminals’

Still, the Trump administration has tied its campaign of mass deportation to efforts to control crime.

In a statement earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees immigration enforcement, credited Trump’s policies with having “unleashed ICE to target the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens, including pedophiles, murderers, gang members, terrorists, and rapists”.

Immigration arrests have been on the rise under Trump. In September, ICE announced it had tallied two consecutive months with more than 50,000 immigration arrests, beating a record set in June, when 43,900 people were detained.

Homeland Security has argued that approximately 70 percent of its immigration detainees are criminals, if pending charges are factored in.

But critics have questioned that statistic, given that the legal system in the US gives suspects the presumption of innocence until they are proven guilty in a court of law.

In other words, many of the accused could be acquitted or see their charges dropped. A large portion of those with criminal charges may also be accused of non-violent crimes.

Analysts have found that a majority of people currently in immigration custody are not considered criminals under the law. According to the Deportation Data Project, which analyses government data sets, some 70 percent of those held in ICE detention have no criminal record.

The Trump administration has nevertheless pushed to increase detentions.

“We need more. We need more arrests, and we need more deportations,” Tom Homan, the White House “border czar”, said in an interview in July.

Pushback on the campaign trail

The aggressive arrest tactics may have repercussions on the Republican campaign for the midterms, though.

Republicans are hoping to defend their majorities in both chambers of Congress, as well as in key state and local elections.

Trump made significant gains in the 2024 elections with Hispanic voters. During his re-election bid, he received nearly 48 percent support among Latinos, according to an exit poll from the Pew Research Center — up 12 percentage points from the 2020 election.

But Pew found that his gains may be eroding. Among the Hispanic voters who supported him in 2024, his approval rating has steadily declined, from a high of 93 percent at the start of 2025 to a low of 57 percent as of last week.

Some Republicans running in the midterm election, including Congress member Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, have even openly criticised the president’s hardline immigration policies.

“Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar said in an advertisement campaign launched in September. She cited the large number of immigrants who were arrested without a criminal record.

Other Republicans, however, blame previous presidencies for creating the conflict over immigration enforcement.

“A mess was created, and now cleaning it up is dirty business,” Jeremy Price, a Republican in Texas, told Al Jazeera. “You’re having to find people, arrest them against their will and remove them from the country because they don’t want to leave.”

Democrats, meanwhile, hope to convert that outrage over immigration enforcement tactics into votes, come November.

“I would hope they’d abolish ICE,” Richard Gonzales, the chair of the Hidalgo County Democratic Party in Texas, said in an interview with Al Jazeera’s Lavelle.

“I mean, in my perspective, I think that they’ve, the agency has just lost its identity, and there’s no way to rehabilitate that.”

text:
State and local governments play a critical role in the detention and deportation machinery. Here's how advocates can make bans on 287(g) agreements more effective and place additional limits on ICE overreach.

by Aleks Kajstura, October 15, 2026

Advocates are getting states to limit the impact of federal immigrant detention policies. By and large, this has involved targeting the 287(g) program, which allows state and local law enforcement to be trained and certified or deputized to carry out immigration enforcement functions for the federal government. However, more work needs to be done to strengthen protections for communities. Progress made in recent legislative sessions shows what works — and what doesn’t — in efforts to curtail local law enforcement cooperation with federal immigration agents.

Banning 287 agreements explicitly is an important tool in an advocate’s toolbox, but can leave many loopholes when treated as a silver bullet.

Banning 287(g) agreements explicitly is an important tool in an advocate’s toolbox, but can leave many loopholes when treated as a silver bullet. That is because much of the collusion with ICE that is undertaken under 287(g) agreements can be performed under other pretenses or even informally.

Instead, advocates should seek to broaden legislation and executive action in order to avoid playing whack-a-mole as ICE tactics shift. This includes going beyond banning 287(g) agreements specifically to include any collusion with state, local, and other law enforcement agencies, or the use of certain infrastructure, to carry out ICE’s civil immigration work. These broader bans target both the letter and the spirit behind 287(g) agreements.

This briefing explains how some states — including Maine, Illinois, and most recently, Massachusetts — pursued broad applicability of their bans on immigration enforcement collaboration, including targeting existing and new agreements, protecting sensitive locations (such as jails, schools, and courthouses), prohibiting housing immigration detainees in their jails, and more. We also examine the crucial role that attorneys general and governors can play in addition to legislating bans on collaboration. While this piece focuses on advocacy at the state level, there are related reforms that advocates can pursue at the city or county level as well.

Ultimately, there is a lot of potential for reform because state governments have indirect control over some federal incarceration. State and local governments control carceral facilities, law enforcement agencies, and a slew of other infrastructure that ICE relies on to conduct federal actions. That gives advocates leverage to oppose the troubling expansion of ICE detention.

Through this guide to recent law changes in several states, we hope to give advocates a roadmap for how to craft successful legislation and executive action in their state that does more than pay lip-service to banning local law enforcement collaboration with ICE, and produces real results.

Commonalities in successful legislation

There are a few provisions that make limits on ICE more effective: making the ban on collaboration applicable to a wide variety of agencies, ensuring that existing agreements are terminated or rendered unenforceable, and prohibiting civil immigration enforcement around sensitive locations, such as schools, courthouses, or hospitals.

Key provisions in recently-passed legislation to limit state and local support for ICE. Key Provisions Maine Illinois Massachusetts Broad definition of law enforcement agencies ✓ ✓ Applies to current agreements ✓ ✓ Prohibits civil immigration enforcement in sensitive locations ✓ ✓

Broad applicability

It is important to ensure that all types of law enforcement are covered so that ICE doesn’t simply go down the list of agencies until they find one that is willing to cooperate.

Legislation is most effective when it broadly defines the law enforcement agencies that it applies to. Each state has a variety of law enforcement agencies, and some may be more obvious than others. ICE already launders requests through multiple agencies to circumvent bans on collusion. Therefore, it is important to ensure that all types of law enforcement are covered so that ICE doesn’t simply go down the list of agencies until they find one that is willing to cooperate. Sufficiently broad legislation is not limited to state governments, but also includes local police departments, private university campus police, and often other government agencies involved in the criminal legal system, such as prosecutors.

For example, here are the definitions from Maine and Massachusetts:

Maine:

“Law enforcement agency” means an agency in the State, including an employee or agent of the agency, charged with enforcement of state, county or municipal laws or with managing custody of detained persons in the State and includes but is not limited to municipal police departments, sheriff’s departments, the State Police, a university or college campus police department, safety department or the equivalent, the Department of Corrections and the Department of Public Safety.

Massachusetts:

“Law enforcement agency”, (i) a state, county, municipal or district law enforcement agency, including, but not limited to: (A) a city, town or district police department; (B) the office of environmental law enforcement; (C) the University of Massachusetts police department; (D) the department of the state police; (E) the Massachusetts Port Authority police department, also known as the Port of Boston Authority police department; and (F) the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority police department; (ii) a sheriff’s department in its performance of police duties and functions; (iii) a public or private college, university or other educational institution or hospital police department; (iv) a federal law enforcement agency; or (v) a humane society police department.

The bar on types of collusion needs to be equally broad. Although New Jersey passed otherwise-broad bills, one of the new statutes contained carveouts for anyone charged with any one of a long list of offenses. Simply charging someone with one of these crimes — no conviction necessary — is enough to exempt law enforcement from the ban on information sharing. As a result, police and prosecutors can easily identify loopholes for collusion that are large enough to nullify the new protections against ICE.

Similarly, the bans need to address not only 287(g) agreements specifically, but any actions typically taken under such agreements. Maine’s legislation is a good example of this; it functionally bans 287(g) agreements, but does so by prohibiting a broad range of activities or use of public funds for immigration enforcement. That approach bans many kinds of activities beyond those that would fall under a 287(g) agreement. As a result, law enforcement is prohibited from engaging in even informal collusion. In contrast, banning the agreements by name unnecessarily narrows the reforms that advocates seek.

Prohibiting new agreements while nullifying existing ones

Many agencies (covering 77.2 million people or 32% of the country) have existing 287(g) agreements already in place, so it’s not enough to only ban agencies from entering into new agreements. Ideally, agreements already in place should be nullified immediately, but at the very least legislation should impose a tight deadline for termination.

Agreements already in place should be nullified immediately, but at the very least legislation should impose a tight deadline for termination.

Over the objections of advocates, Massachusetts’ anti-ICE collaboration law grandfathered in agreements between ICE and Massachusetts’ prisons, while banning collaboration from jails and other law enforcement agencies. When grandfathering in the Department of Corrections’ agreement, legislators argued that allowing some collaboration might deter ICE from conducting as many community sweeps. However, our recent analysis of ICE arrest data shows collaboration has not been a deterrent at all: states like New Jersey, which have tried to compromise between protections and collusion, ended up having arrest rates comparable to that of enthusiastic collaborators like Georgia. Conversely, states that refused ICE collaboration have suppressed arrest rates.

Protecting certain locations

It’s important that everyone feels they can safely go to school, attend their court dates, and seek medical attention. These are all activities that benefit not only the individual but the community and society at large. However, ICE sweeps and targeted actions at such locations undermine public safety — a fact that used to guide federal policy prohibiting ICE enforcement in these places.

In order to restore public trust in important social institutions, many states bar immigration enforcement in and around “sensitive locations,” such as courthouses, schools, or hospitals. Advocates should take full advantage of states’ jurisdiction over public spaces in order to impose some geographic limits on ICE. Restoring these common-sense limits on ICE offers an additional layer of protection that advocates fighting to limit ICE encroachment to communities should seek to add.

Restricting access to detention infrastructure

Preventing ICE from using state and local lockups to house detained immigrants is another crucial way to slow down the mass deportation machine. Even though ICE has a multibillion-dollar budget rivaling that of most nations’ militaries, they nonetheless lack a nationwide network of detention centers and jailers.

In addition to renting bed space to ICE, state and local facilities voluntarily hold people who are already in police custody until ICE can come take them. As detailed in our recent briefing on ICE arrest data, the average number of daily detainer-related arrests more than doubled since the last presidential administration, growing by 144% from 2024 to 2026. Fortunately, state and local governments have the power to put a stop to this practice, known as “detainers.”

Our analysis found that since 2025, states that prevented local law enforcement from complying with detainers saw fewer ICE arrests overall. For example, in Oregon, only a small number of ICE arrests involved law enforcement, and the rare detainer arrest was usually connected to the U.S. Marshals or Federal Bureau of Prison facilities.1

States can strengthen these protections further by not just banning collaboration with ICE, but with other federal law enforcement agencies that have been deputized into the mass deportation agenda. ICE uses other federal agencies as stand-ins to circumvent facility bans on ICE detainees. Under this strategy, ICE and other federal agencies refer people for federal prosecution for immigration-related “crimes,”2 moving them into the custody of the U.S. Marshals and thus enabling them to use contracted local jails where ICE itself is prohibited from doing so. Once those people are finished with their sentence or the prosecution is dropped, they are brought back into ICE custody. While no state law can prevent federal agencies from working together, states can prevent federal agencies from using local jails in their chain of custody.

Advocating for reform through the executive branch

Advocates should look beyond legislative reforms and push for action in the executive branch as well. Governors and attorneys general can play an effective role in curbing ICE overreach. Although narrower in scope, executive action is a good alternative if legislation is unattainable. Executive action can also move faster and is therefore useful as a stopgap measure until legislation is passed.

Attorneys General

Attorneys general are states’ top lawyers. An attorney general provides guidance to agencies tasked with implementing laws in a legal landscape that is constantly shifting in response to evolving ICE tactics. Attorneys general can therefore be a key force in curtailing ICE collaboration even without legislation.

Although narrower in scope, executive action is a good alternative if legislation is unattainable.

Sometimes state laws unrelated to immigration already prohibit 287(g) agreements, and attorneys general serve an important role in highlighting their applicability for state and local police who attempt to work with ICE in ways that are inconsistent with state law. The Maryland attorney general explained the risks of constitutional violations when collaborating with ICE and highlighted ICE tactics designed to fool local law enforcement into unwitting collaboration, pointing out, for example, ICE’s habit of labeling someone as a “fugitive” even when the person is not wanted for any crime. Although the state now has legislation that explicitly bans collusion with ICE, this part of the guidance predates the recent legislative reforms in the state.

Beyond risking constitutional violations, collaboration with ICE can have mundane legal consequences, too. When local police collaborate with ICE, even insurance companies are wary of covering the increased liabilities.

Local governments rely on attorney general guidance, so attorney general involvement can have a big impact on local action. Therefore, it’s important that advocates not overlook their role in guiding local agency behavior — for better or worse. South Carolina exemplifies the impact that an attorney general can have; that state’s attorney general encouragedparticipation in ICE agreements, resulting in a jump from 3 to 15 agreements in just a few months.

Governors

Executive orders, such as those issued by governors in Virginia and Massachusetts (pre-dating the recent legislation in those states), can take the place of legislation in a pinch, but are narrowly applicable. Executive orders can only directly address things under the control of the executive branch of the state, such as state police and state-owned lands; that means city and county agencies are often out of reach of a governor’s unilateral actions.

Executive orders can also be used to ensure that the laws passed by the legislature are effective. For example, the Illinois governor issued an order creating an accountability commission tasked with documenting ICE activity in the wake of legislative reforms in order to identify any further changes needed to curb federal overreach.

Conclusion

ICE is taking advantage of state and local resources to fuel the federal crimmigration agenda. But advocates can harness states’ power to limit ICE’s overreach and keep incarceration policies under state and local control. While there are many approaches, advocates should strive for broad legislation to stop ICE from exploiting common loopholes. Advocating for legislation while simultaneously seeking gubernatorial and attorney general action leads to the quickest and most comprehensive results, putting the brakes on ICE as quickly and effectively as possible.

As the elections approaches and the House of Representatives prepares for the 120th Congress, the resolution calls on the House of Representatives to pass real protections for immigrant communities.
“We need an immigration system that gives people a fair chance.
It’s time to expand pathways to citizenship and ensure all working families can live and work with dignity and safety.
But we have resisted, organized, advocated, and continue doing the work to prepare families for citizenship and help them navigate the immigration system.
Background: 40 years ago, Congress passed the Immigration Reform and Control Act, creating a pathway to citizenship for approximately 2.7 million immigrants.
text:
Chicago, IL – Today, Congresswoman Delia C. Ramirez (IL-03), Ranking Member of a Committee on Homeland Security Subcommittee, immigration advocates, and community members unveiled the People’s Vision for Immigration Reform, a resolution outlining policy priorities to preserve and expand pathways to citizenship. As the elections approaches and the House of Representatives prepares for the 120th Congress, the resolution calls on the House of Representatives to pass real protections for immigrant communities.

The resolution calls on Congress to transform our immigration system and advance humane immigration reform with:

Pathways to citizenship for the millions of undocumented, long-term residents of the United States who are our family members, friends and neighbors;

Humanitarian protections that welcome with dignity those who are seeking safety and asylum in the United States, upholding our domestic and international legal obligations to provide refuge to those in need; and

Expanded legal pathways for family and employment immigration, recognizing that family unity and strengthened protections for all workers in the United States are foundations of thriving communities for all.

“For years, administration after administration, Congress after Congress, has promised relief and has asked our communities to wait for the ‘right time,’ for the ‘politically convenient time,’” said Congresswoman Ramirez. “So today, we announced the People’s Vision for Immigration Reform – a resolution that reaffirms the commitment of Members of Congress to act in defense of our immigrant communities and preserve and expand pathways to citizenship. Now is the time to build a system that honors the contributions of our immigrant neighbors. No more excuses or peros.”

The resolution’s original cosponsors include Representatives Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), Jesus “Chuy” Garcia (IL-04), Lateefah Simon (CA-12), Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC-00), Yvette D. Clarke (NY-09), Analilia Mejia (NJ-11), Jasmine Crockett (TX-30), Maxine Dexter (OR-03), Sylvia R. Garcia (TX-29), Maxwell Frost (FL-10), Federica S. Wilson (FL-24), Jan Schakowsky (IL-09), Jonathan Jackson (IL-01), Melanie Stansbury (NM-01), Yassamin Ansari (AZ-03), Emily Randall (WA-06), Judy Chu (CA-28), Adelita S. Grijalva (AZ-07), and Al Green (TX-09).

“Immigrants have bound our communities together, continue to contribute to our economy, and embody everything that Americans are made of and striving to be. All of which they do while asking nothing in return but the opportunity to reach for and obtain the American Dream,” said Congresswoman Yvette Clarke. “The 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States must not be only the opportunity to reflect on how far we have come; it must be an obligation to remember the terrible price that we pay to reach here. The People’s Vision for Immigration Reform is in large part the only future for this nation worth fighting for.”

“It’s time to send out a strong vision of where we need to be. We have spent an awful lot of time in Washington talking about immigration enforcement this year, but not nearly enough time talking about how we fix the system that has been broken for decades,” said Congresswoman Sylvia Garcia. “We need an immigration system that gives people a fair chance. We can start by making progress now. That’s why I’m leading the discharge petition of the American Dream and Promise Act; we are just one signature away from getting a forced vote. We need to get serious about real reform, not another round of empty promises.”

The bill is endorsed by a coalition of more than 60 national and and local organizations, including Immigration Law Center (NILC), Fair Immigration Reform Movement (FIRM) and FIRM Action, National Immigrant Justice Center (NIJC), League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), Haitian Bridge Alliance, United We Dream (UWD), Refugees International, National Partnership for New Americans (NPNA), Immigrant Legal Resource Center (ILRC), Center for Law and Social Policy (CLASP), Human Rights First, Bend the Arc: Jewish Action, Justice in Motion, Indivisible, Service Employees International Union (SEIU), National Health Care for the Homeless Council, United Parent Leaders Action Network (UPLAN), Children's Rights, Unitarian Universalists for Social Justice, Community Change Action, Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights (ICIRR) and ICIRR Action, CAIR Chicago, Grassroots Collaborative, Warehouse Workers for Justice, National Korean American Service and Education Consortium (NAKASEC), Indivisible Chicago Alliance, Hana Center, Here to Stay Community Land Trust, Illinois Unidos, PASO, Organized Communities Against Deportation (OCAD), Massachusetts Immigrant and Refugee Advocacy Coalition, Jewish Council on Urban Affairs (JCUA), Colorado Immigrant Rights Coalition (CIRC), Popular Democracy, Florida Immigrant Coalition (FLIC), SIREN, Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, Maine People's Alliance, We are CASA, Workers Defense Action Fund, Make the Road States, Voces de la Frontera, Make the Road New York, Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA), Council of Mexican Federations in North America (COFEM), Sunflower Community Action, East Bay Sanctuary Covenant (EBSC), Federación de Clubes Michoacanos en Illinois (FEDECMI), Nebraska Appleseed, and Pineros Y Campesinos Unidos Del Noroeste (PCUN).

“Over the last 40 years we’ve seen the consequences, not only the inability of Congress to prioritize legislation, but of the overreach of the Trump administration that has taken a sledgehammer to refugee admissions, temporary protected status, health care and food access and the basic simple notion that all people in this country deserve due process under the law,” said Lawrence Benito, ICIRR Executive Director. “We know we need permanent solutions, not chaos and fear. We’re here today to recommit to dignity and respect for all through legalization and keeping families together.”

“Let me be clear: Our economy works because of workers, and for generations, immigrant workers have poured their sweat, their strength, and their labor into building this country. Working families deserve to go to work, provide for their families, and return home safely without fear of being detained or disappeared,” Laura Garza, Executive Director at Arise Chicago. “Now is the time to demand real protections for communities. It’s time to expand pathways to citizenship and ensure all working families can live and work with dignity and safety. As communities mobilize across the country, we stand together in our power to change our country’s direction.”

“Immigrants deserve a system that provides dignity, fairness, and a real opportunity for a life in this country. Congress must do its job to defend our neighbors by creating viable pathways. Otherwise, the executive branch will be able to continue to sow chaos in our communities, return refugees to danger, and trample our Constitution,” said Keren Zwick, Executive Director at the National Immigrant Justice Center (NIJC). “NIJC stands ready to advance lasting solutions, even as we continue to fight the problems this administration created.”

“At PASO, we see the resilience of our communities, but resilience should never mean having to live in fear. Instead of being supported, our communities are increasingly being targeted because of their immigration status. But we have resisted, organized, advocated, and continue doing the work to prepare families for citizenship and help them navigate the immigration system. We have done our part, and now the federal government must do theirs. Because the truth is, no matter how much we prepare our communities, if the federal government fails to create real pathways to citizenship, our families will continue to face barriers,” Marien Casillas Pabellon, PASO Executive Director.

“While ICE and DHS terrorize our communities and attack and deport our neighbors, Congress has not acted. While most Americans support creating and ensuring legal pathways to citizenship for immigrants, Congress has done nothing. Their silence enables this administration's campaign of terror against immigrants and their families. Today, as voters, we must demand that our elected representatives take action to create pathways to citizenship and legal status and protect immigrants and their families from abuse by our government,” said Kathy Tholin with Indivisible Chicago.

“Asians are the fastest-growing racial group in the US, and 1 out of 7 undocumented immigrants is Asian. We are longstanding generations, mixed-status families, and new Americans who call this country home. We are all affected by the militarized violence, immigration backlogs, unaffordable costs, and attacks by this President and some Congress members against anyone they think doesn’t belong,” said Danae Kovac, HANA Center Executive Director. “Immigration affects all of us, and let me be clear: our country needs pathways to citizenship. HANA Center will continue to fight alongside Congresswoman Ramirez for Citizenship for All, not only for a pathway to citizenship, but also for the healthcare, education, climate justice, and more that we all need and deserve. Together, we, the people, can create an America where every person belongs and thrives.”

“It is long past time to lift up families and embrace the worth of each of our neighbors. It is time to reject the politics of fear and division that have marked too much of the discussion around immigration in recent years,” said Ed Yohnka, ACLU Illinois Director of Communications and Public Policy. “In recent months, we have seen how years of rhetoric meant to stall meaningful immigration reform can be turned to justify a military-style invasion of our communities and cause too many hard-working people to live in fear and isolation. Immigration policy does not have to be this way. Immigration policy can be based on a commitment to family unification, a commitment to fairness and due process, and a recognition of the dignity and worth that people from other countries and other cultures bring to the United States.

“As a recently naturalized citizen, I have a message to those like me who can now exercise that power. The power of our vote. Let’s show our humanity in how we treat our neighbors, but also let’s show solidarity at the ballot box,” Fasika Alem, United African Organization (UAO) Programs Director. “Elections matter. Make a plan and vote.”

“Our church is home to Indigenous people and to immigrants, old and new. People without documents worship in our assemblies and lead our ministries. Scripture commands: ‘Love the stranger as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.’ For decades, our church has urged compassionate ways for longtime undocumented neighbors to gain legal status,” said Bishop Erik Christensen of the Metropolitan Chicago Synod of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America. “Forty years ago, Congress opened a path to citizenship and those who received status in time became citizens, homeowners, and neighbors. Now is the time to finish that work.

"As a Haitian immigrant, experiencing the agonizing pain and fear of the Haitian community every day who have lost TPS, I particularly welcome the resolution, because it brings to light all the changes needed in our immigration system to ensure the safety of our immigrant friends and family members who are here and deserve justice and dignity,” said Tessa Petit, Florida Immigrant Coalition Executive Director and Co-Chair of FIRM. “It is time for immigrants to no longer be treated as political pawns and sub-creatures, and this resolution will engage Congress to put an end to the abuse of our communities.”

“1 of every 4 ICE arrests happen in Texas. In just over three months, ICE shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, shot Wilber Rafael Garces Perez in Austin, hospitalized Miguel Parra-Hernandez after striking him with an ICE vehicle in Houston, and has separated countless of families,” said Lizeth Chacon, Workers Defense Executive Director. “Immigrant workers and their families strengthen and build our state – Texas is their home, and for many it has been for more than 30 years. It's time for Congress to act, for there to be an end to ICE violence and a real pathway to citizenship for all immigrant workers and their families.”

“For 25 years, my mother and I were both undocumented. We were able to adjust to legal permanent residency because we qualified for a U visa, something that only undocumented immigrants who are victims of a violent crime could apply for. There are over 12 million undocumented immigrants in the United States who have no pathway to citizenship and I sure wish not a single one ever needs to apply to a U visa,” said Jose-Arnulfo Cabrera, National Campaigns and Congressional Affairs Deputy Director, Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA). “But that is how broken our immigration system is and why Congresswoman Ramirez’s resolution is quite important today.”

The violence of the Department of Homeland Security under the Trump administration has only served to underscore citizenship's importance. Last week, a five year old child had to watch his father get shot by agents of our government. He is only the latest child to be failed by the unimageable cruelty of the DHS's at-all-costs approach to mass deportations,” said Ben D’Avanzo, National Immigration Law Center. “But he was also failed by our completely broken immigration system that has allowed families to go without health care, be abused by their employers, and stripped of longtime protections. This resolution represents the right pathway, one that upholds our core values and refuses to pit immigrant communities against each other.”

“LULAC is proud to support Congresswoman Ramirez’s resolution to protect immigrant families, defend workers, and create pathways to citizenship. As America celebrates 250 years of independence, we should remember who helped build this country,” said Dr. Ray Serrano, National Director of Research & Policy, League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC). “Congress needs to act. Keep families together. Protect workers. Give people a fair chance at citizenship. Our families helped build this country. We deserve a place in its future.”

text:
California is seeking to block the Trump administration’s practice of making immigration arrests in and around state courthouses with a new lawsuit alleging arrests have continued after a federal court order.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued U.S. Department of Homeland Security Thursday, saying that the Trump administration’s unlawful decision to arrest immigrants near California courthouses “systematically made our communities less safe.”

A directive launched in May 2025 allowed US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to make arrests in or near courthouses when they have credible information that a “targeted alien” will be present, according to the lawsuit. Previous memos from the administration offered more guardrails to federal agents, the lawsuit said.

More than a year later, a Northern District of California court vacated the immigration arrest policy, but that didn’t stop the federal government from conducting enforcement activities at state courthouses, the lawsuit said. Despite the court order, there were 60 civil immigration arrests at superior courts around the state, according to the lawsuit.

The practice keeps people from going to court without the threat of an immigration arrest, the lawsuit said.

“Even if they do not effectuate a civil arrest, officers have a regular presence inside or near courthouses and have been spotted searching for individuals to arrest in hallways, security lines, courtrooms, and other areas where people perform their court business,” the lawsuit said.

The case, filed in the US District Court for the Central District of California, asks the court to prohibit agents from conducting civil immigration arrests at California courts in addition to deeming the policy of making arrests around state courthouses a violation of federal law.

Immigration enforcement carried out at state courthouses violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the Tenth Amendment right for states to self govern powers that aren’t delegated by the US Constitution, the lawsuit alleged.

DHS didn’t immediately responded to a request for comment.

title: Challengers ask court to pause agreement between Texas and the DOJ on deportation proceedings
description:
In 2026, Texas filed a lawsuit in the Wichita Falls division of the Northern District of Texas, where it alleged that the EOIR does not have the power to adopt the administrative-closure rule.
The case was assigned to the only federal judge in that division, Chief U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor.
Within hours after the case was filed, the U.S. Department of Justice and Texas filed a motion to have O’Connor enter a final judgment in the state’s favor.
O’Connor denied their request on the ground that they lacked a legal right to sue, known as standing.
In particular, he rejected the cities’ contention that the elimination of the rule would cost them money because their taxpayers are likely to be deported.
text:
Three cities and a group that provides legal services to immigrants came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to pause an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice that they described as the product of “egregious collusion.” A ruling in the challengers’ favor would temporarily restore a Biden-era regulation, adopted through notice-and-comment rulemaking, that allows immigration judges to suspend some deportation proceedings – when, for example, a crime victim or witness is seeking immigration relief, such as asylum – while the challengers’ appeal in the lower federal courts is ongoing.

The Executive Office for Immigration Review, which is part of the Department of Justice, adopted the regulation at the center of the dispute, which provides what is known as “administrative closure,” in 2024.

In 2026, Texas filed a lawsuit in the Wichita Falls division of the Northern District of Texas, where it alleged that the EOIR does not have the power to adopt the administrative-closure rule. The case was assigned to the only federal judge in that division, Chief U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor.

Within hours after the case was filed, the U.S. Department of Justice and Texas filed a motion to have O’Connor enter a final judgment in the state’s favor. The federal government also asked O’Connor both to throw out the rule altogether and to issue an order making clear that the EOIR could not adopt a similar rule in the future. O’Connor granted those requests.

Three cities with substantial immigrant populations – Baltimore, Maryland; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio – sought to join the case to defend the administrative-closure rule on appeal, along with Centro Legal de la Raza, which provides legal services to immigrants. O’Connor denied their request on the ground that they lacked a legal right to sue, known as standing. In particular, he rejected the cities’ contention that the elimination of the rule would cost them money because their taxpayers are likely to be deported.

After the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit turned down their request to block the consent judgment between Texas and the Department of Justice and thereby reinstate the administrative-closure rule while their appeal continued, the challengers came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to intervene.

Lawyer Joshua Salzman of Democracy Forward, representing the challengers, called the consent judgment “indefensible.” “If a judgment procured through such open collusion is allowed to remain in effect,” he wrote, “any agency can avoid the strictures of the” federal law governing administrative agencies “by advertising its unwillingness to defend a disfavored regulation and by immediately acquiescing to nationwide relief.”

description:

text:
A federal judge ordered the Department of State to open the 2027 Diversity Visa lottery. The Trump administration failed to begin registration for the green card program on schedule per immigration policy. U.S. District Judge Ohta granted a preliminary injunction on October 14, 2026. Further, Ohta is requiring the State Department establishe a registration period for the fiscal year 2027 program. This ruling allows all prospective applicants to enter the green card Diversity Visa lottery. The State Department is required to continually process entries until all 55,000 visas are issued or until the 2027 fiscal year comes to an end.

Ohta ordered the department to publicly announce and open the registration period by midnight Eastern time on Thursday, October 15, 2026, according to Curtis Morrison, an attorney representing Red Eagle Law L.C., who brought the lawsuit. The registration period must last a minimum of 30 days. A spokesperson for the State Department claimed that the Department of State delayed the registration period in order to put American interests first. They also added that the department prefers not to comment on pending or ongoing litigation.

The Trump administration has openly opposed the Diversity Visa program. They argued that their failure to open the 2027 lottery before the end of the previous fiscal year was due to conflicts with regulations which govern the program’s timing. Red Eagle Law then sued Secretary of State Marco Rubio, challenging these claims under the Administrative Procedure Act. The firm argued the delay caused financial harm to them. The firm relies on work representing Diversity Visa applicants. These applicants did not functionally exist due to the fact that the program ended alongside the previous fiscal year without allowing new applicants. This caused financial losses to the firm they would be unable to recover.

Ohta concluded that the failure to open registration effectively suspended the program without sufficient explanation. The government argued that reopening the lottery after having missed the standard registration timetable would conflict with a federal rule requiring the registration period to last 30 days. Red Eagle argued that missing the registration timetable should not prevent the court from ordering the State Department to administer the program, regardless. Ohta rejected the government’s argument.

The judge also found that Red Eagle’s statement had standing. The firm’s economic losses could cause irreparable harm and be irrecoverable. This marks a reversal from an earlier stage of the case. Red Eagle’s request for a temporary restraining order that would have forced the department to open registration immediately was denied without prejudice by Ohta. Under the new injunction, that process must now begin for the 2027 program. The court will retain jurisdiction over implementation of the order.

text:
Oscar Belgal, the New York man shot by federal immigration officers last week, appeared remotely in immigration court Thursday.

His lawyers say he still needs surgery to remove a bullet lodged in the back of his neck. Federal officials previously described his injury as “superficial,” saying he was hit by a bullet or fragment.

Belgal, 28, a native of the Dominican Republic, barely spoke during the brief hearing, according to the Associated Press. His injury wasn’t visible on the video feed as he appeared from the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, where his lawyers say he is being held in solitary confinement.

Karene Brown of the Legal Aid Society told Judge Dara Reid that Belgal has been on 24-hour lockdown without access to a phone to speak with his family. Brown said she had asked ICE to move him out of solitary confinement, but the agency had not honored the request. Reid said she had no say in where he is housed within the facility.

In a court filing obtained by ABC News, Belgal’s lawyers also said he has received only ibuprofen for pain. They said the left side of his face remains numb and that he has difficulty hearing in his left ear.

Belgal tried to speak to the judge about his living conditions, but his lawyer advised him not to and cut him off, the Associated Press reported.

Belgal was shot on Oct. 8 while in his car with his 5-year-old son. His lawyers allege that masked officers in civilian clothes approached the vehicle without identifying themselves, smashed a window and fired as Belgal tried to drive away.

The Department of Homeland Security said the officers believed their lives were in danger and fired after Belgal hit two government vehicles and accelerated toward them. NYPD body-camera footage shows officers arriving moments after the shooting.

Belgal’s lawyers filed a federal petition seeking his release. On Wednesday, a federal judge ordered the administration to explain why he should remain in custody and temporarily barred his deportation. His next immigration court hearing is scheduled for Oct. 29.

title: Inside ICE, Officials Question String of Trump Admin “Midterm Panic Moves” - The Intercept

Days later, on the weekend of September 25, ICE leadership quietly issued internal orders for a major change that would overhaul nationwide immigration enforcement.
After news of the orders broke in the right-wing Daily Wire, the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, denied the story.

text:
After agents with Homeland Security Investigations, a division of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Monday morning, officials who spoke to The Intercept raised questions about whether the raid was political in nature.

Though the investigation into Omar has reportedly been ongoing for years, an ICE official working in immigration enforcement suggested the timing of the raid raised questions.

“She’s always been a thorn in the side of the Trump administration,” said the ICE official, who spoke to The Intercept on the condition of anonymity to protect their livelihood. “This has to be politically motivated.”

The raid is the latest of what several officials inside ICE told The Intercept were a series of moves — policy changes, sweeping initiatives, and, in Omar’s case, a specific operation — that reflect a scramble to help lift Republicans’ dimming prospects in November’s midterm elections.

In the last month, ICE has undertaken steps like removing vehicle stop training, announcing surges into sanctuary cities, and freezing then quickly unfreezing non-criminal deportations — what one official called a “midterm panic move.”

According to analysts, these politically charged moves are rapidly degrading the reputation of law enforcement agencies among many Americans.

“Throughout the Trump administration, we have seen them use law enforcement for overtly political purposes, often directly targeting blue states or blue politicians for their actions” said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a policy analyst and senior fellow at the American Immigration Council. “This is something that has really been a significant challenge for the reputation of law enforcement, because we have seen so many issues along these lines where there are allegations of these overtly political actions.”

Reporting had linked the raid on Omar’s home immigration paperwork — she arrived in the U.S. as a refugee in 1995 and naturalized five years later — but a second ICE official familiar with the matter questioned that explanation.

“There is something more than that, there have to be other charges for the substantiation of the warrant because a judge wouldn’t sign something beyond statute of limitations,” said the official, who is with Homeland Security Investigations, the arm of ICE that carried out the raid, who also spoke to The Intercept on the condition of anonymity.

An article in the New York Post suggested the investigation might be related to an effort by Omar in 2019, just after she arrived in Congress, to correct her birth year in a Minnesota state legislature library.

The statute of limitations for crimes related to citizenship, according to a Justice Department website, is 10 years. Civil denaturalization proceedings do not have a statute of limitations, but must meet certain conditions, according to Reichlin-Melnick.

“In order to subject someone to civil denaturalization,” Reichlin-Melnick said, “the government has must prove either that the person committed fraud or that they were ineligible for naturalization in the first place.”

“A Waste of Time”

According to accounts from inside ICE, the moves, allegedly motivated by the midterms, are creating chaos and confusion inside the agency — and fostering resentment among employees.

“We are highly trained agents who should be working child exploitation and trafficking cases, instead we are being used as pawns in our administration’s games,” said the Homeland Security Investigations official, touching on a shift away from the ICE branch’s traditional areas of focus. “I think everything happening with the agency right now is related to the midterms and to stoke divisive fires.”

Politically motivated operations started ramping up inside Homeland Security Investigations after federal agents were ordered to pursue a criminal voter fraud probe across nine states in early September, according to the first ICE official.

“The voter fraud initiative was just inefficient and ridiculous,” the official said. “Knocking on doors to question people about voting before you even have evidence to present to them is a non-starter.”

The official added, “Directing your entire workforce to do that for weeks instead of real criminal investigations is a waste of time.”

“It Backfired”

With the midterms themselves approaching, fresh controversies engulfed ICE, prompting the administration to react with a string of messy policy changes and public announcements.

As the voter fraud investigations were underway, public backlash erupted after immigration officers from ICE’s other division, Enforcement and Removal Operations, or ERO, shot and wounded a 28-year-old Venezuelan man during a traffic stop in Austin, Texas, on September 20.

Days later, on the weekend of September 25, ICE leadership quietly issued internal orders for a major change that would overhaul nationwide immigration enforcement. The orders directed all deportation officers to stop arresting undocumented immigrants without criminal histories. After news of the orders broke in the right-wing Daily Wire, the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, denied the story.

Despite the denial, ICE officials operating across the country told The Intercept that the orders were legitimate and stayed in place for nearly a week.

“We reverted back to Biden-era enforcement,” said one official with Enforcement and Removal Operations, who was ordered to stop all arrest of non-criminal immigrants, including those who had standing deportation orders from immigration judges. “The DHS denied it but the orders stayed in place for 4-5 days and we followed them.”

Another deportation officer, who also asked for anonymity, described the orders as a “midterm panic move” in response to the ICE shooting in Austin.

“Our FODS” — field office directors — “told us through our team group chats and word-of-mouth to keep it out of the press, it was never in writing. I think leadership wanted to dial things back after the Austin shooting, but the orders got leaked and it backfired.”

On the same day as the leak and denial, the Department of Homeland Security seemed to take a harder public line by announcing a “nationwide public safety surge in sanctuary cities” targeting “criminal illegal aliens.”

Vehicle Stops “Shit Show”

On October 1, a week after the stand-down order, the Washington Examiner reported on another leaked DHS guidance that announced the formally amended ICE’s vehicle stops policy.

The Department of Homeland Security issued another direct denial, downplaying the significance of the guidance, which took aim at keeping unexperienced personnel from engaging with vehicles.

“Wrong, this is nothing new. This memo makes no changes to how ICE conducts vehicle stops,” the department said. “ALL officers have always received vehicle stop training.”

In 2025, the DHS cut training time requirements for ICE’s academy by approximately 40 percent, including cuts to driving and firearms training. The cuts came ahead of a hiring spree that added about 12,000 people to ICE’s ranks to meet the Trump administration’s deportation goals.

The recent amendments to ICE’s vehicle stops policy marks the third time this summer that department and ICE leadership ordered Enforcement and Removal Operations officials to change how they engage with vehicles. Previously, ICE halted and then amended its policy after immigration officers shot and killed two men during traffic stops in Texas and Maine in July. These orders were also challenged by official government social media channels.

“There’s clearly a disconnect between leadership on the ground level and what’s coming out of Washington” said one official. “It’s a total shitshow.”

Then, on Thursday, October 8, plainclothes ICE officers opened fire on a vehicle during a targeted enforcement operation in New York City. At least seven rounds were fired into the car, according to reports. The driver, a 28-year-old Dominican man, was struck in the neck as his 5-year-old son sat in the backseat.

“The footage looks like a carjacking, they fucked up again,” said another Homeland Security Investigations official after reviewing video of the incident. “ERO was never given the freedom to work like they have in the past 2 years. They were always much more restrictive with their general enforcement.”

“Now comes these free-for-all mandates, and these guys who weren’t used to ‘enforcement’ and dealing with the public who were thrust into this world. Couple that with no tactical training — disaster.”

Fisher Phillips invites you to join us for an informative, in‑person half‑day seminar exploring the key California legislative and legal updates that will shape the workplace in 2027 and beyond.

With Governor Newsom’s final term drawing to a close, he signed a final flurry of workplace‑related bills into law. Except as provided otherwise, most measures signed into law will take effect on January 1, 2027. This program will give your organization a clear, practical overview of what is changing and what you need to do to stay compliant.

What You’ll Learn

Participants will gain insight into the most significant new laws and legal developments affecting California employers, including:

Artificial Intelligence in the Workplace

SB 947 (No Robo Bosses Act) – This bill prohibits employers from relying solely on an “automated decision system” when making disciplinary or termination decisions. It requires a human review to corroborate such decisions, and provides workers with a written “post‑use” notice.

SB 951 (AI Layoff Notices) – This bill amends California’s WARN Act to require employers to provide specified information in WARN notices when a layoff, relocation, or termination is caused “in whole or in substantial part” by an AI system or other automated technology.

Workplace Surveillance & Privacy

AB 1331 (No Surveillance in Bathrooms) – This bill prohibits employers from using a “workplace surveillance tool” to monitor employees in a bathroom and gives employees the right to leave such a tool behind when entering a bathroom.

AB 1883 (Privacy Protections for Employees’ Emotional States and Neural Data) – This bill prohibits employers from using an AI‑enabled surveillance tool to recognize or predict an employee’s emotional state or to collect “neural data” generated by measuring an employee’s nervous system.

SB 690 (Effort to Curb Digital Wiretapping Lawsuits) – This bill removes the private right of action for claims under the “pen register” provision of the California Invasion of Privacy Act, applying retroactively to pending lawsuits filed on or after January 1, 2025.

Wage & Hour and Pay Equity

SB 1237 (Increased Penalties for Pay Data Reporting Failures) – This bill significantly increases the maximum civil penalty for repeated failures to file required annual pay data reports with California’s Civil Rights Department, from $200 to $1,000 per employee.

AB 1697 (More Time to Prepare for Stay‑or‑Pay Ban) – This bill delays implementation of last year’s stay‑or‑pay ban until January 1, 2027, giving employers an additional year to restructure such contracts and accommodate collective bargaining agreements.

AB 2646 (Major Wage Hike in Agricultural Industry) – This bill imposes a statewide minimum wage of $19.75 per hour for certain agricultural workers, including H‑2A employees and their local‑worker counterparts.

Employment Discrimination & Leave

SB 1149 (Bereavement Leave) – This bill expands California’s bereavement leave law to allow employees to take up to five days of leave upon the death of a “designated person” — any person related by blood or whose association is the equivalent of a family relationship.

AB 1803 (Anti‑Hate Speech Training) – This bill expands California’s sexual harassment prevention training requirement, effective January 1, 2028, to also include “anti‑hate speech training” on recognizing, reporting, and confronting workplace speech that vilifies or incites hatred based on protected characteristics.

Workplace Safety & Enforcement

AB 2321 (Revamped Cal/OSHA Investigations) – This bill requires Cal/OSHA’s Bureau of Investigations to investigate any serious injury, illness, or exposure cited as a willful violation, requires immediate referrals to county prosecutors, and makes it a misdemeanor to willfully resist or interfere with Cal/OSHA.

AB 1776 (High‑Profile Fight Over Anti‑Trust Law Changes) – This bill implements changes to California’s anti‑trust law with significant implications for employers and businesses across the state.

Case Law Update

The program will also cover the most important 2026 Case Law developments affecting California employers, including recent court decisions on wage and hour, discrimination, leave, and other key employment issues with practical guidance on how these rulings should shape your workplace policies.

Benefits Update

This session will address recent developments in employee benefits, including new compliance requirements and plan design considerations employers need to know for the year ahead.

Immigration Update

This session will address the latest developments in immigration enforcement and workplace rights, including new notice requirements and practical steps employers can take to prepare for and respond to immigration‑related workplace actions.

Who Should Attend

This seminar is designed for HR professionals, in‑house counsel, business owners, and anyone responsible for managing employees.

What You’ll Take Away

Key legislative changes from the latest session and their impact on employers in 2027

Practical steps to update workplace policies and maintain compliance

Strategies to reduce risk and avoid costly litigation

Don’t miss the chance to stay ahead of these critical changes in 2027.
